Akhtar said the matter was immediately communicated to Bahrain Post, which clarified that the ballots were not delivered directly by them. The Bangladesh ambassador in Bahrain is also overseeing the issue. ‘Bahrain Post has informed us that they will conduct an on-site investigation and report back.’

On Tuesday, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party raised concerns before the election commission over the viral video related to the distribution of postal ballots in Bahrain.

A four-member BNP delegation, led by Nazrul Islam Khan, chairman of the party’s central election steering committee, placed their concerns during a meeting with chief election commissioner AMM Nasir Uddin.

Nazrul Islam alleged irregularities in the overseas distribution of postal ballots, claiming that videos circulating on social media showed leaders of a particular political party handling a large number of ballot papers in Bahrain.

Some 1,533,683 voters have registered to vote through postal ballots, of whom some 772,000 are expatriate Bangladeshis residing in different countries across the world.

title: Selim Al Deen’s 18th death anniversary observed
body:
Theatre troupes and cultural organisations observed the 18th anniversary of death of legendary playwright Selim Al Deen on Wednesday with seminars, processions and commemorative programmes at multiple venues.

At Jahangirnagar University, the drama and dramatics department organised a daylong programme on the campus with the support of the university administration to recall the life and works of Selim Al Deen, regarded as one of the most influential playwrights of post-Tagore Bengali theatre.

The theme of this year’s observance — Chhute jete jete thomke daray ekjona [One pauses while rushing ahead] — was taken from Al Deen’s play Prachya.

The programme began in the morning with a memorial procession and floral tributes.

Teachers, students, researchers, theatre activists and cultural enthusiasts joined the procession, titled Smaran Jatra, which started from the old arts building and ended at Selim Al Deen’s grave on the JU campus.

The JU drama and dramatics department, Bangladesh Gram Theatre, Dhaka Theatre, Swapnadal, Anwita Selim Al Deen Bidyapith, JU Teacher Student Centre, Taluknagar Theatre, Sammilita Sangskritik Jote of Savar, Bunon Theatre and Arshinagar Theatre, among others, placed floral wreaths at Selim Al Deen’s grave.

Mohibur Rouf Shaibal, associate professor of drama and dramatics at JU and coordinator of the anniversary programme, said that Al Deen’s works vividly portrayed the human, political, economic, religious and social realities of Bengal, securing him a distinct place in both national and international theatre practice.

‘At a time when local cultures face challenges in a globalised world, his vision shows how to remain rooted while creating world-class art. Remembering him is not just about tribute, but about inspiring a new generation through the practice of his dramatic philosophy’, he added.

Later on the day, a seminar was held at the Set Lab of the old arts building.

A keynote paper titled ‘Selim Al Deen and the Decolonised Identity of Bengali Theatre’ was presented by Professor Aminul Islam of the JU drama and dramatics department at the event.

Academics from the university took part in the discussion, reflecting Al Deen’s intellectual legacy and his contribution to shaping a distinct theatrical language rooted in local culture.

Separately, the drama and film department of the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy organised a special seminar at the National Theatre Hall in Dhaka to mark the anniversary.

The seminar featured a keynote presentation on ‘Bengali Aesthetic Roots and Dualist Art Philosophy’, by Reza Arif, an associate professor of drama and dramatics at Jahangirnagar University. The seminar was presided over by JU Professor Lutfor Rahman and moderated by BSA director Deepak Kumar Goswami.

Theatre activists Zahid Ripon, Rubaiyat Ahmed and Abu Sayed Tulu spoke on the paper.

Dhaka Theatre staged Deyal, written by Selim Al Deen and directed by Anik Islam at the National Theatre Hall of the BSA. Dhaka Theatre will also stage their productions ‘Nimajjan’ today and ‘Rangmohal’ on Friday.

Selim Al Deen Sangrahashala also organised a two-day festival at studio theatre hall of the BSA. On the opening day, Pantomime Movement of Chattogram staged Prachya and the theatre department of Jagannath University staged Joiboti Konyar Mon.

Theatre troupe Swapnadal arranged a three-day programme, including the screening of Al Deen’s play Hargaj at the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy on January 17.

Born on August 18, 1949, at Senerkhil village of Sonagazi upazila in Feni district, Mohammad Moinuddin Ahmed, commonly known as Selim Al Deen, began his career as a copywriter before joining Jahangirnagar University in 1974 as a lecturer in the Bangla department.

He later founded the university’s drama and dramatics department and served as its first chairman.

In 1981, he co-founded Bangladesh Gram Theatre with theatre activist Nasiruddin Yousuff, aiming to develop a theatre movement grounded in indigenous forms and narratives.

Selim Al Deen received numerous awards, including the Independence Award 2023, the Ekushey Padak in 2007, the Bangla Academy Award in 1984, the Best Tele-playwright Award in 1994 and the National Film Award for best dialogue in the same year.

title: SEC students continue protest demanding SUST affiliation
body:
Sylhet Engineering College students have been observing a shutdown programme on the campus in demand of incorporating the college as an institute under the Shahjalal University of Science and Technology.

The students said that they started enforcing the shutdown programme locking the administrative building and three academic buildings of the college on Tuesday evening.

They said that they boycotted academic activities, including scheduled examinations, and kept suspended all kinds of administrative works on Wednesday to press home the demand.

The students said that they have been protesting to eliminate the long-standing discrimination in the country’s four specialised public engineering colleges, including the SEC.

In the context of the movement, the interim government’s education adviser had formed a high-level committee to investigate into the demand of affiliating the four engineering colleges to the universities concerned, SEC students said.

They claimed that the committee recently submitted its report, in which it recommended that Sylhet Engineering College would be included as a full-fledged institute under the SUST.

However, no initiative is being taken so far to implement the recommendation, the students told New Age in the afternoon.

They alleged that the recommendation is not being implemented due to reluctance of the Directorate of Technical Education.

A student, who wanted not to be named, claimed that they had issued a two-day ultimatum to the college authorities on Sunday to begin the initiative to affiliate the Sylhet Engineering College as a full-fledged institute of the Shahjalal University of Science and Technology.

‘But the authorities did not take any effective step by this time, forcing us to launch the shutdown programme,’ he alleged.

The agitating students hoped to continue the shutdown programme until their demand is met.

SEC principal Md Asaduzzaman told New Age that the students staged demonstrations on the college campus locking the administrative and academic buildings.

‘The higher authorities concerned were informed about the situation,’ he said in the afternoon, adding that steps would be taken after receiving directives of the higher authorities.

title: DU statistics dept welcomes freshers
body:
The department of statistics at Dhaka University held its freshers’ reception for first-year undergraduate students of the 2024–2025 academic session on Wednesday at the TSC auditorium on the campus.

Departmental chairman Professor Zafar Ahmed Khan presided over the programme, said a press release.

Pro-vice-chancellor of the National University Professor Md Lutfar Rahman and dean of the faculty of science at DU Professor Abdus Salam addressed the event. Assistant Professor Kanchan Kumar Sen delivered the welcome remarks.

Speakers encouraged students to engage in co-curricular activities alongside academic work to build themselves as skilled and responsible individuals. They also stressed the importance of moral and human values in shaping a better society.

The programme concluded with a cultural performance.

title: BUFT National Career Fest 2026 held
body:
BGMEA University of Fashion and Technology, through its Career Development Club, organised the BUFT National Career Fest 2026 on January 14–15 on its permanent campus at Turag in Dhaka.

The two-day event was presented by BGMEA, KDS, and Prime Bank, powered by Centro, Fashion Step Group, Fakir Fashion, Shin Shin Group, FPG, and Masco Group, and co-powered by Auko-Tex Group, RH Corporation, and Asian Apparels Limited.

Over 300 organisations took part in the event, drawing more than 10,000 job seekers and approximately 40,000 visitors, said a press release.

The fest was graced by Naznin Kawshar Chowdhury, executive chairman, NSDA; Faruque Hassan, chairman of the BUFT board of trustees; Mohammad Hatem, president of BKMEA; Inamul Haq Khan, senior vice-president, BGMEA; Nafis Ud Doula, director of BGMEA; Mohammad Shohel, director, BGMEA; Mohiuddin Ahmed Selim, chairman, ITET; Shibbir Mahmud, chairman, Swisstex Limited; Ehsanul Karim Kaiser, convener, interim committee of ITET; and MM Mahbub Hasan, SVP, Prime Bank PLC.

The welcome address was delivered by Professor Ayub Nabi Khan, adviser to BUFT, while Professor Md Alamgir Hossain, acting vice-chancellor of BUFT; the club’s adviser Md Abdul Mukit; the club’s president Abid Hossain; and the club’s general secretary Mahmud Fantasir also addressed the gathering.

title: BMU launches e-logbook in postgrad residency prog
body:
Bangladesh Medical University has introduced e-logbooks in its postgraduate residency programme, beginning with five departments in a pilot phase.

The initial rollout covers medicine, general surgery, anaesthesia analgesia and intensive care medicine, radiology and imaging, and hepatology, said a press release.

The university plans to expand the system to all departments, with the ICT office leading the implementation.

The update was shared at a meeting on BMU campus in Dhaka Wednesday.

BMU vice-chancellor Professor Md Shahinul Alam, pro-vice-chancellor for administration Professor Md Abul Kalam Azad, pro-vice-chancellor for research and development Professor Md Mujibur Rahman Hawlader, treasurer Professor Nahreen Akhtar, registrar Professor Md Nazrul Islam, director of ICT cell Professor AKM Akhtaruzzaman, associate professor of internal medicine department Md Nazmul Hasan, Assistant Professor Khaled Mahbub Murshed, among others, attended the meeting.

title: ACC files 12 cases against PK Halder, 35 others
body:
The Anti-Corruption Commission has filed 12 separate cases against Prashanta Kumar Halder and 35 others on charges of embezzling Tk 5.31 billion by taking loans from FAS Finance and Investment Limited in the names of various fictitious companies.

Assistant director of the ACC’s public relations department, Md. Tanzir Ahmed, disclosed the information on Wednesday.

According to the ACC, loans totalling Tk 4,339,618,009 were shown as approved between 2014 and 2017 in the names of 12 companies from FAS Finance and subsequently misappropriated. Including interest, the outstanding loan amount has stood at Tk 5,310,869,009.

The cases were filed on January 13. Deputy director of the ACC headquarters Md Mashiur Rahman is the complainant in cases no. 1 and 2, while assistant director Md Imran Akon is the complainant in the remaining 10 cases.

ACC investigations revealed that the accused, in collusion with one another, created new and paper-based companies to obtain loans. Most of these companies had no real business operations. Although one or two instalments were paid in a few cases, many loans saw no instalment payments at all.

Despite this, the loans were rescheduled at board meetings without any objections.

Notable accused include former managing director of Reliance Finance Limited and NRB Global Bank Limited Prashanta Kumar Halder, former chairman of FAS Finance and Investment Limited Md Siddiqur Rahman, former managing directors Md Russell Shahriar and Md Mofiz Uddin Chowdhury, former chairperson Mahfuza Rahman Baby and former chairmen Mohammad Abdul Hafiz and Abdul Motalib Ahmed. Several former directors of FAS Finance and Investment Limited and managing directors of the concerned borrowing companies have also been named as accused.

The commission further found that no business operations or even the existence of the borrowing companies could currently be traced at the head-office addresses used in their names. It has been alleged that the loans were approved using forged and fraudulent documents.

The cases have been filed under Sections 406, 409, 467, 468, 471 and 109 of the Penal Code, 1860; Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947; and Section 4(2) of the Money Laundering Prevention Act, 2012.

title: Ctg tribunal sets January 19 for charge hearing
body:
A Chattogram Divisional Speedy Trial Tribunal on Wednesday set January 19 for holding the hearing on charge framing against 39 accused, including former ISKCON organiser Chinmoy Krishna Das Brahmachari, in the murder case of lawyer Saiful Islam Alif.

Speedy Trial Tribunal judge and district judge Md Zahidul Haque passed the order at 3.00pm after the case was transferred as ready for trial from a lower court and the tribunal held its first proceeding.

Of the 23 accused currently in custody, 22 were produced before the tribunal, while Chinmoy was not brought from jail for security reasons, said assistant public prosecutor Md Raihanul Wazed Chowdhury.

He said that the court reviewed the case records in the presence of the accused produced and the judge confirmed attendance by calling each accused by their names. The tribunal also ordered that all accused in custody be produced on January 19.

During the day’s proceeding, relatives of the accused protested on the court premises, alleging that no lawyer was being allowed to appear for the defence. Chattogram District Bar Association president Abdus Sattar and senior lawyers later went to the spot and told them that the court would ensure justice.

Meanwhile, a large number of police were deployed in and around the court premises, and security measures were tightened from the morning centring the case proceedings.

On October 25, 2024, Chinmoy led a large gathering of the Hindu community in Chattogram.

On October 31, 2024, a sedition case was filed against 19 people, including Chinmoy, on charges of desecrating the national flag.

On November 22, Chinmoy led another large rally in Rangpur following which he was arrested at the Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in the capital Dhaka on November 25 in the sedition case.

Next day, a Chattogram court rejected his bail petition, sending him to jail.

The court’s decision sparked clashes between his followers and members of the law enforcement agencies on the court premises.

At one stage of the clash, lawyer Saiful was hacked to death outside the court premises.

Several cases were filed against Chinmoy and others following Saiful’s killing.

On April 30, 2025, the High Court granted bail to Chinmoy in the sedition case, but the Appellate Division later cancelled the bail.

In the murder case, the police on July 1, 2025, filed a charge sheet naming Chinmoy as the prime accused and listing 38 others. During the charge-sheet acceptance hearing, the court rejected the investigation officer’s recommendation to discharge one person, raising the total number of charge-sheeted accused to 39.

Of the 39 accused, 16 are still absconding, the assistant public prosecutor said.

title: BCG arrests 2 with 75,000 Yaba pills in Teknaf
body:
The Bangladesh Coast Guard arrested two alleged drug traffickers with 75,000 yaba pills in Teknaf of Cox’s Bazar on Tuesday.

A press release, signed by BCG media officer Lieutenant Commander Siam-ul-Haq and issued on Wednesday, said that acting on a tip-off, a special team from coast guard station Teknaf conducted an operation at around 1:00pm in the Naf River near Nightongpara under Teknaf police station.

The team intercepted a wooden boat, searched it, and recovered the pills, worth about Tk 3,75,00,000, along with detaining two suspects.

The seized boat and narcotics, as well as the arrested, were handed over to Teknaf model police station for legal action.

title: Painter electrocuted in Dhaka
body:
A 35-year-old painter electrocuted while working on a four-story building in Adabar area of Dhaka on Wednesday.

The identity of the deceased could not be known immediately. Inspector Faruk, in-charge of the Dhaka Medical College and Hospital police camp, said the painter was electrocuted and fell from the building while working on its exterior in the Shekhertek area.

He was later taken to Dhaka Medical College and Hospital, where doctors declared him dead at around 5:30pm.

title: Arguments in Abu Sayed killing case Jan 20
body:
The International Crimes Tribunal-2 on Wednesday set January 20 for placing arguments in the crimes against humanity case filed over the killing of Begum Rokeya University, Rangpur student Abu Sayed during the July mass uprising.

The three-judge panel of the ICT-2, led by Justice Md Nozrul Islam Chowdhury, passed the order as the testimony in the case came to an end on Wednesday.

Twenty five prosecution witnesses, including the investigation officer, testified in the case.

Chief prosecutor Muhammad Tajul Islam, prosecutors Md Mizanul Islam and Gazi MH Tamim took part in the hearing for the prosecution, while Aminul Gani Titu argued for accused former BRUR proctor Shariful Islam and Sujad Miah stood as state-appointed defence counsel for the other fugitive accused.

Chief prosecutor Muhammad Tajul Islam in his opening statement, described Abu Sayed as a symbol of courage in the uprising.

Six persons—former BRUR proctor Shariful Islam, former assistant registrar Rafiul Hasan Russel, former staffer Md Anwar Pervej, former assistant sub-inspector Amir Hossain, former constable Sujan Chandra Roy, and former BRUR Chhatra League general secretary Imran Chowdhury Akash—of the 30 accused were produced before the tribunal on Wednesday.

The tribunal framed charges against all 30 accused on August 6, 2025.

Azizur Rahman Dulu represented Sujan Chandra Roy, Aminul Gani Titu appeared for Shariful Islam and Salauddin Regan represented Imran Chowdhury Akash.

The tribunal appointed six state defence counsels on July 22 to represent fugitives in absentia. ICT-2 issued arrest warrants on June 30 against 26 fugitives, including former BRUR vice-chancellor Professor Md Hasibur Rashid.

The investigation agency submitted its report on June 24, accusing 30 individuals, including the former commissioner of Rangpur metropolitan police. Four arrestees were interrogated on June 18 and 19 after the tribunal formally showed them arrested on April 9.

According to the prosecution, on July 16, 2024, shortly before Sayed’s death, the then-proctor allegedly forced students off campus with the help of Chhatra League activists, after which two policemen fired on Sayed at close range.

Sayed’s family filed a complaint on January 13, 2025, naming 25 individuals.

title: Denmark to boost military presence in Greenland from today
body:
Denmark will beef up its military presence in Greenland ‘from today’, the defence ministry said Wednesday, just before high-stakes talks were to start in Washington over US president Donald Trump’s threats to take over the Arctic island.

‘The Danish armed forces are, from today, deploying capabilities and units related to exercise activities. In the period ahead, this will result in an increased military presence in and around Greenland, comprising aircraft, vessels and soldiers, including from NATO allies,’ the Danish defence ministry said in a statement.

Since returning to office nearly a year ago, Trump has repeatedly said the United States needs to take control of the vast, strategic and sparsely populated Arctic island for reasons of ‘national security’.

He has accused Denmark of neglecting security in and around Greenland, and said Wednesday the Danish autonomous territory was ‘vital’ for his planned Golden Dome air and missile defence system.

Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen has warned that a US attack on a NATO ally would end the alliance.

‘Security in the Arctic is of crucial importance to the Kingdom of Denmark and our Arctic allies, and it is therefore important that we, in close cooperation with allies, further strengthen our ability to operate in the region,’ defence minister Troels Lund Poulsen said in Wednesday’s statement.

The exercise activities in 2026 could include guarding critical infrastructure, providing assistance to local authorities in Greenland, including the police, receiving allied troops, deploying fighter aircraft in and around Greenland, and conducting naval operations, the ministry said.

Denmark last year hosted exercises in Greenland in which NATO allies Germany, France, Norway and Sweden took part, it said.

Danish foreign minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen and his Greenlandic counterpart were to hold talks Wednesday in Washington with US secretary of state Marco Rubio and vice president JD Vance.

Just hours before the meeting Trump said that US control of Greenland — an autonomous territory belonging to NATO ally Denmark — was ‘vital’ for his planned Golden Dome air and missile defence system.

‘NATO becomes far more formidable and effective with Greenland in the hands of the UNITED STATES. Anything less than that is unacceptable,’ he wrote on social media.

He said NATO ‘should be leading the way’ in building the multi-layer missile defence system.

‘IF WE DON’T, RUSSIA OR CHINA WILL, AND THAT IS NOT GOING TO HAPPEN!’ Trump wrote.

Just prior, Danish defence minister Troels Lund Poulsen had sought to ease US concerns about security in Greenland, telling AFP Denmark was boosting its military presence there and was in talks with allies on ‘an increased NATO presence in the Arctic.’

Trump has repeatedly threatened to take over the vast, strategic and sparsely populated Arctic island, and he has sounded emboldened since ordering a deadly January 3 attack in Venezuela that removed its president.

title: SC rejects Cumilla-4 BNP candidate’s plea on loan status
body:
The Appellate Division on Wednesday rejected an application filed by Cumilla-4 BNP candidate Manzurul Ahsan Munshi seeking to lift its earlier stay on a High Court decision that asked the authorities not to include his name on the list of loan defaulters.

Following the apex court’s January 8 stay order, Bangladesh Bank included Manzurul’s name in the loan defaulter list.

The chamber judge, however, advised Manzurul’s lawyer to have the rule heard and disposed of by the High Court.

On December 8, 2025, the High Court issued the stay order on a petition filed by Manzurul, three days before the announcement of the election schedule on December 11.

The High Court had directed Bangladesh Bank not to include Munshi’s name in the Credit Information Bureau list.

Manzurul’s lawyer, Saifullah Mamun, said that his client sought vacation of the chamber judge’s stay, arguing that the loan had been rescheduled after the stay order issued on January 8.

The national election is scheduled for February 12.

In a revision petition, Manzurul challenged a November 5, 2025 order of the Dhaka Fifth Joint District Judge’s Court, which rejected his plea seeking a directive not to list him as a loan defaulter.

He argued that his company is negotiating a settlement of the defaulted loan.

Meanwhile, the Election Commission is scheduled to hear an appeal on Saturday filed by Manzurul’s rival candidate and National Citizen Party nominee, Hasnat Abdullah, challenging Munshi’s candidacy.

Manzurul Ahsan Munshi, managing director of MAM Power Limited, is contesting the 13th Jatiya Sangsad election for Cumilla-4 as a BNP candidate.

His company allegedly owes about Tk 88 crore to Premier Bank and more than Tk 12 crore to IDLC Finance Limited.

Lawyer Mohammad Hossain represented IDLC while lawyer Bivuti Tarofder appeared for Premier Bank.

title: Iran threatens to strike US bases if attacked
body:
A senior adviser to Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei warned president Donald Trump on Wednesday that an Iranian strike in June on an American base in Qatar had demonstrated its ability to respond to any attack.

Trump should recall the attack on the Al Udeid air base, which proved ‘Iran’s will and capability to respond to any attack’, Ali Shamkhani wrote in a post on X after Washington repeatedly refused to rule out new military action against Iran.

The strike on Al Udeid was in retaliation for US support for Israel’s war against the Islamic republic in June. Shamkhani, a former defence minister, was himself badly wounded by an Israeli strike but survived.

Some personnel have been asked to depart the United States’ Al Udeid military base, two diplomatic sources told AFP on Wednesday, with the Gulf state saying ‘regional tensions’ were behind the move.

The decision comes after Washington threatened to respond to an Iranian government crackdown on protests while Tehran has said it would strike US military and shipping assets in the event of a new attack.

The measure was taken ‘in response to the current regional tensions’, Qatar’s International Media Office said in a statement.

Meanwhile, Iran vowed fast-track trials for people arrested over a massive wave of protests, after Trump threatened ‘very strong action’ if the Islamic republic goes ahead with hangings.

In Tehran, authorities held a funeral ceremony for over 100 members of the security forces and other ‘martyrs’ killed in the demonstrations, which authorities have branded as ‘riots’ while accusing protesters of waging ‘acts of terror’.

The protest movement across Iran, initially sparked by economic grievances, has turned into one of the biggest challenges yet to the clerical leadership since it took power in 1979.

Demonstrators have defied the authorities’ zero-tolerance for dissent by turning out in protests all around the country, even as authorities insist they have regained the upper hand.

Iran’s judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei said on a visit to a prison holding protest detainees that ‘if a person burned someone, beheaded someone and set them on fire then we must do our work quickly’, in comments broadcast by state television.

Iranian news agencies also quoted him as saying the trials should be held in public and said he had spent five hours in a prison in Tehran to examine the cases.

Footage broadcast by state media showed the judiciary chief seated before an Iranian flag in a large, ornate room in the prison, interrogating a prisoner himself.

The detainee, dressed in grey clothing and his face blurred, is accused of taking Molotov cocktails to a park in Tehran.

Trump on Tuesday said in a CBS News interview that the United States would act if Iran began hanging protesters.

‘We will take very strong action if they do such a thing,’ said the American leader, who has repeatedly threatened Iran with military intervention.

‘When they start killing thousands of people — and now you’re telling me about hanging. We’ll see how that’s going to work out for them,’ Trump said.

Iranian authorities called the American warnings a ‘pretext for military intervention’.

Rights groups accuse the government of fatally shooting protesters and masking the scale of the crackdown with an internet blackout imposed on January 8.

Internet monitor Netblocks said in a post to X on Wednesday that the blackout had now lasted 132 hours.

Some information has trickled out of Iran however. New videos on social media, with locations verified by AFP, showed bodies lined up in the Kahrizak morgue just south of the Iranian capital, with the corpses wrapped in black bags and distraught relatives searching for loved ones.

Iranian prosecutors have said authorities would press capital charges of ‘waging war against God’ on some detainees.

According to state media, hundreds of people have been arrested.

State media has also reported on the arrest of a foreign national for espionage in connection with the protests.

No details were given on the person’s nationality or identity.

The US State Department on its Farsi language X account said 26-year-old protester Erfan Soltani had been sentenced to be executed on Wednesday.

‘Erfan is the first protester to be sentenced to death, but he won’t be the last,’ the State Department said, adding more than 10,600 Iranians had been arrested.

Rights group Amnesty International called on Iran to immediately halt all executions, including Soltani’s.

Norway-based NGO Iran Human Rights said it had confirmed 734 people killed during the protests, including nine minors, but warned the death toll was likely far higher.

‘The real number of those killed is likely in the thousands,’ IHR’s director Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam said.

Iranian state media has said dozens of members of the security forces have been killed, with their funerals turning into large pro-government rallies.

At Wednesday’s funeral ceremony in Tehran, thousands of people waved flags of the Islamic republic as prayers were read out for the dead outside Tehran University, according to images broadcast on state television.

‘Death to America!’ read banners held up by people attending the rally, while others carried photos of supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Another image could be seen at the rally showing Trump’s assassination attempt, captioned: ‘This time it will not miss the target’.

It appeared to be referring to the assassination attempt against Trump during a campaign rally in 2024.

title: SC ends 2-decade legal saga, terms case ‘judicial tyranny’
body:
The Appellate Division has ended a two-decade legal saga involving the service status of 988 National University employees appointed between 2003 and 2004, when the Bangladesh Nationalist Party–led alliance was in power.

The full verdict was delivered by a seven-member bench headed by chief justice Syed Refaat Ahmed, who retired from the job on December 27, 2025.

The judgment, written by Justice Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury, who is now the chief justice, was briefly announced on May 27, 2025. The verdict was published on the Supreme Court website on January 13.

In its verdict, the Appellate Division declared the terminations illegal and described the earlier handling of the case as an act of ‘judicial tyranny’.

Over the years, the case produced seven different verdicts, exposing judicial inconsistency and leaving hundreds of employees in prolonged uncertainty.

The National University’s syndicate had repeatedly changed its decisions on their appointments with changes in governments and vice-chancellors.

In 2006, the High Court Division declared the appointments lawful after hearing a public interest litigation filed by former deputy speaker Fazle Rabbi Miah in 2004.

Four years later, in 2011, the High Court reversed its position by allowing a review petition filed in 2010 by a third party, former liberation war affairs minister AKM Mozzammel Hossain, and declared the appointments illegal.

On appeal, the Appellate Division scrapped both the 2006 and 2011 verdicts and sent the case back to the High Court Division for rehearing.

After rehearing, the High Court Division in 2012 issued a fresh verdict, which led to the termination of 988 officers and employees of the National University.

The dismissed employees challenged the decision, but in 2016, the Appellate Division upheld the terminations, leaving them without jobs and without effective legal remedy.

Some of the dismissed employees later sought review of the 2016 verdict, but their petitions were rejected.

Eight years later, after the fall of the Sheikh Hasina-led Awami League regime in August 2024 amid a mass uprising, the Appellate Division revisited the matter in a review petition filed by the National University following a syndicate decision on September 5, 2024.

The court observed that the matter should have ended with the High Court judgment delivered on August 22, 2006, as neither the petitioner nor the National University had appealed against it.

It noted with ‘anxiety and sorrow’ that some of the affected employees had died while the case remained pending for years.

The court held that the reopening of the case had severely affected not only the careers but also the livelihoods of the employees and their families.

The Appellate Division ordered the reinstatement of all affected employees with their respective seniority, directing that the period they remained out of service be treated as extraordinary leave.

According to sources at the university’s registry office, the reinstated employees rejoined their posts on June 1, 2025, following a syndicate decision on May 30, 2025.

Senior lawyer Md Asaduzzaman appeared for the university while senior lawyers Salah Uddin Dolon, Md.Ruhul Quddus and Siddique Ullah Miah appeared for the staffs.

title: Political will for increasing women’s participation urged
body:
Politicians, academics and professionals on Wednesday at a dialogue expressed concern over the participation of fewer number of women in politics of Bangladesh and said that political will was crucial to increasing women’s participation in the area.

Referring to the women candidates participating in the Jatiya Sangsad elections scheduled for February 12, they said that some political parties had nominated women candidates for less than five per cent of seats in the elections and many others nominated no women candidate.

They made the observations while speaking at a dialogue organised by the Centre for Governance Studies, a non-government think-tank, at the CIRDAP auditorium in the capital Dhaka.

The discussion was moderated by CGS president Zillur Rahman.

One of the panellists, Nasim Firdaus, founder and president of the Bangladesh Women Leadership Alliance, said that politicians should change their attitudes so that more women could participate in politics and others fields as women were more than 50 per cent of the total population of the country.

‘In the workforce of different sectors, we found a significant absence of women in many sectors. Questioned about the lack of women in leadership, it was often claimed that they were not sufficiently trained and it was a lame excuse,’ Nasim said.

Bangladesh Jasod general secretary Nazmul Haque Prodhan said without the participation of women, the development activities would be delayed as they were more than half of the total population.

Bangladesh Nationalist Party organising secretary Shama Obaid Islam, who is contesting for the Faridpur-2 constituency in the forthcoming national polls, said that she wanted more women leadership in the party.

To attain this, the party could adopt a provision that in every committee across the country there should be a fixed number of women leaders.

Universal Medical College and Hospital Limited chairperson Priti Chakraborty, Bangladesh Women Entrepreneurs Association president Nasrin Fatema Awal, Dhaka University women and gender studies  professor Syed Md Shaikh Imtiaz, Transgender leader  and rights activist Ho Chi Minh Islam, State Reform Student Movement president Lamiya Islam, Gono Odhikar Parishad senior vice-president Faruk Hasan, Robi Axiata corporate sales manager and Tagra BD founder Tahreem Khan Zahid, Khelafat Majlis organising secretary Kazi Minhazul Alam and advocate Elina Khan, among others, spoke at the discussion.

title: Flats for FFs occupied by others: welfare assoc
body:
Of the 870 flats meant for impoverished freedom fighters at the Bijoy Rakeen City housing project, 766 are occupied by influential individuals who did not participate in the War of Independence, alleged freedom fighter Abu Md Ishtiaq Aziz Ulfat, administrator of the Muktijoddha O Muktijoddha Poribar Kalyan Samiti, a welfare association, on Wednesday.

At a press conference at the National Press Club in the capital Dhaka, Ishtiaq said, ‘The fascist Awami League regime facilitated illegal allocations of the flats to the party leaders, police officers and senior government officials, instead of genuine freedom fighters.’

The authoritarian AL regime was ousted on August 5, 2024, in the wake of a mass uprising.

At the press conference, Ishtiaq also revealed other large-scale irregularities, corruption, and abuse of power in the Bijoy Rakeen City housing project at Mirpur in the capital.

In 1994, the then prime minister Khaleda Zia allocated 16.2 acres of land at Block-D in the Mirpur-14 area to provide housing for marginalised freedom fighters, he said.

Mentioning that the Bijoy Rakeen City project was initiated on this land, he said that nearly 1,950 flats were built under the entire project, while 870 of those were designated for freedom fighters.

Citing that about 95 per cent of the freedom fighters were poor, and grassroots, working people, he claimed that freedom fighters were neglected after the country’s independence, and they still were facing negligence.

Alleging that Awami League leaders distorted the history of the independence war, he said, ‘Awami League tried to erase the names of Maulana Bhashani, Suhrawardy and Ziaur Rahman from the history of Bangladesh’s emergence. In the same way, they built flats on land allocated for marginalised freedom fighters and handed those over to non-freedom fighters.’

Citing that the welfare association’s previous president, former additional inspector general of police AT Ahmedul Haque Chowdhury, abused his administrative authority to sign a 57–43 per cent share-based agreement with the private Rakeen Development Company.

‘As a result, the freedom fighters’ ownership over the association’s land was undermined, and the project eventually turned into a commercial housing venture,’ said Ishtiaq, also the president of Jatiyatabadi Muktijoddha Dal.

The association administrator claimed that of the current 516 members of the association, 334 were not genuine freedom fighters.

He also said that an aggrieved group of freedom fighters filed a case with the High Court over the ‘illegal possession’ of the flats by non-freedom fighters.

Other freedom fighters and members of the welfare association were present at the press conference.

From the press conference, demands were made for a comprehensive investigation into all allocations and contracts related to the Bijoy Rakeen City project, cancellation of flat allocations to non-freedom fighters and illegal beneficiaries, verification of the list of genuine freedom fighters, and legal action against those responsible.

title: BNP demands fresh postal ballot
body:
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s central election steering committee on Wednesday alleged that a political party was attempting to manipulate the upcoming Jatiya Sangsad elections by luring marginalised voters with money transfers through bKash and collecting copies of national identity cards.

The party also demanded that redesigned ballots be sent to registered voters for postal voting in the country, as the BNP’s symbol was placed in the middle of the postal ballots sent to expatriate voters in a way that made it less visible when folded.

BNP’s central election steering committee chief and the party’s standing committee member, Nazrul Islam Khan, made the remarks at a press conference at the committee office in the capital’s Gulshan area.

He also said that the activists of a specific party were collecting the copies of the voters’ NID cards as part of a plan to rig the polls.

‘We have formally informed the Election Commission of our concerns, but we have not seen any visible action yet,’ Nazrul said.

He expressed his hope that the commission would strictly implement the electoral code of conduct.

Nazrul talked to journalists after returning from a meeting between BNP chairman Tarique Rahman and the leaders of the 12-party alliance.

During the meeting, Tarique Rahman exchanged pleasantries with the leaders, Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha reported.

On Tuesday, a BNP delegation led by Nazrul met chief election commissioner AMM Nasir Uddin at the EC headquarters in Dhaka.

In Wednesday’s press conference, Nazrul also alleged that the design of postal ballots sent to expatriate voters favoured three political parties.

He said that the ballot paper was arranged in five columns and 14 rows, placing the symbols — scales, water lily bud and hand fan — on the top row.

By contrast, he claimed, the BNP’s symbol was placed in the middle of the sheet in a way that makes it less visible when the paper is folded.

‘This is not a coincidence. It is intentional and meant to favour those three parties,’ he said.

According to him, the BNP has formally requested the commission to correct the design of postal ballots and send the fresh ones to the registered voters in the country to prevent a repeat of what he termed a ‘tactical approach’.

The party also alleged irregularities in the overseas distribution of postal ballots.

Nazrul said that viral video clips showing expatriates mishandling postal ballots in Bahrain and Oman were alarming, as postal votes could play a decisive role in the election outcome.

Urging all parties to follow the electoral code of conduct, he said that the BNP was complying with commission directives, while some political forces were allegedly acting in a coordinated manner to tilt the contest in their favour.

He cited party chairman Tarique Rahman’s postponement of a planned visit to northern districts at the commission’s request as an example of compliance.

‘Despite this, we see senior leaders of other parties openly campaigning, holding rallies and seeking votes for their symbols without any apparent restrictions,’ he said, alleging selective enforcement of electoral rules.

title: CWAB threatens boycott demanding Najmul’s resignation
body:
The Cricketers Welfare Association of Bangladesh on Wednesday announced a boycott of all cricket if the BCB board director M Najmul Islam doesn’t resign before the first match of the Bangladesh Premier League on Thursday.

The CWAB president, Mohammad Mithun, said that the comments made by Najmul earlier were ‘completely unacceptable’ and ‘hurt’ the cricketers.

‘The words that the board director has used about the players are completely unacceptable to the players. It has deeply hurt the entire body of cricketers. So if he does not resign before tomorrow’s match, then from tomorrow onwards we are announcing boycott from all cricketing activities,’ Mithun said in an online press meet organised by the CWAB on Wednesday night.

Najmul previously labeled former national team captain Tamim Iqbal as an ‘Indian agent’ after the latter commented on recent matters regarding Bangladesh’s participation in the forthcoming ICC T20 World Cup, scheduled to be co-hosted by India and Sri Lanka.

‘You have all been seeing for quite some time now how comments are being made about our cricketers, starting from individuals and, now, using certain words about the entire group. This is never acceptable to us, and we never expect this. I believe a board director should think more carefully before speaking about players,’ Mithun said.

Mithun also said that they had given the BCB a lot of time on various issues, including the First Division Cricket League, but didn’t get any responses.

‘Still we haven’t seen any positive result. And the words that this board director is repeatedly using have deeply hurt the entire cricket community, and the players are in no way willing to accept this,’ he said.

Earlier, Najmul, the chairman of the finance committee of the BCB, said that if the Bangladesh national cricket team didn’t take part in the upcoming T20 World Cup, the BCB wouldn’t have suffered any loss. The loss would completely be of the cricketers, and they wouldn’t be compensated.

He also said that the decision of participating in the T20 World Cup in India was now a matter of national interest and that would be prioritised.

The BCB, however, expressed its ‘sincere regret’ for the remarks made by Najmul that ‘may be deemed inappropriate, offensive, or hurtful’.

‘Such comments do not reflect the values, principles, or official position of the Bangladesh Cricket Board, nor do they align with the standards of conduct expected from individuals entrusted with the responsibility of serving Bangladesh cricket,’ BCB said in a press release.

The BCB also said that it didn’t endorse or take responsibility for such statements or remarks.

‘The Bangladesh Cricket Board also makes it clear that it will take appropriate disciplinary action against any individual whose conduct or comments show disrespect towards cricketers or cause harm to the reputation and integrity of Bangladesh cricket,’ the press release read.

‘The Board unequivocally reaffirms its full support for and respect towards all cricketers, past and present, who have represented the country with dedication and pride. Players remain at the heart of Bangladesh cricket, and their contributions and welfare continue to be a top priority,’ it added.

The BCB are in an ongoing discussion with the ICC on their request of relocating their matches of the T20 World Cup outside India.

The debacle started after the Indian Premier League franchise Kolkata Knight Riders scrapped Mustafizur Rahman from their squad upon receiving ‘advice’ from the Board of Control for Cricket in India.

title: Bancharampur UNO Ferdous Ara dies
body:
Ferdous Ara, upazila nirbahi officer of Bancharampur upazila in Brahmanbaria, died on Wednesday at a hospital in Dhaka.

She breathed her last at around 7:00am, said additional deputy commissioner-general Ranjan Chandra Dey.

He said Ferdous Ara fell sick on Monday and was admitted to a hospital in the capital with severe migraine pain.

According to family sources, her janaza and burial will take place at her in-laws’ house in Daudkandi.

Deputy commissioner Sharmin Akhter Jahan expressed deep sorrow over her untimely death. She also prayed for the eternal peace of the departed soul.

title: Elderly patient dies as local operators obstruct ambulance to Dhaka
body:
An elderly patient died inside an ambulance on Tuesday night after some local ambulance operators allegedly obstructed his transfer to Dhaka at multiple points in Shariatpur.

The local operators also assaulted the ambulance driver from Dhaka and the patient’s relatives.

The deceased is identified as Jamshed Ali Dhali, 60, resident of Kutubpur area under Damuda upazila.

Zobaid Hossain Roman, grandson of Jamshed, said that Jamshed got sick on Tuesday morning.

His relatives rushed him to the Shariatpur Sadar hospital where the physicians advised the relatives to transfer Jamshed to the National Institute of Neurosciences and Hospital in the capital Dhaka for further treatment.

The hospital’s physician, Rashed Ahmed, said that the patient was admitted with stroke related complications on Tuesday morning.

Jamshed’s relatives rented an ambulance from the hospital premises at Tk 6,000 at about 12:30pm on Tuesday and after they took him inside the ambulance the driver demanded an extra Tk 1,000.

The relatives then rented another ambulance at Tk 5,000, which went there from Dhaka.

When they reached Kotapara area on Dhaka-Shariatpur road at about 2:00pm, some local ambulance syndicate members blocked the ambulance.

At that time, the syndicate members were saying why the relatives rented ambulance from outside instead of hiring the local one. They also assaulted the ambulance driver and the patient’s relatives twice.

The ambulance driver from Dhaka, Salman, alleged that eight to 10 people led by Sumon Khan who owns some ambulances operated at Shariatpur Sadar hospital area blocked the ambulance twice in Kotapara area and Jamtala area at Rajnagar union under Noria upazila for a total of one and a half hours.

‘Later some locals helped us and we finally started for the National Institute of Neurosciences and Hospital,’ he said, adding, ‘on the way the patient died.’

At about 9:00pm on Tuesday, the relatives came to Palong model police station in Shariatpur and informed the police about the incident verbally.

Sumon Khan claimed that he only asked the ambulance driver why he took patient from Shariatpur.

He claimed that he did nothing more than that and the allegation against him was baseless.

Shariatpur Palong model station officer-in-charge Shah Alam said that they could not take any legal action as the complaint was verbal.

‘If they file written complaint, we will take legal actions,’ he said and admitted that local ambulance drivers in Shariatpur often harassed patients.

Earlier, on August 14 past year, a newborn died after the ambulance carrying him was blocked for one and a half hours by a local ambulance syndicate in Shariatpur, as the baby’s father had hired an ambulance for Tk 5,000 on its return trip to Dhaka, while local drivers demanded Tk 10,000.

title: Tejgaon College students block Farmgate again for justice
body:
Students of Tejgaon College on Wednesday once again blocked the Farmgate crossing in the capital Dhaka for about five hours, demanding the arrest of and exemplary punishment for those responsible for the death of their fellow student after a clash, causing immense sufferings to city commuters.

Although the students initially blocked the Indira Road minutes after 11:30am, they later blocked the Farmgate crossing from about 12:30pm to 4:30pm, halting traffic in the area and surrounding areas, including Manik Mia Avenue, Karwan Bazar, Shahbagh, Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Tejgaon and Mohakhali.

Tejgaon College student Easin Arafat Rabbi alleged that over a month had already passed, but the main killers had not been arrested yet.

Amid the hours-long blockade, a group of the agitating students locked in an argument with a bus driver and vandalised the vehicle.

Dhaka Metropolitan Police assistant commissioner (petrol) for Tejgaon zone Md Altaf Hossain Mollah told New Age that police officers tried to convince the protesting students to withdraw the blockade, but they refused to do so.

‘We assured them that a Detective Branch team was investigating the case to serve justice. The team has already identified and arrested four individuals in connection with the murder case filed against a group of unidentified people,’ said Altaf.

A traffic police personnel said that they diverted vehicles to Bijoy Sarani and Sonargaon crossings to ease public sufferings.

On the night of December 6, a clash broke out between a group of Tejgaon College students and a group of outsiders.

The college authorities, on December 10, filed a case against a group of unidentified miscreants with the Sher-E-Bangla Nagar police station regarding the incident, in which Rana was seriously injured, alleging that a dispute over smoking inside the hall led to the clash between outsiders and residential students.

Following the death of Rana, the case was transformed into a murder case and the metropolitan police’s detective branch has been investigating the case, the police said.

Earlier, on January 4 and 11, the protesting students blocked the Farmgate crossing, demanding justice for Rana.

title: Right message, wrong messengers
body:
MULTIPLE things can be true at once. The Iranian people are engaged in a legitimate popular struggle against an entrenched political elite that has failed to meet their material needs and has answered demands for freedom and dignity with unconscionable violence and repression. At the same time, the US has no political, legal or moral basis to intervene in Iran. The dire state of the country, as is true of Venezuela and Cuba, the two other nations targeted by the latest neo-neoconservative regime change enthusiasts blinded by imperial hubris and a fetishization of military power, is in significant part the result of Washington’s own policies.

Since 1979, the US has pursued policies aimed at ensuring the failure of the Iranian Revolution. In the decades that followed, and with particular acceleration under the Trump administration, this effort crystallized into a sanctions regime designed not to promote democracy or human rights but to drive ordinary Iranians into a state of immiseration. This strategy, deployed against governments that Washington unilaterally deems problematic, occasionally for defensible reasons but far more often for refusing to subordinate themselves to US imperial and corporate power, has been linked to an estimated 38 million deaths worldwide since 1971.

In Iran, as elsewhere, this policy has rested on the cynical belief that mass suffering will produce political unrest advantageous to the interests of the United States and, in this case, of Israel as well. The quiet part was said out loud by Senator John Fetterman, who mocked the government’s recent inability to quell economic discontent through modest financial inducements and celebrated this as ‘a testament to how our nation and Israel broke Iran.’

The disregard for international law, democratic principles, and human life that underpins this slow violence (see for example Madeleine Albright’s 1996 insistence that sanctions killing as many as half a million Iraqi children was ‘worth it’) is more evident today than ever. The hypocrisy of an administration that has enabled a genocide in Gaza, decapitated a government in pursuit of oil, threatens to militarily seize the territory of a sovereign country, and condemns repression in Iran while defending public execution of Renee Good by ICE is not lost on anyone.

Beyond sanctions, the template for deeper US involvement in Iran appears poised to follow a familiar, troubling playbook. If Washington moves toward directing regime change under the guise of ‘supporting’ Iranian freedom, the most likely beneficiary would be the exiled son of the former Shah, who has not lived in the country for decades. Such an intervention would amount to a second US-backed ouster of an Iranian government to reinstall a member of the Pahlavi dynasty.

The Shah’s son, who has cultivated warm ties with Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, and has been rebuffed by Iranian human rights activists, does not represent a pathway toward Iran’s democratization. The pursuit of US intervention today then might well produce consequences as calamitous and as unpredictable as those unleashed in 1953. This broader history must therefore remain central to any serious assessment of the current crisis in Iran.

BEFORE Venezuela possessed the largest proven oil reserves in the world, that distinction belonged to Iran. More than a century ago, a weak, illegitimate, and cash-strapped Qajar Dynasty sold the rights to petroleum prospecting to British mining magnate William Knox D’Arcy, a speculative venture in a country with no existing oil industry and no guarantee of viable deposits. At the time, petroleum had not yet come to grease the wheels of the West or serve as the engine of its industrial and military power.

As a result, the 1901 oil concession was not met with the same resistance that had greeted earlier attempts by the Qajars to treat the country as their personal fiefdom, outsourcing development and selling national resources to the highest foreign bidder. The Iranian people had long resisted such Western encroachment, repeatedly forcing their government to retreat from foreign contracts. Yet popular pressure failed to materialize for what would become the most consequential concession of all, one that laid the foundation for decades of imperial intervention in Iran.

The discovery of a vast sea of oil in 1908 prompted the creation of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company (rebranded the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company in 1935 and again as British Petroleum in 1954). By 1914, citing financial uncertainty for the company and a desire to modernize the British naval fleet from domestic coal to more efficient foreign oil, the British government moved to acquire a majority stake in APOC. The timing proved decisive. The world war that followed fueled a global oil boom, and Iranian production expanded rapidly, with APOC supplying a substantial share of Britain’s wartime needs.

After the war, in 1925, a coup ended Qajar rule, and Minister of War Reza Khan crowned himself Shah, inaugurating the Pahlavi Dynasty. He renegotiated the oil concession on marginally better terms, but the increased revenues enriched the Pahlavi elite far more than ordinary Iranians. The result was a growing inequality that fed a revived anti-imperial consciousness.

British control, combined with a failure to defend national sovereignty, radicalized Iranians across social classes. Nowhere was this discontent more acute than among exploited oil workers, who lived and labored in squalid, dangerous conditions, excluded from advancement and constrained by a rigid colonial hierarchy that starkly contrasted with the privileged lives of foreign staff.

THAT the Shah served at the pleasure of British commercial interests became evident in 1941, when London, and Moscow, deposed him, citing his perceived closeness to Germany, and installed his son, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, to secure oil for the war effort and keep it from falling into German hands. For good measure, British and Soviet forces occupied the country for the next five years.

After the war and occupation, Iranians renewed their demands for sovereignty, beginning with reclaiming what they saw as their inalienable birthright: control of the natural wealth beneath their soil. Mohammad Mossadegh embodied this struggle. A European-trained lawyer and leader of the National Front coalition, he became the first fully democratically elected prime minister in 1951, sidelining the authority of the Shah and riding a wave of widespread popular support. His ascent was so significant to both Iran and to broader geopolitics that it prompted Time Magazine to name him ‘Man of the Year’ and hailed him as the ‘Iranian George Washington’ by 1952.

Yet he committed what, in the early Cold War, was an unforgivable offense: he nationalized Iran’s own natural resources. This move was wildly popular. The depth of exploitation was evident in that the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company made more in profits in 1950 than it had paid Iran in royalties over nearly the entire previous half century. Mossadegh insisted he was willing to compensate the company, a practice consistent with recent nationalizations, not only in places like Mexico but in Britain itself, which had nationalized its coal industry under the Labour government in 1947. The British nonetheless refused any negotiated settlement.

London instead responded with economic warfare, imposing a de facto embargo designed to starve Mossadegh’s government, obstruct his reform agenda, and grind the population into submission, not unlike more recent sanctions regimes. The campaign only intensified nationalist fervor; some Mossadegh’s allies declared it preferable for Iran’s oil to be destroyed ‘by an atom bomb’ than to remain under British control. When economic coercion failed, London turned to overthrowing the government, a plot Mossadegh uncovered, leading to the expulsion of British personnel from the country.

In Washington, Downing Street found willing accomplices. The pretext for intervention was that the economic turmoil, engineered by British policies, might in turn create a political vacuum that the Soviets or domestic communists would exploit. In reality, CIA documents acknowledged that Mossadegh was not a communist but a committed nationalist, and that Iran’s communist party was marginal, among the population and within the military. Despite this intelligence, the United States turned toward regime change, establishing the first ever model for covert coups that would follow around the world.

In 1953, after the CIA fomented an artificial uprising and Mossadegh was arrested by a US-backed military loyalist, the Shah, who had fled the country in anticipation of a failed plan, was restored to power. For their trouble, American oil companies were granted a 40 per cent share in the new consortium that controlled Iranian oil, while another 40 per cent went to British Petroleum.

LACKING popular legitimacy, the Shah depended heavily on US backing to maintain control. His rule was enforced through the expansion of the secret police, SAVAK, which functioned as an instrument of state terror rooted in surveillance, repression, and torture. US arms transfers helped sustain this coercive order. By the end of the Shah’s reign, US weapons sales to Iran were in the billions annually, with cumulative purchases over the decade perhaps as high as $20 billion.

As the regime poured staggering resources into armaments, it failed to adequately provide for the well-being of its population. The economic shocks of the 1970s drove millions into the slum-like peripheries of cities like Tehran. These dispossessed joined a broad coalition of women, religious clerics, merchants, laborers, students, and activists who mobilized against the monarchy. Political ferment deepened as President Carter, in a display of strategic myopia, publicly toasted the Shah, praising Iran as an ‘island of stability,’ and crediting his ‘great leadership,’ asserting that he had the ‘respect and the admiration and love’ of his people.

That the revolution which soon followed would assume an Islamic character, or culminate in the creation of a theocratic state, was not predetermined. It drew on the influence of the exiled religious figure, soon to be Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Khomeini, as well as an Islamic political vocabulary shaped by Ali Shariati, whose synthesis of Marxism, Iranian history, and Shi’a Islam resonated widely. Yet it was driven above all by a general popular discontent. As in revolutions everywhere, ideology supplied meaning, but material conditions set the stage. Iranian scholar Hamid Dabashi captures this reality in his observation that ‘Khomeini may not have led a revolution for the price of melon, but many of his followers thought they did.’

If there was a shared ideological thread running through the protests then, it was anti-imperialism. Demonstrators rejected the forced Westernization and authoritarian secularism of the Pahlavi state and rallied behind the slogan ‘Neither East nor West,’ an expression of Third World nationalism and assertion of self-determination. So too did the memory of Mohammad Mossadegh animate the uprising. His figure, representing a crushed experiment in democracy and an anti-imperialist past, remained deeply embedded in Iranian political consciousness.

The Pahlavi government met this movement with escalating violence. This repression, historian Ervand Abrahamian writes, ‘placed a sea of blood between the shah and the people,’ ensuring the monarchy could not survive and hastening the defection of the military. The revolution soon set in motion events that culminated in the student seizure of the US Embassy in Tehran who feared that Washington intended to rehabilitate, and reinstate, the Shah after admitting him for cancer treatment. The result was a prolonged 444-day standoff that institutionalized mutual hostility and cast a long shadow over both countries and the region.

This animus deepened as the US backed Iraq in its invasion of Iran soon after the revolution. The eight-year war killed roughly one million people and revealed Washington’s willingness to bleed regional powers to maintain its geopolitical influence. Continued US support for Israel and the Islamic Republic’s resistance further solidified the adversarial relationship.

The events of 1979, shaped by the blowback from 1953, also set the US on a trajectory of deeper imperial entanglement. These moves included a tightening partnership with Saudi Arabia, a more direct response to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, and laid the foundations for the Gulf War. Taken together, they created the conditions for the catastrophic, mass murderous ‘War on Terror’ that was to come, revealing a direct line from US policy toward Iran to the wider architecture of American empire across the Greater Middle East.

THE popular protests in Iran are just, and the exceedingly violent response is an affront to the most basic principles of human rights and dignity. But rolling back the regime through US intervention, rather than through the actions of the Iranian people themselves, cannot plausibly be described as support for democracy. It represents the opposite. It is an attempt to reimpose a former client state and reclaim a strategic foothold lost in 1979, in service of a broader ideological project aimed at reasserting US hegemony in the region and beyond.

The Iranian people deserve freedom, and have the right to determine their own political destiny. The horrific slaughter of protesters and imprisonment of dissidents must end. Yet US intervention would both co-opt the movement and almost certainly foreclose any real possibility of justice or democracy.

The precedent here is unmistakable. There was once what was presented as a compelling case for removing Saddam Hussein, given his record of atrocities. But regime change in Iraq, pursued under the ulterior aims of an imperial America, carried out through lies, deceit, and illegality, and urged on by an exile elite with no local legitimacy, became one of the defining crimes of the century. To follow a similar course in Iran today would not only risk replicating those failures. It would reopen wounds that remain painfully fresh, even as they are all too easily forgotten.

CounterPunch.org, January 14. Eric Ross is an organizer, educator, researcher, and PhD Candidate in the History Department at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. He is a coordinator of the national Teach-In Network sponsored by the RootsAction Education Fund.

title: AI in job market
body:
ARTIFICIAL intelligence has entered people’s daily lives in such a way that the moment of shaping the future from fantasy to reality has remained unknown to many. It is currently used in office software, industrial machinery, medical image analysis and job application selection. The tasks that used to take a lot of people’s time are now being done automatically. The result is not a theoretical question, but a real concern: will this technology accelerate progress, or will employment opportunities shrink?

This debate is now being discussed in depth around the world. The World Economic Forum has highlighted the importance of technological change, stating that it will change the structure of a large number of jobs. Even if some jobs are lost, new types of jobs will be created that are unimaginable today. This view is also consistent with the research of Erik Brynjolfsson and Andrew McAfee. According to their analysis, technology cannot simply be seen as a ‘job destroyer.’ Rather, it is like a tide — which pushes back some work, again bringing new possibilities to the fore.

THE experience of the manufacturing sector is relevant here. A few decades ago, there was great concern when robots were introduced in Japanese factories. But in reality, many factories are not shrinking but expanding. Productivity has increased as heavy and monotonous work has gone into the hands of machines, and more workers have been employed in jobs that are not possible without human skills. A similar trend is being seen in the field of artificial intelligence. Algorithms are capable of processing data quickly, verifying applications and handling big data, but are still dependent on humans to give instructions, monitor and interpret results.

According to the International Labour Organisation, regular and repetitive office work which is performed by a large number of women around the world, may be most at risk due to artificial intelligence. However, at the same time, MIT’s Task Force on the Work of the Future has shown that the importance of professions that require human judgment, empathy, and creativity is not decreasing; rather, it is increasing. That is, while artificial intelligence is able to reduce the boredom of work, it cannot fully occupy human space.

This debate is particularly relevant in the context of Bangladesh. Every year, the country’s universities are entering the job market with a large number of graduates who expect quality employment. However, employers have long pointed out the lack of necessary skills. Meanwhile, the pressure on employment has intensified as artificial intelligence is spreading in different sectors faster than expected.

Occupations that rely on repetitive work — such as data entry, basic accounting, and call centre services — are at clear risk. Even in the ready-made garment sector, the use of AI-based automation is increasing. If not prepared, Bangladesh may lose its competitiveness in the long run.

But there is another side to this story. Around the world, AI has created entire new job categories. Data annotation, where workers train AI by tagging and reviewing information, has become a billion-dollar industry in countries like India and the Philippines. Bangladeshi firms are slowly entering this space. Software companies are hiring machine learning trainees, content reviewers and people who can design or refine prompts for AI tools. These roles didn’t exist ten years ago.

HISTORY offers encouraging examples. When ATMs first appeared, people assumed bank tellers were finished. Yet economist James Bessen later showed that teller jobs actually grew because banks opened more branches and workers focused on customer service instead of counting cash.

Despite being one of the most automated countries in the world, South Korea has not been hit by a massive employment crisis. On the contrary, they have been able to develop skilled human resources, including robot experts, data engineers and digital strategists, who have made technological change easily acceptable. This experience proves that if investment is made in skills, automation is not a risk, but opens the way to new opportunities. This lesson is very relevant for Bangladesh, as the impact of technology is largely dependent on policy, education and preparedness.

These fears cannot be ignored. Economist Daron Acemoglu has repeatedly warned that if companies apply technology without training workers, inequality will multiply. Wealth will be concentrated in the hands of a few skilled people, while the rest of the people will lag behind. Where social protection is not strong, such as in Bangladesh, this risk becomes deeper and more serious.

Youth unemployment is already a major concern. The problem is clear: without rapid action, artificial intelligence can sharply increase the gap between the skilled and the unskilled, town and village, the privileged and the disenfranchised.

A smart approach can turn this moment into an advantage. Three steps are essential: The education system in Bangladesh is still giving more importance to textbook memorisation than solving problems, which needs to be changed. The main goal of education should be to develop digital skills, communication abilities, critical thinking and creativity. Countries like Singapore are introducing students to artificial intelligence from an early stage; Bangladesh should also adopt such a bold and modern approach.

Businesses should use new technologies to ensure retraining of older employees instead of laying them off. Brief and practical training can also help employees adapt to new responsibilities - machine operators can become digital technicians, clerks can work as data assistants, and supervisors can learn to supervise artificial intelligence systems.

The European Union has taken the lead in formulating policies on the ethical and transparent use of artificial intelligence. Bangladesh also needs to analyse these models and develop policies that encourage innovation on the one hand and protect workers’ rights and livelihoods on the other.

Afroza Akter is a lecturer in English, Bangladesh University of Business and Technology.

title: Polygamy: betrayal of women
body:
RECENT headlines — wife’s approval no longer essential for second marriage — are not only media hype. They reflect the profoundly worrying path of a High Court ruling. The court upheld Section 6 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961 and made it clear that a Muslim man’s second marriage does not depend on his first wife’s agreement.

Section 6 says that a husband must get written permission from the Arbitration Council before getting married further while he is still married. If he fails to accomplish this, the marriage cannot be registered. And, he will face criminal charges and have to pay the whole dower immediately. The application must explain why the marriage is suggested and whether the current wife or wives have agreed. The High Court sees this structure in the most limited way: the council’s authorisation is the most important thing and the wife’s assent is for information. This is the most harmful kind of constitutional minimalism. The court has selected the interpretation that gives men the most power and takes away women’s freedom although the law is at least unclear.

The verdict also wipes out Bangladesh’s own more freeing precedents. The High Court Division ruled in the 1999 Jesmin Sultana v Mohammad Elias case that polygamy is almost impossible to execute fairly because of the Qur’anic rules on treating wives fairly; and, hence, it is almost always illegal. It suggested that Section 6 should be changed to a law that makes polygamy illegal. The Appellate Division told the judges off and informed them to take out the part about polygamy in the Elias v Jesmin case.

The rationale, however, remains a strong obiter that connects Islamic interpretive resources with gender justice. The current High Court bench does not engage with this line of reasoning and instead falls back on a sterile textualism. They claim that because Section 6 does not clearly require ‘consent’ as a condition precedent, the wife’s assent cannot be legally necessary. This is not neutrality. It is a deliberate decision to favor a narrow interpretation of the statute above one that enhances rights and promotes equality.

The court’s answer is to trust arbitration councils, which can decide if a second marriage is ‘necessary and just.’ But there is strong evidence that these groups are frequently male-dominated, politically controlled local institutions that lack clear rules, open thinking or meaningful scrutiny. The court successfully provides local patriarchal power institutions control over women’s bodily and emotional autonomy by saying that the first wife’s agreement is not needed as long as the council agrees. The wife’s lived experience of betrayal, economic instability and psychological trauma is reduced to a variable in a bureaucratic equation rather than being regarded as a constitutional issue.

Article 27 of the constitution guarantees equal treatment under the law. Article 28(2) makes it clear that men and women have equal rights. The combined effect of Article 31 and 32 safeguards women’s rights to dignity, safety and meaningful legal protection. A legal system that interprets polygamy as a right for men and solely checks for ‘procedural’ compliance by an arbitration council is fundamentally at conflict with the protection. Bangladesh is also a member of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women. The CEDAW Committee has made it clear that polygamous marriage is not fair to women and states should work to make it illegal. General recommendation No 21 and No 29 say that polygamy is bad for women’s dignity, financial stability and emotional health. The High Court may have approached Section 6 from a constitutional and international perspective, applying the ‘necessary and just’ criteria to hold that the current wife’s informed, voluntary agreement was the minimum required. Instead, it separates personal law from the equality effort, regarding polygamy as a religious area that is almost sacred and not subject to full constitutional review.

There are other Muslim-majority places where courts are not powerless. Pakistan’s Supreme Court in the Mst Khurshid Bibi v Baboo Muhammad Amin case, famously usedijtihadto recognise a woman’s right to judicial dissolution (khula) even without the husband’s permission, emphasising substantive justice over rigid formalism. Bangladeshi jurisprudence has often toyed with more egalitarian interpretations of the Muslim family law only to be pulled back by conservative setbacks. The current decision continues that backward trend, showing that when women’s rights clash with patriarchal views of ‘personal law,’ the court prefers to respect traditional methods instead of changing them for the better.

This is not a theoretical disagreement about doctrine. Research on polygamy in Bangladesh shows that women are left alone to raise their children while their husbands marry again and again, frequently without going through the arbitration council. Global research also shows that polygamy makes women’s poverty, emotional misery and risk of violence worse in a systematic way. The court normalises this material abuse by saying that a second marriage is legal’ with council authorization even if the first wife is against it. It turns women into legally manageable externalities of male desire as long as a form is filled out and a charge is paid.

A rights-oriented High Court could have declared that ‘necessary and just’ under Section 6 cannot be met if the current wife’s informed, voluntary consent is not present, except in particular cases that are clearly in her best interest. Arbitration councils are required to regard the wife as an essential party endowed with veto-like power, supported by rationale and appellate scrutiny, used Articles 27, 28 and Bangladesh’s CEDAW duties to show that polygamy is constitutionally questionable and ought to be strictly enforced, not encouraged and urged the parliament to follow the spirit of Jesmin Sultana by working towards the legislative end of polygamy, as the Special Marriage Act 1872 does for interfaith marriages. This law makes polygamy and conversion for marriage illegal. The court has instead endorsed the most benign, patriarchal interpretation and, then, denied responsibility by citing the arbitration councils.

The illustration doing rounds on social media, a hennaed hand in bangles shackled to a pen signature, shows the truth that the judgment is unable to see. A woman does not need permission from an arbitration council to do what she wants. The High Court’s decision turns a small procedural protection into a way to justify gender-based subordination. This decision cannot be the last word. The Appellate Division and the parliament have a choice: they can either keep using the terms ‘valid law’ and ‘religious accommodation’ to hide patriarchal dominance or they may face polygamy as a structural form of discrimination that no amount of bureaucratic authorisation can clean up.

Samanta Azrin Prapty is a legal researcher and writer.

title: Bangladesh’s governance challenges
body:
