The seven-member planning and development committee includes Appellate Division judge Justice AKM Asaduzzaman, High Court Division judges Justice Md Atabullah and Justice Md Bazlur Rahman, along with the law, public administration and finance secretaries, and the Supreme Court registrar general.

Muajjem Hussain said the government’s approval of 213 posts was part of the broader proposal, marking an initial step toward establishing a fully functional secretariat independent of executive control.

Other approved posts for the Supreme Court Secretariat include two protocol officers, three accounts officers, three assistant accounts officers, 19 administrative officers, 26 personal officers, and one auditor.

The organogram also includes one photographer, one computer operator, 21 shorthand-cum-computer operators, one cashier, one data entry operator, one office assistant-cum-computer typist, 19 drivers, two storekeepers, one ‘cash sarkar’, one electrician, five photocopy machine operators, two dispatch riders, 48 office assistants, two peons and one sweeper.

The government has also approved nine jeeps, six micro-buses, four buses, five photocopy machines and one digital camera for use by the officers and staff.

According to the gazette, the expenditure for posts, vehicles and office logistics will be met from the budget allocation for the Supreme Court Secretariat.

Supreme Court registrar general Md Habibur Rahman Siddiquee has been appointed acting secretary of the Supreme Court Secretariat until further orders.

On December 11, 2025, chief justice Syed Refaat Ahmed said that the long-awaited Supreme Court Secretariat — formally launched at one of its new administrative offices on the SC campus — brings to an end a 26-year pursuit to secure genuine judicial independence.

On November 30, 2025, the law ministry issued a gazette promulgating the Supreme Court Secretariat Ordinance, fulfilling one of the core commitments in the chief justice’s judicial reform road map announced on September 21, 2024, weeks after he assumed office.

title: Adviser says no to interest rate cuts
body:
Finance adviser Salehuddin Ahmed on Saturday hinted at no cuts in the interest rate on lending to entertain populist demands.

He made the hint while addressing the publication ceremony of the seventh edition of the Banking Almanac in the city’s CIRDAP auditorium.

In November 20025, Bangladesh Bank decided to keep its policy rate unchanged at 10 per cent amid mounting pressure from businesses to lower borrowing costs as high interest rates continue to strain corporate finances and restrict investment.

Noting policy decisions were not to entertain populist demands, the finance adviser said that policy decisions should be made for the sake of the country.

He also explained the probable adverse impact of sudden change in the major policy decisions.

Bangladesh Association of Banks chairman Abdul Hai Sarkar, who was among the discussants arranged by the Banking Almanac at the fag end of the interim government that assumed power on August 8 in 2024, three days after the ouster of the Awami League regime through the July uprising, blamed pilfering of money from many banks established by AL between 2009 and 2024 for the precarious situation the banking sector was currently in and also for the high interest rates on lending.

‘Still there are scopes for cutting the rates if the government relied on less borrowing,’ Hai said.

Presided over by former adviser to the caretaker government and acting chairman of the Banking Almanac’s editorial board Hossain Zillur Rahman, the discussion was also participated in by finance secretary Khairuzzaman Majumder, secretary of the financial institutions division Nazma Mobarek, and BB deputy governor of Bangladesh Bank Nurun Nahar.

They explained how the interim government in the past 17 months since its taking office tackled the economic headwinds inherited from the previous regime.

Khairuzzaman Mozumder said that economic stability had returned and the exchange rate of Taka had strengthened, with Bangladesh Bank now purchasing dollars to maintain stability.

During this time, the average inflation rate had dropped below double digit although it still remained at elevated level of more than 8 per cent, they observed.

The finance adviser said that monetary policy and interest rate hike were not enough to pull down the inflation in the country where effective supply and monitoring always remained challenging.

Expressing satisfaction on the overall macro-economic recovery, he said that the current government never gave impression of elevating the country to the level of Singapore.

The country would stand on strong footings if the current reforms programme continued, he said.

Hossain Zillur Rahman identified five issues, including economic democracy, economic ease of life and governance, saying that these would the key for achieving an accelerated economic growth.

title: NCP-Jamaat seat deal to be made public soon: Nahid
body:
The Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami-led alliance is fully prepared to contest the 13th Jatiya Sangsad elections, and the final seat-sharing deal will be announced publicly within a day or two, National Citizen Party convener Nahid Islam said on Saturday.

Nahid made the remarks while speaking to journalists after a meeting with a European Union election observer delegation led by chief observer Ivars Ijabs at Hotel InterContinental in Dhaka.

The alliance has completed its internal preparations, and only the public announcement of seat sharing remains pending, he said.

He said that the Jamaat–NCP alliance had already begun electioneering across the country, while confusion and disorder still prevailed in other political alliances over seat distribution.

Nahid, however, expressed concern over the lack of a level playing field in the election, saying political parties had little confidence that equal opportunities were being ensured.

He alleged that special privileges and state protocol were being extended to a particular political party, which was sending a message of administrative bias and could create an uneven electoral environment.

The NCP leader also accused sections of the mainstream media of bias, saying negative and false reports were being deliberately published about his party.

He said that some media outlets were targeting the NCP with misleading news, which was undermining fairness in the electoral process, and added that the party had repeatedly raised the issue with the government and the Election Commission.

Regarding loan defaulters, Nahid said that many candidates with outstanding bank loans had initially been declared valid, while only a small number had been disqualified despite a much larger figure being involved.

He demanded a tougher stance from the Election Commission to ensure that defaulters were not allowed to contest the polls.

On election monitoring, Nahid said that the European Union would send a large observer mission for the upcoming parliamentary elections.

He said that the EU wanted the polls to be free, competitive and credible so that a democratic transfer of power could take place smoothly after the results were announced.

Raising concerns over security, Nahid said that the public shooting and killing of Inquilab Mancha convener Sharif Osman Bin Hadi had created fear in the electoral field.

He said that the continued failure to arrest the perpetrators had left candidates and activists feeling unsafe ahead of the election.

title: Commitment to independence key to progress, says Tarique
body:
Bangladesh Nationalist Party chair Tarique Rahman on Saturday said that the country could be guided in the right direction if politicians remained committed to the ideals of the 1971 War of Independence, the 1990 democratic movement and the student-led mass uprising of August 5, 2024 while working to uphold national independence and sovereignty.

He said that the country had gone through repeated upheavals and conflicts in both the political and economic spheres since independence, adding that it continued to face difficult challenges alongside differing views.

Tarique said that although sustaining accountability and the democratic process would involve pressure and hardship, maintaining democratic continuity over time would ultimately enable positive changes.

The BNP chair made the remarks while speaking at an exchange of greetings with editors and journalists representing newspapers, radio and television channels, news agencies and online media platforms at Hotel Sheraton in the capital.

Tarique assured the editors and journalists that if his party formed a government with the support of the people, it would welcome constructive criticisms aimed at solving the country’s problems and helping it move forward, rather than criticisms for criticisim’s sake.

He said that several points had become clear from the discussion, notably that the future depended on safeguarding freedom and security, whether for individuals or journalists, and that there was shared concern over democratic and political rights belonging to all citizens.

Tarique said that the country had longstanding problems and continued to face challenges, stressing that there was no desire to return to the situation before August 5, citing past tragedies and the events of August 5, 2024 as stark reminders.

He urged the people of all political persuasions to resolve differences through dialogue instead of allowing them to deepen the divisions that could split the nation.

Tarique said that after returning to the country he had felt that the new generation was seeking guidance and hope, adding that this desire extended across all generations, even though political actors could not meet every expectation.

He made an appeal to members of all political parties and to society at large to engage in discussions over differences of opinion, saying that the democratic process and accountability must be upheld at all costs at both national and local levels, including elections to local government bodies and trade organisations.

Tarique said that while reform debates had focused mainly on constitutional and legal issues, insufficient attention had been given to people’s everyday needs, safety and security across all sections of society.

He said that with an around 20 crore population, a significant portion of it being young people, it was essential to create employment opportunities at home and abroad for them.

A failure to do so, he said, could jeopardise the hopes inspired by the August 5 mass uprising, the 1990 movement, and the 1971 War of Independence.

Speaking at the event, Jaijaidin editor Shafik Rehman said that there should be a universal pension system for journalists.

If Tarique Rahman comes to power, he hoped, such a scheme would be ensured for journalists and their families under a general government law, without the need for a separate statute specifically for the profession.

The Daily Star editor Mahfuz Anam said that they wanted democracy, independent journalism, and good governance.

He warned that the country’s future challenges, particularly climate change, were not receiving sufficient attention from political parties.

Manab Zamin editor Matiur Rahman Chowdhury said that they wanted to write and speak freely, adding that since August 5, 2024 the media had been partly independent and partly controlled.

He explained that mob violence had limited the media ability to act courageously and that their work was often hindered, recalling incidents when newspaper offices were set on fire.

New Age editor and Bangladesh editor’s Council president Nurul Kabir said that he extended his greetings to Tarique Rahman with the hope that he could take steps to support the democratic development of Bangladesh and its society politically, socially, culturally, and in terms of media.

Democracy, Kabir said, cannot flourish anywhere in the world without legal, political, social, and cultural freedom for the media.

Highlighting past challenges, he said that many journalists in Bangladesh had faced legal cases, attacks, and injustices, often without a proper legal framework to defend themselves.

Kabir urged that the legal rights of the journalists currently imprisoned should be guaranteed without waiting for any political change, expressing the hope that such measures could be implemented promptly with the support of those in power.

He said that many journalists who had supported the previous regime had faced legal cases and were currently in prison.

The legal rights of those incarcerated as accused must be ensured, he affirmed.

On behalf of the editors’ council, Kabir hoped that if Tarique Rahman had any influence in the matter, he would be able to take measures to guarantee these rights without waiting to come to power.

Amar Desh editor Mahmudur Rahman said that Tarique Rahman had been absent from the country for 17 years and was unaware of what had happened during that period.

He claimed that Tarique had only heard from prominent figures and news media contacts, suggesting that this did not reflect the full history of Bangladesh over the past 17 years.

In response, Tarique said that although he could not stay in the country for a long time, he had remained in constant contact with the nation and its people.

‘Those of you who were in the country will certainly know things better than me, but it is not that I know nothing at all,’ he said.

BNP secretary general Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, Jugantor editor Abdul Hye Sikder, Kaler Kantho editor Hasan Hafiz, Ekushe Television CEO Abdus Salam, BD News editor Toufique Imrose Khalidi, among others, spoke at the event.

title: Mob violence and post-uprising policing
body:
A MASS uprising occurs when long-standing public grievances reach a breaking point, as frustration with injustice, hardship and exclusion deepens and fear of the state gradually erodes. Such uprisings are rarely triggered by a single incident. Rather, they emerge from sustained political exclusion, denial of justice, economic distress, corruption, repression and the steady erosion of institutional legitimacy — particularly when elections cease to offer meaningful change, criminal justice institutions lose credibility, media freedoms shrink and security forces are perceived as instruments of coercion rather than protection. Under these circumstances, citizens increasingly view protest as the final available means of asserting their voice. A single catalytic event — whether an act of state repression, a sudden economic shock, or a deeply symbolic injustice — can then convert long-simmering frustration into collective action. Mass participation becomes possible when people recognise that their grievances are widely shared and sense that the state’s coercive authority is either weakening or has lost its moral legitimacy.

In the aftermath of a mass uprising, societies often enter a fragile transitional phase marked by heightened public hope and a sense of popular empowerment, alongside deep institutional uncertainty. The collapse, or loss of legitimacy, of the old order creates political and administrative vacuums. Citizens, emboldened by the success of street mobilisation, may come to believe that rapid change can be achieved through crowds rather than formal processes. Meanwhile, state institutions — particularly law enforcement and the bureaucracy — remain weakened by prolonged politicisation and misgovernance. This results in governance gaps and a deterioration of law and order. The sharp contrast between elevated public expectations and the limited capacity of transitional authorities fuels impatience, contestation and competing narratives about the direction of the uprising. These tensions often manifest in mob violence, targeted attacks and declining respect for legal authority, as witnessed in post-uprising Bangladesh. Whether such volatile moments lead to democratic consolidation or renewed instability ultimately depends on restoring institutional credibility, rebuilding the legitimacy of law enforcement, ensuring inclusive political processes and channelling the moral energy of the uprising into durable governance reforms.

However, once the immediate objectives of an uprising are achieved, the mindset of street-based mobilisation can persist. Instead of relying on laws, courts, elections, or administrative procedures, people may continue to turn to street pressure to resolve grievances. Over time, this weakens respect for legal processes and institutions, as public action begins to substitute for lawful mechanisms. In such contexts, the central challenge becomes restoring trust in institutions and encouraging citizens to resolve disputes through established legal and democratic means rather than through the power of the crowd.

The mob attacks on The Daily Star and Prothom Alo in December 2025, triggered by the killing of student leader Sharif Osman Bin Hadi, starkly exposed the volatile mix of grief, political anger and weakened institutional authority in post-uprising Bangladesh. Violence escalated into collective punishment through vandalism, arson and looting, leaving journalists and staff trapped and fearing for their lives. While police initially prioritised evacuation and fire control to prevent further loss of life — a restraint later criticised for allowing the mob to act with impunity — subsequent arrests and assurances of accountability could not undo the serious damage inflicted on press freedom, public trust and the rule of law. The physical harassment of veteran journalist Nurul Kabir, the principled editor of New Age, while he stood in solidarity with fellow journalists, further underscored the growing vulnerability of independent media and ethical journalism amid episodes of mass fury and mob violence.

These incidents are not isolated. They form part of a wider pattern marked by more than 1,600 roadblocks, repeated mob actions and street-based vigilantism since August 5, reflecting a deeper crisis of trust in institutions and a dangerous normalisation of vigilante justice over lawful process.

The police, traditionally entrusted with maintaining public order and upholding the rule of law, often find themselves ill-equipped to operate effectively in volatile post-uprising environments, where the burden of restoring order falls disproportionately upon them. In post-uprising Bangladesh, this challenge has been shaped by a convergence of structural, institutional and psychological factors. Prolonged politicisation has entrenched a culture of command-driven policing, in which obedience to directives routinely outweighs professional judgement. Such institutional inertia suppresses initiative at the field level, weakens situational responsiveness and fosters hesitation during fast-evolving and emotionally charged confrontations — difficulties further compounded by fractured morale carried over from the uprising itself.

Persistent capacity constraints further undermine police effectiveness. Inadequate training in crowd control, negotiation and de-escalation limits officers’ ability to manage spontaneous or leaderless violence. Resource shortages, weak intelligence flows and the absence of clear operational guidelines during political transitions compound these deficiencies. Equally significant is the pervasive fear of political repercussions. Officers are often uncertain whether decisive action will later be interpreted as excessive force or political bias. This atmosphere of uncertainty encourages hesitation, selective enforcement and, at times, withdrawal from contested spaces, allowing violent groups to operate with impunity and eroding public confidence in the police as a neutral guardian of order.

Recent protests and street confrontations have also revealed a growing pattern of public hostility towards the police, driven by the perception that law enforcement represents a discredited past order rather than a neutral civic institution. This hostility steadily erodes police legitimacy, morale and deterrent authority. Audio-visual evidence from demonstrations shows sustained verbal abuse, institutional vilification and humiliation of officers, including crude slogans and threats of social exclusion, such as calls to deny education to the children of police families. This antagonism has affected all ranks, from frontline constables to senior leadership. Misinformation, public insults and aggressive rhetoric undermine even sincere efforts at dialogue and de-escalation. At times, verbal hostility has escalated into physical violence, with angry mobs attacking police using bricks, sticks and improvised weapons, leaving officers injured while performing their duties. Yet, despite provocation, police remain bound by law and professional ethics, unable to respond with retaliatory discrimination. Such assaults deepen the cycle of violence, weaken the rule of law and corrode public trust at moments when restraint and accountability are most urgently required.

Another major challenge lies in the blurred boundary between political expression and criminality. Post-uprising societies often tolerate a wide latitude of protest in the name of democratic space, but such tolerance can unintentionally normalise coercion and violence. When unlawful acts go unpunished or are selectively addressed, a culture of impunity takes root. In Bangladesh, inconsistent enforcement of the law — particularly when perpetrators invoke political or moral justification — has emboldened groups to bypass legal mechanisms and resort to force.

Bangladesh’s post-independence governance is marked by a fundamental paradox. Despite emerging from a liberation struggle to establish a liberal democratic Constitution, the country largely retained colonial administrative, police and judicial structures designed for imperial control. This unresolved colonial legacy, most evident in the police system governed by the Police Act of 1861, prioritises obedience over public service and lacks effective mechanisms for accountability and community engagement. As a result, a deep structural contradiction persists, weakening democratic accountability, eroding public trust and contributing to managerial failures and serious abuses, including extra-legal practices.

Cosmetic changes are insufficient. What is required is evidence-based, context-sensitive reform anchored in a modern police law and supported by broader criminal justice and governance reforms. These must address systemic gaps, enforce internal discipline, restrain deviant behaviour and remove those unfit for service. Yet successive regimes have failed to undertake decisive police reform in line with public expectations. Only recently, following sustained advocacy by the police, civil society and the media, has an ordinance been issued to establish a Police Commission — an initiative widely welcomed, despite concerns over its limited independence, as a long-overdue step. Even so, reforms delayed for decades cannot be expected to yield immediate results.

Consequently, under the post-uprising transitional government, the police have struggled to contain mob violence. In other domains of policing, progress remains limited, while inertia and capacity deficits continue to erode professionalism. Although the 2024 uprising produced a significant shock — a convulsion within the system — it has yet to translate into sustained structural reform. Without such transformation, the gap between democratic aspirations and colonial-era policing will persist, with serious implications for governance, security and the rule of law.

Addressing the law and order crisis in a post-uprising society such as Bangladesh requires a multidimensional policy response.

First, depoliticisation of the police is fundamental to restoring lawful order. Law enforcement agencies must be structurally insulated from partisan influence so that operational decisions are guided by law and public safety rather than political expediency. Genuine operational autonomy, combined with transparent and credible accountability mechanisms, would enable officers to act decisively and impartially while reassuring citizens that power is not being abused.

Second, capacity building must be understood as a qualitative, not merely quantitative, endeavour. Beyond manpower and equipment, police training must emphasise democratic policing values, crowd psychology, conflict sensitivity and de-escalation skills, alongside human rights–compliant use of force. In volatile post-uprising environments, preventive engagement is often more effective than reactive force.

Third, the rule of law must be enforced in a visible, consistent and non-discriminatory manner. Any selective tolerance of mob action, regardless of emotional or political framing, undermines legal norms and signals impunity. Swift, impartial and transparent investigations — particularly into high-profile attacks on the media or public institutions — are essential to reaffirm that no cause justifies lawlessness.

Fourth, rebuilding public trust must be treated as a central policy objective. Community engagement, structured dialogue forums and accessible grievance-redress mechanisms can narrow the distance between citizens and law enforcement. When people believe their concerns can be addressed institutionally, the appeal of street justice diminishes.

Fifth, reform cannot be confined to the police alone. The entire criminal justice system and broader organs of the state require comprehensive renovation, reorganisation and professionalisation. Courts, prosecution services, correctional institutions and oversight bodies must function efficiently, independently and transparently. Delays, politicisation and administrative weakness fuel frustration and push citizens towards extra-legal remedies. A credible justice system, working in coordination with law enforcement, is indispensable for restoring faith in lawful processes.

At the same time, the wider machinery of government must address structural socio-economic inequalities through a holistic and inclusive approach. Persistent poverty, unemployment, discrimination and social exclusion create fertile ground for anger and mob behaviour. Development policies must therefore ensure equitable access to education, healthcare, employment and social protection. When citizens experience dignity, opportunity and fairness, social tensions diminish and the foundations of a peaceful society are strengthened.

Bangladesh currently faces a profound challenge in the form of widespread unemployment and underemployment among educated youth. Many see little realistic prospect of securing decent employment despite years of academic effort, breeding frustration and hopelessness that undermine social stability. When education fails to translate into opportunity, young people begin to question the fairness and legitimacy of the entire system. This dynamic was clearly reflected in student protests that began as a quota reform movement for public sector jobs and evolved into a broader political mobilisation. In this context, unemployment becomes not merely an economic issue but a powerful catalyst for mass mobilisation and, at times, mob violence. Sustainable and inclusive job creation therefore remains the most effective long-term response to social unrest.

Finally, political leadership bears a decisive responsibility in shaping post-uprising norms. Clear, consistent and unequivocal condemnation of violence — regardless of political affiliation or perceived justification — is essential. Leaders must resist rhetoric that legitimises anger or romanticises unlawful acts as revolutionary justice. Democratic gains can only be preserved through restraint, moral clarity and adherence to constitutional processes.

In the broader canvas of state governance, the police may be likened to a goalkeeper in football — the final line of defence rather than the sole guardian of order. Just as a team depends on the coordinated performance of all eleven players, effective governance requires multiple institutions to fulfil their respective responsibilities. When other organs of the state fail, the police inevitably face the consequences. If attacks are relentless, even the most capable goalkeeper cannot stop every shot. Similarly, it is neither realistic nor fair to expect the police alone to compensate for systemic governance failures.

In conclusion, the deterioration of law and order in post-uprising Bangladesh is not merely a policing failure but a broader governance challenge rooted in transition, mistrust and institutional weakness. Restoring order requires more than force; it demands legitimacy, consistency and reform. Only through a balanced approach — combining firm enforcement with institutional reform and public engagement — can Bangladesh navigate its fragile post-uprising phase and move towards a stable, law-governed democratic order.

Dr Md Motiar Rahman is a retired additional inspector general of police.

title: Hopes beyond uncertainty in Bangladesh politics
body:
THE political landscape of Bangladesh has been characterised by uncertainty and fragmentation for most, if not all, of its history, shaped from the very outset of its independence in 1971 following a historic victory over West Pakistan. Such uncertainty and fragmentation in the political environment have escalated significantly over the past one and a half decades, largely due to the process of depoliticisation and its consequences under an authoritarian regime masquerading as a hollow or bubble democracy, orchestrated by the Bangladesh Awami League and its purported alliances. However, the July 2024 mass uprising that deposed the previous tyrannical regime inspired the potential to bring about stability and consensus within the national political landscape. Nonetheless, the months and years that have passed since July 2024 indicate that such novel hopes and aspirations remain highly ambitious and continue to appear as little more than a distant dream for many. As a result, a crucial question of unity versus fragmentation currently lies at the heart of contemporary politics in Bangladesh and is likely to persist in the years ahead.

Bangladesh is at a turning point in its history due to economic challenges, dysfunctional democracy and socio-cultural upheavals. Its political destiny is being shaped by the ongoing contradiction between the aspiration for national unity and the reality of political fragmentation. Nevertheless, there may still be grounds for cautious optimism, even amid the many uncertainties confronting the nation. Bangladesh was not only born out of a unifying struggle, but is also a resilient and courageous nation with a proud and glorious past. For instance, the unifying spirit that shaped the nation emerged through the language movement of 1952, the 1969 mass uprising, the liberation war of 1971, the anti-dictatorship movement of the 1990s, and finally the July 2024 mass uprising against fascism, all of which forged a strong sense of collective identity rooted in linguistic, cultural and political rights. Unity during these periods was grounded in a shared vision of emancipating the masses from political, economic, social and cultural marginalisation. Nonetheless, concerns about political fragmentation have repeatedly resurfaced, obstructing the nation’s progress and weakening the promise of democratic consolidation.

Notably, following the July 2024 mass uprising, national politics in Bangladesh became abruptly fractured, giving rise to numerous competing narratives that rendered the political landscape increasingly volatile and unpredictable. To some extent, several of these narratives were not part of the July Revolution’s original agenda, and their continued articulation has introduced both liberal and extremist tendencies into Bangladesh’s current political environment. The absence of the previously dominant political party, the Bangladesh Awami League, alongside the emergence of a new party, the NCP, and the continued prominence of two other major parties, the BNP and Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, together with many smaller parties, has fostered entrenched political polarisation. In such a context, politics often turns into a zero-sum contest, where an electoral defeat in Bangladesh is perceived as an existential loss rather than as a legitimate democratic alternative. Consequently, functional democracy, nurtured through healthy competition and mutual tolerance, has been largely absent in Bangladesh for decades.

The lack of institutionalised democracy within political parties and across various state institutions has created a situation in which personal and party interests frequently take precedence over national objectives, perpetuating a persistent cycle of uncertainty in democratic governance. Even in situations that demand consensus, the major political parties regularly fail to cooperate on matters of national interest. More often than not, the national parliament is used as a platform for confrontation, disruption or abstention rather than as a forum for addressing pressing national concerns. The credibility and legitimacy of democracy are further weakened by disputed elections, allegations of manipulation and the systematic silencing of dissenting voices. Such fragmentation among major political parties leads many citizens to believe that they are being marginalised and excluded from their rightful participation in the institutionalisation of democracy. Restrictions imposed on the media, civil society and critical voices have contributed to political apathy, particularly among young people and ordinary citizens. Achieving political unity becomes increasingly difficult when ruling parties and their incumbents constrain freedom of expression and obstruct the political activities of the opposition.

Uneven economic growth over the years has failed to benefit all social groups equally, giving rise to deep and often entrenched inequalities. Particularly under the previous regime, rent-seeking practices intensified alarmingly, resulting in the transfer of vast sums of money abroad. Several additional factors—such as rising living costs, prolonged unemployment, widespread corruption, lack of accountability, institutional weakness and spatial inequalities—have contributed to social, cultural and economic fragmentation, which has converged with existing political divisions and further deepened the overall crisis.

However, the other side of these fragmentations and uncertainties may also offer the possibility of renewed hope and unity in Bangladesh’s political future. The mass uprising of July 2024, which effectively overthrew a tyrannical regime, marks a decisive and historic moment, signalling the potential for a fundamental shift away from the country’s debased political system. Political parties and any future government must therefore exercise greater responsibility in safeguarding public welfare and engaging in ethical and democratic political practices. The lesson of unity may emerge from the collective experience of the July 2024 movement, where unity is increasingly articulated in political discourse through ideas of nationalism, development and stability. Yet genuine national unity must be grounded in pluralism, an independent judiciary, tolerance and trust in institutions. There remain possibilities for overcoming present uncertainties and fragmentation, despite political diversity. A democratic society does not require unanimous agreement; rather, it depends on the peaceful coexistence of diverse perspectives within shared ethical, legal and constitutional boundaries.

Several additional factors highlighted by the July 2024 movement also point towards the potential for optimism and greater stability in national politics. Bangladesh possesses a large, dynamic and energetic youth population. Although many young people are disillusioned with conventional party politics, they are increasingly participating through digital platforms, social movements and issue-based activism. Their demands—centred on employment opportunities, fairness, transparency and dignity—have the potential to transform the political landscape beyond traditional party loyalties. Moreover, despite external pressures and repeated attempts to control civilian voices, Bangladesh continues to maintain a tradition of vibrant civil society engagement, relatively active media and intellectual debate. As a result, both future governments and their opposition forces are likely to face sustained pressure to function as moral and political counterweights, thereby preserving the prospects of reform and accountability in political life.

In addition, the interim government has introduced several long-awaited reforms that could help restore public confidence and reduce uncertainty by strengthening institutional effectiveness, particularly within the legislature, the administration, the judiciary and the electoral system. However, the success of these reforms will once again depend on genuine commitment to democratic norms and principles. Thus, despite persistent uncertainty, a number of developments encouraged by the July 2024 mass uprising suggest that hopes for unity, stability and democratic renewal may yet prevail over fragmentation and doubt in Bangladesh’s evolving political landscape in the years to come.

Dr Shafiqul Islam is a political analyst and full-time faculty member at the department of political science and sociology, North South University.

title: Labour compliance challenges
body:
THE interim government in November 2025 passed the Labour (Amendment) Ordinance 2025, bringing about extensive changes in the Labour Act that impact the labour framework. While the reforms are positioned to strengthen worker rights and align with international standards under the International Labour Organisation, its immediate implications for employers are profound and demanding.

The legislation broadens the law’s scope, mandates new administrative obligations and significantly enhances enforcement mechanisms. Employers, especially those employing a large number of workers, now face a substantially more complex and high-stake compliance environment.

The labour law is only applicable to those falling within the definition of worker set by the law. As such, only those are able to enjoy the rights provided in the law and also exercise those rights in labour courts. One of the most consequential aspects of the amendment is the expansion of the definition of ‘worker’ in Section 2(65) of the law.

The previous definition offered broad exclusions, explicitly stating that a worker ‘does not include a person mainly in a managerial, administrative [or supervisory] capacity,’ meaning that a large category of white-collar employees working in these capacities did not enjoy labour law protection and were governed by employment contracts and company policy. The amendment removes this exclusion from the core definition. The new, more inclusive definition states: ‘“worker” means any individual, including someone who is undergoing training... who is employed in any establishment or industry... to perform skilled, unskilled, manual, technical, business development, or clerical work as an employee or officer, by whatever designation called….’

The inclusion of ‘officer’ and the functional category of ‘business development’ tasks immediately pulls a number of previously exempted white-collar staff into the category of ‘worker.’ This means that, depending on the type of organisation, a significant number of employees previously excluded from labour law protection are entitled to labour law protection and enforcement mechanisms.

The maternity benefit entitlement has been changed to expand welfare support for female workers. The ordinance has replaced the earlier eight weeks’ maternity benefit period with 60 days and extended the total paid leave to 120 days from the date of delivery. The period is the total new paid leave entitlement while the 60 days is the standardised equivalent used to adjust administrative time frame previously specified in weeks. It requires at least six months of service before entitlement and maintains the exclusion where a woman has two or more surviving children although it now refers to the mother as ‘mother/parturient.”

Payment methods for the maternity benefit are modernised as benefits may now be given in cash, bank deposit or electronic fund transfer and the wage calculation method is simplified, using monthly wages divided by 26n instead of a three months’ average.

However, for other core provisions, such as notice requirements, proof of delivery, payment timelines and employer obligations in case of the worker’s death, all time frames are adjusted from eight weeks to 60 days. The restriction on job termination during pregnancy and post-delivery also aligns with this sixty days, reflecting the modernisation and digitalisation of procedures without changing the basic protections.

This change primarily impacts employers by requiring them to update all internal human resource manuals, policy documents and reporting software to replace “eight weeks’ with ‘sixty days’ to ensure a full procedural compliance.

The ordinance shifts the balance of industrial power by making it substantially easier for workers in larger establishments to organise and register a trade union. Under the previous requirement, a trade union could only be registered if at least 20 per cent of the workers in the establishment are its members.

The new structure specifies clear numerical ceilings for membership requirements based on the total worker count. As little as 20 workers in an establishment may now jointly apply to register a trade union. However, the union must meet specific membership thresholds based on the total number of workers in the establishment.

The ordinance converts the establishment of a provident fund from an optional provision to a statutory obligation once a minimum threshold of workers is reached, introducing substantial administrative and financial responsibilities for management. The previous provisions were optional and were not triggered until 75 per cent of the workers united to demand its establishment. The new ordinance makes it mandatory for factories and establishments employing 100 or more permanent workers to establish and maintain a provident fund.

The amendment also introduces an option for workers to participate in the national ‘Pragati’ pension scheme as an alternative to the employer-constituted provident fund. The investment provisions have been simplified, limiting investments to government-approved sectors while the earlier version detailed specific investment categories such as ICB Mutual Fund Certificates or government securities.

A comprehensive framework addressing workplace harassment and discrimination has been introduced, demanding the institutionalisation of internal complaints and compliance committees. The ordinance explicitly mandates equal pay for equal work, prohibiting wage discrimination based on gender or disability.

The responsibilities against violence and harassment at work have been significantly expanded. The previous provision was exclusive to the protection of women. The amendment introduced broad and mandatory duties for the owner, employer and authority to ensure that the workplace environment is not hostile and are required to formulate and implement a workplace policy against violence and harassment which is applicable for everyone.

In addition, the mandatory requirement of the establishment of a ‘committee for disposal of complaints on discrimination, violence, and harassment’ has been added.

Under the ordinance, the requirement of establishing an alternative dispute resolution authority dedicated to the resolution of individual and collective labour disputes has been added. This authority is mandated to operate on the crucial principles of impartiality and fairness, notwithstanding any other existing laws.

While labour courts retain their statutory jurisdiction, the introduction of a dedicated ADR authority reflects a legislative intent to strengthen pre-adjudicatory dispute resolution mechanisms. The framework is designed to operate alongside, rather than in substitution of labour courts.

The Labour Act (Amendment) Ordinance marks a significant transformation in labour landscape, expanding protections for workers while imposing more rigorous compliance obligations on employers. From broadened worker definitions and enhanced maternity benefits to mandatory social security and equality frameworks, the ordinance modernises labour regulation to align with rising international standards. Employers must now proactively adapt their policies, processes and reporting mechanisms to meet the heightened requirements, ensuring both legal compliance and a fair, safe and inclusive workplace.

Saqeb Mahbub, a barrister-at-law, is a partner and Afrin Sadia Nusrat is an associate at law firm Mahbub and Company.

title: GAS CRISIS: A system full of holes
body:
DHAKA has developed a strange winter ritual. As the temperature drops, gas pressure disappears from pipeline kitchens, LPG shops pull down their shutters and the officially ‘fixed’ price quietly retreats into the world of press conferences and PDF notices. What remains in the real market is a different arithmetic altogether: a 12-kg LPG cylinder that costs Tk 1,300 on paper and Tk 2,300 in flesh and blood. The difference, it seems, is the price of believing in regulation.

Liquefied petroleum gas was once marketed as a sensible alternative, a modern solution for households abandoned by pipeline gas. Over the last decade, private LPG has steadily become the cooking fuel of urban middle-class life and peri-urban necessity. Estimates suggest that more than 4 million households now depend on LPG, with annual consumption crossing one million tonnes. This dependency was supposed to bring competition, efficiency and price stability. Instead, it has delivered a recurring hostage situation where consumers are trapped between shortages, whispers of global crises and a regulatory authority that sets prices but not reality.

Officially, the story is neat. Each month, the regulator announces a new price based on international benchmarks, currency rates and a formula polished since 2021. January’s increase was modest on paper, about Tk 53 for a 12-kg cylinder. That should have pushed retail prices slightly above Tk 1,300. Yet even before the announcement took effect, cylinders were selling at Tk 2,200 to Tk 2,500, if they were available at all. In some neighbourhoods, consumers walked from shop to shop like pilgrims searching for a shrine that still believed in fixed prices.

The gap between the declared price and the street price is not a market anomaly any more; it is a permanent feature. Even in ‘normal’ months, consumers quietly accept paying Tk 150–200 more than the official rate. This silent surcharge has now ballooned into Tk 500–1,000, justified by murmurs of supply shortages and rising costs somewhere up the chain. Curiously, the shortage always appears at the retail end, never at the announcement podium.

The usual explanation this winter is imports. LPG imports reportedly fell by roughly 40 per cent in December, dropping from an average of around 130,000 tonnes a month to about 90,000 tonnes. Winter demand, higher freight costs, shipping disruptions and geopolitical complications have all been invoked. These are not implausible factors. Bangladesh imports almost all of its LPG, and global prices do fluctuate. But supply shocks do not automatically translate into lawless pricing unless enforcement collapses. Scarcity may explain queues; it does not explain why a fixed price becomes optional.

The more uncomfortable truth is structural. Bangladesh’s LPG market is nominally competitive but practically cartelised. A handful of large operators dominate imports, storage and bottling. Retailers, often small family-run shops, are squeezed between distributor prices and consumer anger. When wholesale supply tightens, retailers either shut down or sell at inflated prices to survive. Regulation exists, but monitoring is sporadic, fragmented and largely symbolic. Price fixing without price policing is not regulation; it is theatre.

Meanwhile, households are forced to absorb the shock. For a lower-middle-income family, paying Tk 2,300 for a cylinder that should cost Tk 1,300 is not an inconvenience; it is a budgetary earthquake. Cooking fuel already eats into disposable income, especially as food prices remain stubbornly high. LPG consumption for a family typically lasts 25 to 35 days. At current black-market prices, annual extra expenditure per household can easily exceed Tk 10,000. Multiply that by millions of households and the invisible tax imposed by market failure runs into tens of billions of taka.

The irony deepens when pipeline gas enters the picture. Winter gas pressure shortages are a familiar annual drama, but they now interact cruelly with the LPG crisis. When pipeline gas falters, households rush to LPG as backup, spiking demand overnight. This seasonal pattern is entirely predictable, yet planning seems permanently surprised by it. Strategic reserves are minimal, coordination between pipeline gas management and LPG supply is non-existent, and consumers are left to juggle cylinders like emergency rations.

There is also a philosophical contradiction at work. Policymakers routinely argue that private sector participation improves efficiency and lowers prices. Yet in LPG, private dominance has coincided with chronic price distortions. Government-supplied LPG, limited in volume and geography, remains far cheaper. A 12.5-kg cylinder from public suppliers costs Tk 825, a figure that feels almost mythical in today’s market. The existence of this price exposes an uncomfortable question: if LPG can be sold at that level by public entities, why must private consumers pay nearly three times more? The answer, inevitably, lies not in global markets alone but in margins, mark-ups and market power.

Regulatory responses, so far, have been predictably cautious. Letters are written, assurances are exchanged and inspections are promised. Selling above the fixed price is technically punishable, but punishment requires presence, proof and persistence. The absence of visible penalties has taught the market a simple lesson: the risk of enforcement is lower than the profit of overpricing. Confidence in regulation erodes not because prices rise, but because rules appear optional.

The social cost of this erosion is significant. Energy insecurity breeds resentment, distrust and a sense of abandonment. Consumers begin to view both government and business as complicit, even when individual actors may be constrained by larger failures. This cynicism is corrosive. It normalises exploitation as an inevitable feature of daily life and lowers expectations of governance itself.

There is also a long-term policy danger. LPG was meant to be a transition fuel, supporting urbanisation while cleaner and more reliable energy systems evolved. If LPG becomes synonymous with profiteering and crisis, public support for energy reform weakens. Households may revert to unsafe alternatives, including biomass or illegal connections, undermining environmental and safety goals.

What makes the situation particularly bitter is its predictability. Winter demand spikes. Import dependence creates vulnerability. Weak enforcement invites opportunism. None of this is new. Yet each year, the same script is performed with minor variations, as if repetition itself could substitute for resolution.

A functioning LPG market does not require heroic interventions. It requires transparent supply data, mandatory disclosure of distributor prices, real-time monitoring in high-demand seasons and swift penalties that hurt enough to deter. It also requires the political will to confront concentrated market power rather than politely requesting cooperation. Without these, monthly price announcements will continue to resemble seasonal greetings: well-intentioned, widely circulated and largely ignored.

For now, the consumer remains the most reliable shock absorber in the system. They absorb price hikes, shortages, policy failures and the quiet consensus that this is simply how things work. In winter kitchens across Dhaka and beyond, cooking has become an exercise in economic survival, where the flame on the stove burns brighter than faith in regulation.

Perhaps the cruellest satire of all is this: the price of LPG is officially set every month, adjusted to the decimal, calculated with international benchmarks and announced with confidence. And then, in the market, it is quietly laughed at. In that laughter lies the real measure of the crisis — not of gas, but of governance.

HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently, he teaches at IUBAT.

title: Illegal occupation of roads, footpaths must stop
body:
UNAUTHORISED parking on roads and footpaths and makeshift shops in the places are not only a nuisance but a systemic failure that renders the city infrastructure hostile to residents. A photograph that New Age published on January 10 shows that dozens of CNG-run auto-rickshaws and makeshift shops occupy most parts of a road stretch near a hospital at Jurain. The photograph is a grim indictment of Dhaka’s urban mismanagement. Dhaka roads are notoriously unfriendly for pedestrians, especially for those with disabilities, because of flawed structures and the rampant grabbing of space by vendors and illegal parking. This woe is compounded by motorcyclists who, in a display of flagrant lawlessness, treat footpaths as personal thoroughfares and parking bays. Such practices obstruct the smooth traffic and force pedestrians onto the path of oncoming traffic, leading to frequent accidents and altercations. Despite these issues making the headlines countless times, the authorities have failed to take up effective measures. A lax enforcement of traffic rules, coupled with an ill-conceived parking policy and a chronic lack of designated spaces, has encouraged this anarchy. Every time a reclamation drive is launched, the victory is short-lived.

The persistence of this chaos is not accidental but is fuelled by a lucrative, deeply entrenched nexus of corruption. Numerous reports identified syndicates composed of local political leaders, ward councillors, law enforcement officers and city officials who benefitted from the illegal allotment of public space. Such syndicates have unfortunately continued. It is estimated that approximately 300,000 hawkers occupy Dhaka’s roads and footpaths, paying extortion money ranging from Tk 20,000 to Tk 500,000 for an ‘allotment’ from intermediaries. On a daily basis, the vendors pay between Tk 300 and Tk 1,000 to operate, resulting in a staggering daily extortion sum of roughly Tk 9 crore. This money reportedly flows to police stations and political activists, ensuring that the occupation remains protected from meaningful intervention. While the authorities frequently pledge to break this syndicate, their efforts have largely been confined to ineffectual, periodic eviction drives. These raids penalise the foot soldiers of the trade, the hawkers, while leaving the powerful beneficiaries of the extortion racket untouched. Consequently, the roads and footpaths of the capital remain crowded and off-limits to pedestrians and vehicles.

The authorities, therefore, need to move beyond ad hoc, sporadic measures and address the root of the crisis to truly reclaim the roads and footpaths. This requires an urgent enforcement of a comprehensive parking policy and hawkers’ management policy to stop illegal parking on roads and illegal occupation of footpaths. Most important, the authorities need to show the will to identify and prosecute the syndicates that profit from such occupation.

title: Weak policing threatens peaceful elections
body:
THE year 2025 was largely a time of law and order failures. What makes this worrying is that this was the year preceding the national elections, set for February 12, after the political changeover that happened in August 2024. Law and order, therefore, needs to be improved to the expected, or required, level for the elections to be free, fair and peaceful. But people still pass their days amidst violence and crimes such as murder, robbery, theft, kidnapping and extortion that are happening apace. In the month that ended 2025, a shrine and several graves were vandalised in Thakurgaon on the 27th. Inquilab Mancha convener Sharif Osman Hadi, an aspirant for a Dhaka constituency, was shot at in Dhaka on the 12th and died while being treated in Singapore on the 18th. On the 22nd, a leader of Jatiya Shramik Shakti, the labour wing of the National Citizen Party, was shot at in Khulna reportedly over the share of drug peddling money. On the 26th, a bomb explosion at a madrassah in Dakkhin Keraniganj left four wounded. On November 18, mobs burnt offices of the Daily Star and Prothom Alo. Cultural organisations Chhayanaut and Udichi were also set on fire.

Police statistics show the filing of 3,785 cases of murder, 1,935 of robbery, 9,762 of theft, 1,101 of kidnapping and 1,815 arms-related cases in 2025. Statistics of rights group Ain O Salish Kendra show that at least 197 people died in mob violence in 2025, whilst the figure for 2024 was 128. The rights group further says that at least 102 people died and 4,744 were injured in 401 incidents of political violence in 2025. Whilst all this paints a bleak picture of law and order in the year that went by, what adds to fears, especially in view of the general elections, is that about two-thirds of the arms and much of the ammunition looted from prisons and police stations during the August 2024 political changeover have arguably fallen into the wrong hands. The police say that they are yet to recover 1,333 of the 5,763 looted firearms and recapture 700 of the 2,200 inmates who broke out of jails at that time. Prisons directorate officials say that 27 out of the 98 firearms looted then could be recovered. All this is believed to have resulted from leniency or inefficiency in maintaining law and order that the government showed during the early days of the political changeover.

The government must, in such a situation, take effective measures against all such violence and crimes to make the elections that the nation is moving towards peaceful. With the elections about a month away, it is high time the government acted in the right direction.

title: Holders Palace stunned by Macclesfield
body:
Crystal Palace’s defence of the FA Cup came to an embarrassing end as they were beaten 2-1 by sixth-tier Macclesfield on Saturday in the biggest shock in the competition’s history.

The 117 places that separate Premier League outfit Palace from Macclesfield of the National League North in the English football pyramid is the most ever overcome by an underdog in FA Cup history.

Captain Paul Dawson and Isaac Buckley-Ricketts scored either side of half-time to secure a famous victory for a club that were forced to reform in 2020 after being wound up for unpaid debts.

‘I can’t believe it, we never thought we would be in this position,’ said Macclesfield manager John Rooney, the younger brother of former England captain Wayne Rooney.

‘I didn’t think it was possible but there is that little bit of hope that anything can happen on the day.’

Macclesfield are also still coming to terms with the death of forward Euan McLeod, who died aged 21 less than a month ago, after a car accident when he was travelling home after a match.

Crystal Palace boss Oliver Glasner, who has been linked with the vacant managerial post at Manchester United, made six changes but his starting line-up still included England internationals Marc Guehi and Adam Wharton.

‘I have no explanation for what I have seen today,’ said Glasner.

‘In these kind of games honestly you don’t need tactics, you don’t need a manager.

‘I think if you just show what you’re capable of and having a little bit of pride then you perform in a different way, but today we missed everything.’

Palace are now winless in nine games in all competitions and set-piece defending has been at the heart of that slump.

Macclesfield took full advantage when Dawson powered in a header from a free-kick just before half-time.

Glasner described the goalmouth scramble that led to Macclesfield’s second as ‘slapstick’.

Buckley-Ricketts prodded past Walter Benitez from close range on the hour after Palace fluffed multiple opportunities to clear the danger.

Spanish international Yeremy Pino’s pinpoint free-kick in the 90th minute showed the quality the Premier League side possess.

But they could not save themselves from going down in history for the wrong reasons just months on from beating Manchester City at Wembley to win a major trophy for the first time.

Premier League strugglers Wolves are now unbeaten in four games after thrashing Shrewsbury 6-1 to progress to the fourth round thanks to a Jorgen Strand Larsen hat-trick.

title: BKSP wants RTC in Rangamati by 2030
body:
Bangladesh Krira Shikkha Protisthan intends to support the residents of the Chittagong hill tracts by setting up a regional training centre in Rangamati, which initially will have the capacity to accommodate six different sports disciplines.

Beginning its journey with football and hockey at Savar in 1986, the sports educational institution now operates 21 sports disciplines with seven regional training centres across the country.

Initially, BKSP will concentrate on football and five combat sports: judo, karate, boxing, taekwondo, and wushu. There are plans for future inclusion of archery and gymnastics at the Rangamati centre.

The institute is contemplating the provision of training facilities for aspiring athletes from the remote hilly districts of Rangamati, Khagrachari, and Bandarban, aiming to facilitate their pursuit of sports careers.

Aside from training facilities, the centre would offer residential space and a 12-year educational curriculum through the institute.

BKSP received the nod after government directives to develop a regional training centre in Rangamati were announced during the Deputy Commissioner’s Conference organised by the Cabinet Division at the Osmani Memorial Auditorium in February 2025.

In October 2025, the ministry for youth and sports also announced its plan to set up BKSP’s regional training centre.

The land acquisition for the project is already in progress during the tenure of BKSP’s previous director general Brig Gn Md Munirul Islam, who served BKSP from August 2024 to mid-December 2025.

‘The concerned authority is working on land acquisition, covering roughly 40 to 45 acres. If the construction begins in 2026, we can expect the Rangamati centre to be fully operational by 2029-2030,’ said Munirul.

‘About the progress, everything depends on budget allocations for the fiscal year 2025-2026,’ he added.

The Rangamati centre will be open to aspiring athletes nationwide, with a primary focus on the indigenous communities and providing high-quality training.

‘We have observed that the current facilities available across the country are not comfortable for athletes from hilly areas. Therefore, we want to reach out to them rather than have them come to us, he added.

Additionally, Rangamati was chosen for its geographical landscape, communication facilities, and security considerations, with the broader idea of encouraging interaction between hilly and plain land communities through sport, as stated by the former DG of BKSP.

BKSP selected sports based on the diverse cultures of indigenous communities, the physical characteristics of hilly people, and their strong sporting traditions.

‘For certain training, we need to artificially construct hillocks in Savar or other training centres. However, this will not be necessary in Rangamati… Therefore, we can develop a plan based on the opportunities presented by the natural facilities available,’ said Munirul.

title: Polish farmers march against Mercosur trade deal
body:
Polish farmers descended on Warsaw on Friday to protest a European trade deal with the South American Mercosur bloc, marching just moments after it was accepted by a majority of EU nations in Brussels.

Over a thousand protestors gathered, some arriving on their tractors, to again denounce a deal many fear will lead to unfair competition in the bloc.

‘This will kill our agriculture in Poland,’ said Janusz Sampolski, a farmer who came from a village just south of Gdansk on the Baltic coast, some 340 kilometres (210 miles) away.

‘We will be dependent on supply chains from other countries,’ he told AFP, saying it could threaten Poland’s food security ‘in the event of the threat of war’.

Poland, along with France, Ireland, Austria, and Hungary, voted against the measure, but most of the 27 EU members approved it, diplomats told AFP.

Carrying flags and wearing yellow vests, the demonstrators marched toward Parliament and the chancellery of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Some protestors set off fireworks and lit off flares. Tractors, which several drove into the city, were not let into its limits.

Aside from economic concerns, farmers also warned of food quality and safety risks.

‘Food will be coming to us... produced using pesticides that have been banned in the European Union,’ said Przemyslaw Zbroinski, another farmer from the Gdansk region.

‘Some of the substances [have been banned] for nearly 30 years,’ he added.

The Mercosur deal has been in the works for over 25 years, with the European Commission arguing that it will bolster EU exports while fostering diplomatic ties.

But for Zbroinski, ‘It will definitely end with much harsher and larger strikes, and blockades of countries and capitals’.

title: Thousands of Irish farmers protest EU-Mercosur trade deal
body:
Several thousand Irish farmers protested Saturday against the European Union’s trade deal with the South American bloc Mercosur, a day after EU states approved the treaty despite opposition from Ireland and France.

Tractors streamed into the roads of Athlone, in central Ireland, for the demonstration, displaying signs including ‘Stop EU-Mercosur’ and ones with the European Union flag emblazoned with the words ‘sell out’.

Farmers on Friday also marched in Poland and blocked roads in France and Belgium as the EU gave the green light to the trade deal, which has been welcomed by businesses groups but heavily criticised by European farmers.

The accord, more than 25 years in the making, would create one of the world’s largest free-trade area, boosting commerce between the 27-nation EU and the Mercosur bloc comprising Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay.

Major Mercosur exports to the EU include agricultural products and minerals, while the EU would export machinery, chemicals and pharmaceuticals with lowered tariffs applied.

But many European farmers fear their livelihoods will be undercut by a flow of cheaper goods from agricultural giant Brazil and its neighbours, prompting Ireland, France, Poland, Hungary and Austria to vote against the accord.

The agreement is widely opposed by Irish farmers for fear it will result in an influx of an extra 99,000 tonnes of cheap beef from South America, disrupting Irish agriculture.

The Irish Farmers’ Association (IFA), Ireland’s main farmers’ lobby group, called the result “very disappointing”.

It said it would ‘renew’ focus on securing a majority against the deal in the European Parliament.

‘We expect Irish MEPs to stand behind the farming community and reject the Mercosur deal,’ said IFA president Francie Gorman in a statement.

The Mercosur deal will also need to be agreed by a majority of MEPs in the European assembly in the coming months, where voting coalitions have become more volatile and unpredictable.

title: Ex-delivery driver gives voice to China’s precarious gig workers
body:
A few years ago, Hu Anyan was speeding through the streets of Beijing on a three-wheel motorbike loaded with packages, one of millions of delivery drivers working for China’s online retail giants.

The 46-year-old is now a best-selling author after recounting his experiences in his book ‘I Deliver Parcels in Beijing’.

Around two million copies have been sold since its release in 2023 across more than 20 countries. An English translation was released in October, with a French version due this month.

The simple autobiographical account gives a voice and face to the swarms of anonymous gig workers who weave through China’s bustling cities day and night to deliver online orders, which account for a third of retail sales.

But as a delivery driver, Hu said he ‘always believed (he) was trash’.

‘It was through writing that I built recognition of my own worth,’ he told AFP near the flat he rents in Chengdu.

His story reflects China’s evolution. His parents worked their entire lives in state-owned enterprises. He entered a much more flexible job market in 1999 after a decade of reforms following the Cultural Revolution.

‘Before, technical schools guaranteed a job after graduation, but that was no longer the case for my generation,’ he said.

After a string of unstable jobs, Hu, like many, joined the gig economy in 2017.

He worked 12 hours a night in a huge parcel sorting centre in Guangdong, with a 30-minute break each shift and four days off per month.

‘I was a walking corpse with blurred vision and a wavering consciousness,’ said Hu, who would drink alcohol to sleep during the day.

But it was his account of working as a delivery driver in Beijing that moved readers.

At the time, Hu had no health insurance and no fixed salary. He calculated that at two yuan ($0.29) per delivery, he had to deliver a parcel every four minutes to earn a living. If his pace slowed, he would receive a call from from a company employee.

‘She would say: ‘You still have 60 parcels to deliver and you have 30 minutes left. What’s going on? Do you want to continue working here or not?’ he told AFP.

‘These rules lack humanity and rationality, and they oppress us every day.’

Laid off after his employer went bankrupt, Hu recounted his experience on social media platform Douban ‘without any particular goal’, while juggling odd jobs. A young publisher encouraged him to turn his posts into a book.

The voices of delivery drivers are rare in China, where the state strictly controls worker representation and public expression.

Delivery driver Chen Guojiang, who called online for workers’ rights, was imprisoned for several months in 2021, according to media reports and NGOs. He has since disappeared from social media.

Hu’s book passed the censors, with a few adaptations, sticking to social commentary and refraining from criticism.

But it has resonated like ‘very few other works’ with a generation facing job insecurity and increasing competition in the labour market, said academic Huang Ke, who wrote a thesis on China’s delivery drivers.

‘The number of graduates is increasing, but job opportunities are not keeping pace,’ he told AFP.

Following the book’s release, one Douban user said he understood the irritability of some delivery drivers: ‘You can’t expect someone to be kind and gentle when they find themselves in an environment of insecurity and exploitation.’

Faced with growing social awareness, authorities have introduced measures in recent years to improve the lives of delivery drivers.

But most of China’s 80 million gig workers have ‘no real access to labour law protections because of their ambiguous employment status,’ said Ou Lin, a law professor at Britain’s Lancaster University.

Now financially secure, Hu is inundated with requests for proofreading and advice from aspiring writers.

‘If I hadn’t published this book, it’s quite possible that I would still be delivering orders today,’ he said. ‘That’s how everyone survives.’

Hu said he would be happy if his book helped improve the situation of delivery drivers, but ‘from a social movement perspective, literature is not very effective’.

He wants to believe that, at the very least, ‘customers now say thank you more’ to delivery drivers.

title: Germany’s Merz, business groups hail EU-Mercosur deal
body:
German chancellor Friedrich Merz Friday hailed a ‘milestone’ after European Union countries approved a trade deal with the South American Mercosur bloc while business groups also welcomed the news.

‘The approval of the EU-Mercosur Agreement is a milestone in European trade policy and an important signal of our strategic sovereignty and capacity to act,’ Merz said, after a majority of the bloc’s members backed the controversial pact in a vote.

‘However, 25 years of negotiations were too long. Now it is important to conclude the next free trade agreements quickly.’

German finance minister Lars Klingbeil welcomed the deal as an important signal in support of free trade.

‘While others are closing themselves off and pursuing increasingly aggressive trade policies, we are focusing on new partnerships’.

The accord is deeply divisive -- while it was backed by business, it has been fiercely opposed by many European farmers, and the EU had to override opposition led by France to the pact.

Berlin has long been a vocal supporter of the deal which it believes will open up new markets for its export-dependent economy as it struggles to emerge from a long period of stagnation.

Germany’s VDA auto industry association welcomed the approval of the accord as ‘long overdue and very good news... especially for Germany as an exporting country’.

‘The EU-Mercosur agreement opens up considerable opportunities for the automotive industry,’ said the association’s boss Hildegard Mueller.

Auto parts shipped to Mercosur countries are currently subject to tariffs of up to 18 per cent while passengers cars face levies of up to 35 per cent, she said.

The VCI chemical industry federation hailed approval of the deal as a ‘good day for Europe’.

‘The EU is sending a strong signal in difficult times: Europe wants to help shape the future, not just stand by and watch,’ said the group’s chief Wolfgang Grosse Entrup.

title: Japan to test deep sea rare earth mining to cut China reliance
body:
Japan embarks Sunday on what it says is the world’s first bid to tap deep sea rare earths at a depth of 6,000 metres -- greater than the height of Mount Fuji -- to curb dependence on China.

A Japanese deep-sea scientific drilling boat called the Chikyu will set sail for the remote island of Minami Torishima in the Pacific, where surrounding waters are believed to contain a rich trove of valuable minerals.

The test cruise comes as China -- by far the world’s biggest supplier of rare earths -- ramps up pressure on its neighbour after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested in November that Tokyo may react militarily to an attack on Taiwan, which Beijing has vowed to seize control of by force if necessary.

Rare earths -- 17 metals difficult to extract from the Earth’s crust -- are used in everything from electric vehicles to hard drives, wind turbines and missiles.

The mission by the Chikyu is ‘a first step toward our country’s industrialisation of domestic rare earths’, the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC) said in a statement last month.

The agency touted the test as the world’s first at such depths.

The area around Minami Torishima, which is in Japan’s economic waters, is estimated to contain more than 16 million tons of rare earths, which the Nikkei business daily says is the third-largest reserve globally.

These rich deposits contain an estimated 730 years’ worth of dysprosium, used in high-strength magnets in phones and electric cars, and 780 years’ worth of yttrium, used in lasers, Nikkei said.

‘If Japan could successfully extract rare earths around Minami Torishima constantly, it will secure domestic supply chain for key industries,’ Takahiro Kamisuna, research associate at The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), told AFP.

‘Likewise, it will be a key strategic asset for Takaichi’s government to significantly reduce the supply chain dependence on China.’

Beijing has long used its dominance in rare earths for geopolitical leverage, including in its trade war with US President Donald Trump’s administration.

China accounts for almost two-thirds of rare earth mining production and 92 per cent of global refined output, according to the International Energy Agency.

Media reports this week said Beijing was delaying Japanese imports as well as rare-earth exports to Tokyo, as their two-month-old spat escalates.

China on Tuesday blocked exports to Japan of ‘dual-use’ items with potential military uses, fuelling worries in Japan that Beijing could choke supplies of rare earths, some of which are included in China’s list of dual-use goods.

An earlier spat in 2010 saw Japan move to lessen its dependence on Beijing for rare earths but more than 70 percent still come from China, according to Tokyo -- a stat it is looking to change.

During the test mission, the Chikyu will send a pipe beneath the water to ensure a ‘mining machine’ attached to its tip can reach the seabed and retrieve the rare earth-rich muds, JAMSTEC said.

Deep-sea mining has become a geopolitical flashpoint, with anxiety growing over a push by US president Donald Trump to fast-track the practice in international waters.

Environmental campaigners warn it threatens marine ecosystems and will disrupt the sea floor.

The International Seabed Authority (ISA), which has jurisdiction over the ocean floor outside national waters, is pushing for the adoption of a global code to regulate mining in the ocean depths.

title: Chinese villagers struggle for heat as gas subsidies fade
body:
Almost a decade after China began curbing coal burning to stop thick winter smog, villagers in northern Hebei province are struggling to afford their heating bills with most gas subsidies now phased out.

In 2017, Beijing mandated that dozens of northern areas wind down the use of coal-fired stoves in favour of electric and natural gas-powered systems.

China’s central government allocated funds to refit stoves, but subsidies faded after three years and additional aid has drastically declined, local media reported this week.

In Xushui, a district in Hebei roughly 100 kilometres (62 miles) outside Beijing, villagers told AFP they avoided turning on the heating because it drained their incomes.

‘Regular folks can’t afford it... Spending 1,000 yuan ($143) per month on heat -- no one can stand that,’ a resident in his 60s told AFP at a farmers’ market.

‘Everyone likes that (the air) is clean. There’s not one person that doesn’t like it,’ he said, asking not to be named for fear of ‘trouble’.

‘But... the cost of clean (air) is high,’ he added.

On the clear, sunny day AFP visited, the warmest temperature was just under six degrees Celsius, with lows of minus seven.

Restaurant worker Yin Chunlan said that her elderly in-laws need to pay up to 7,000 yuan per year to heat their six-room village home.

Yin, 48, lives in an apartment in town and says her annual bill is a third of that.

‘But it’s not the same in the village,’ she told AFP.

‘They have to set their heating much higher, and the temperature still isn’t as warm, so it wastes gas and wastes money.’

Yin’s in-laws often pile on extra blankets to stay warm.
