As Felani’s family marks her death anniversary with prayers and charity in Kurigram, their grief is sharpened by the knowledge that the Indian authorities have neither punished the perpetrators nor meaningfully acknowledged acts that violate law and agreements.

What is more upsetting is that border killings by Indian guards have not stopped or even slowed. Rights organisations show that border killings have continued unabated, with 2025 recording the highest number in five years. The Indian guards killed at least 34 Bangladeshis in 2025, Ain O Salish Kendra data show. Ordinary Indian citizens also reportedly killed at least 12 Bangladeshis along the border in the year. Unabated border killings only underscore the emptiness of repeated assurances from Indian authorities to end border killings. Equally disturbing is the routine justification that victims are ‘criminals’ or ‘smugglers.’ Cross-border smuggling is a shared problem involving actors on both sides and should be dealt with in accordance with bilateral agreements and the international law. None of the laws and agreements permits the use of lethal force. Reports of torture, custodial death and shootings of farmers working well inside the Bangladeshi territory further erode the credibility of such claims. The continued use of lethal weapons reflects a shoot-to-kill mindset that dishonours commitments made by India at various levels and violates international border management norms. The failure to ensure justice in emblematic cases like Felani’s has entrenched impunity, emboldening abuses and turning the border into one of the deadliest in the world.

A peaceful and humane border could have been achieved if justice had been ensured in earlier cases, beginning with Felani’s. Dhaka must, therefore, press more forcefully for a zero-killing policy and raise the issue at international forums as it is a violation of rights and international law. Indian authorities should deliver on their promises through independent investigation and accountability. Civil society on both sides should also intensify pressure.

title: Year of chances missed, hopes dashed in health sector
body:
THE year 2025 was a year of chances that the interim government, which assumed office on August 8, 2024 after the fall of the Awami League government three days earlier amid the July uprising, missed out on. This was also a year in which people’s hopes for improvement in health services were dashed. Both happened because of the indolence, if not unwillingness, of the government. But the government has produced several policy documents in the year for the health sector, which many believe, if implemented, would bring about greater good for citizens. However, the policies have largely remained confined to paper. The interim government, as part of reforms in state governance, set up a commission on health sector reforms on November 18, 2024. The commission submitted its recommendations to the government on May 4, 2025. The commission has recommended a separate health commission, increased budgetary allocation, an independent health cadre, an emergency healthcare and ambulance network, an effective referral system and a decentralised local health administration. Experts say that the situation in some areas of the health sector has, rather, worsened because of the suspension of the operational plan-based health services without any plan for an adequate alternative or transition.

No legal protection could be developed to safeguard people’s right to primary health care. In addition, out-of-pocket health expenditure has remained high, leaving patients to struggle to afford services despite government measures such as drug price controls and the appointment of some physicians and nurses. The government created 5,089 supernumerary positions for physicians and appointed some 3,000 physicians in the year, yet people are reported to have experienced no significant improvement in services delivery and they have, rather, continued to face the shortage of physicians, drugs and essential services. The appointment and promotion of physicians could not make any meaningful mark for patients as thousands of positions had already fallen vacant because of retirement, resignation and migration. Inadequate child vaccination programmes and the shortage of anti-venom drugs caused suffering in many areas. Health service delivery was repeatedly disrupted as physicians, nurses, healthcare assistants and medical technicians went on demonstrations throughout the year to push for their demands. The government in June 2024 suspended the operational plans under the Fourth Health, Population and Nutrition Sector Programme, which covered disease control, maternal and child health, vaccination, nutrition, family planning and other essential services. The supply of drugs to community clinics was disrupted, disproportionately affecting people, especially those suffering from hypertension and other non-communicable diseases, in remote areas.

The recommendation for policy shifts to promote domestic pharmaceutical and medical industries for greater self-reliance has not been implemented. All this tells a sorry tale of the health services in the year gone by and leaves a horde of issues for the next political government to attend to.

title: Triangles, tensions and tactical trade-offs
body:
FOR over a decade, global geopolitics has shifted from American unipolarity to a more complex multipolar world, characterised by a tripartite power dynamic involving the US, China, and Russia. This evolution, termed strategic triangularism, involves competitive, cooperative, and confrontational interactions among these powers that shape international order. While previously theoretical, this triangular world order is becoming more evident as the US wields its hegemonic authority, China expands its global influence, and Russia strengthens its strategic presence in Eurasia and the Middle East. These trends indicate a transition from a unipolar world to a more contested, multipolar landscape.

Scholars argue that US power has often been weaponised in ways that deepen global instability — from prolonged military engagements to unilateral sanctions and diplomatic coercion that undermine cooperative international frameworks. Meanwhile, China’s rise over the same period has been marked by extraordinary economic growth, expansive trade networks like the Belt and Road Initiative, and assertive regional policies that challenge US dominance in Asia and beyond. Russia, for its part, having suffered a post-Soviet contraction in influence, has in recent years reasserted its military and geopolitical weight, leveraging energy resources, strategic alignments, and military power to complicate Western policies and revitalise its standing as a global actor. Collectively, the interactions among these three powers do not merely generate competition; they are catalysing a new world order in which power is negotiated within an uneven but persistent triangle of influence and rivalry.

In this evolving triangular order, the United States has traditionally functioned as a system-shaping power. However, under Donald Trump, this dominance has become more overt and imperial, extending beyond traditional alliances. While still relying on NATO and longstanding partnerships, recent years have seen a shift toward coercive leadership, particularly amid increased pressure on European allies to increase defence spending, expand trade, and assert greater strategic autonomy. This approach has blurred the line between alliance management and domination, treating partners as instruments of US dominance rather than equal stakeholders. The renewed US interest in Greenland reflects a 19th-century geopolitical instinct resurfacing today. Scholarly analyses suggest this behaviour reinforces perceptions of US unilateralism and accelerates hedging among allies, many of whom are engaging China economically and accommodating Russia. Consequently, Washington’s actions paradoxically contribute to the emergence of a tripartite world order, defined by recalibrated loyalties and strategic calculations of allies.

China, for its part, leverages economic statecraft, investment networks across Africa, Latin America, and Central Asia, and a spectrum of ‘strategic partners’ that stop short of formal military pacts but create dependency and diplomatic alignment, as highlighted in analyses of Beijing’s global strategy. Russia — while economically constrained — has deepened security and energy ties with Beijing and cultivated alliances with Tehran, Minsk, and other states disaffected by Western policy, using these relationships to sustain its influence and disrupt Western cohesion. These interconnected alliances do not form rigid blocs akin to the Cold War but rather reflect a flexible, contested balance of influence in which allies help define each pole’s strategic capacity and the broader shape of the international order.

Each of the three powers defines the triangular world order through distinct strategic lenses shaped by historical experience, perceptions of power, and geopolitical interests. From the American perspective, the triangle is primarily considered a structure of strategic competition and containment, in which the United States must defend its global primacy against a rising China and a resurgent Russia.

China views the triangular order as both a consequence and an opportunity of its ascendance, interpreting US actions as attempts to preserve an outdated unipolar system and justifying China’s pursuit of an alternative order emphasising multipolarity, development cooperation, and regional leadership, championing ‘win-win cooperation’ and global governance reform.

Russia’s view is shaped by its resurgence in military and energy domains and a longstanding commitment to multipolarity that opposes US hegemony; Moscow sees the triangular order as a chance to reassert great-power status, resist Western encroachment (notably NATO expansion), and leverage its strategic partnership with China to balance American power without subsuming its autonomy. Collectively, these differing perspectives underscore that the triangle is not a symmetrical axis of united purpose but a dynamic, contested arena in which each power’s worldview and strategic priorities continually redefine what global order means to them.

The new world order is increasingly taking shape as a multipolar, fragmented system in which power is distributed among the United States, China, and Russia. Under this emerging architecture, the US envisions a bloc-orientated order driven by America First policies, economic and geopolitical competition, and a recalibration of alliances — essentially a return to a bloc logic reminiscent of the Cold War but with three rival poles rather than two. Trump’s administration has reinforced this shift by reviving Monroe Doctrine-like rhetoric and pressing for US dominance in the Western Hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific, while simultaneously challenging traditional institutions and alliances, underscoring a transactional, assertive US posture that reshapes old commitments and pressures partners to align more closely with American strategic interests.

Meanwhile, China and Russia are promoting multipolarity, inclusive governance, and alternatives to US-centric systems through institutions like the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and BRICS, appealing especially to states dissatisfied with Western dominance.

For the Global South, this means countries are no longer compelled to choose strictly between East and West but can leverage competition among great powers for infrastructure, investment, and diplomatic support — yet they also face heightened pressures to navigate a complex field of influence that can amplify dependency or domestic vulnerabilities.

For a country like Bangladesh, strategically positioned in the Indo-Pacific and a participant in major regional frameworks, the tripolar order presents opportunities for diversified partnerships, development financing, and geopolitical relevance, but also risks entanglement in great-power rivalries that could complicate its autonomy and economic priorities in areas such as trade, security cooperation, and infrastructure investment.

Drawing on recent scholarly debates on tripartite ordering and the erosion of the post-1945 system, the emerging triangular world order is likely to be less rule-bound and more power-negotiated, with profound consequences for the Global South. Analysts argue that a US–China–Russia triangle does not amount to a stable concert of powers but rather an uneven, competitive geometry in which norms are subordinated to interests and smaller states face intensified pressure to align, hedge, or absorb spillover shocks. In the Global South, this environment reduces the protective value of multilateralism while increasing exposure to sanctions, proxy rivalries, and economic coercion. Bangladesh exemplifies this dilemma: strategically located, economically integrated, and diplomatically active, yet structurally vulnerable to great-power competition in trade, security, climate finance, and humanitarian crises. The triangular order thus magnifies both opportunity and risk — offering leverage through diversification, while simultaneously narrowing the margin for error in foreign-policy choices.

The engagement strategies of the US, Russia, and China towards the Global South differ significantly. The United States remains the most coercive actor, using sanctions, conditional aid, and diplomatic pressure, prioritising a transactional approach over developmental support. In contrast, Russia acts as a more insulated power, engaging selectively through energy and arms without pushing for deep political changes in partner states. China has become a key partner for the Global South, offering infrastructure financing and development cooperation via initiatives like the Belt and Road, emphasising sovereignty and non-interference, which appeals to countries wary of Western conditionality. These distinct approaches create a hierarchy of risks and opportunities, prompting Global South states to navigate their relationships based on interests rather than ideology.

An emerging consensus in scholarship holds that the Global South must move beyond episodic hedging toward a deliberate, strategically disciplined multialignment that engages all three poles without sliding into dependency on any single power. For Bangladesh, this is not an abstract prescription but an immediate strategic necessity. Dhaka already balances US market access and security engagement, Chinese infrastructure financing and industrial investment, and Russian cooperation in energy and defence — most visibly in projects such as the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant, participation in the Belt and Road Initiative, and continued access to Western export markets. The challenge now is to convert this pragmatic balancing into a more institutionalised strategy — deepening economic and diplomatic ties across South and Southeast Asia, Africa, and the Middle East; strengthening regional mechanisms within BIMSTEC, the Indian Ocean Rim Association, and UN peacekeeping networks; and diversifying sources of finance, technology, and security cooperation to reduce exposure to sanctions pressure or geopolitical coercion. Equally critical is closer coordination with similarly positioned states — such as Vietnam, Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya — to amplify collective bargaining power on issues ranging from climate finance and labour migration to supply-chain resilience.

Cooperation among the Global South is no longer a matter of ideological solidarity but of strategic survival. In a world where power increasingly overrides principle, Bangladesh’s long-term autonomy will depend not on choosing sides, but on calibrated multialignment anchored in robust South–South collaboration and sustained national resilience.

Simon Mohsin is a political and international affairs analyst.

title: Law enforcers to remain deployed in Feb 8-14
body:
The Bangladesh government has decided to deploy the members of the law enforcement agencies across the country for a seven-day nationwide security operation from February 8 to February 14 to ensure that the 13th National Parliamentary Election and the referendum, scheduled for February 12, are conducted freely, fairly, and peacefully.

The home ministry has issued a circular with details stating that the deployment of law enforcement agencies across the country will take place in two phases.

Personnel already deployed during the first phase would continue their duties, while the second phase will focus on polling centres, with law enforcement officers serving for a total of seven days from February 8 to February 14.

This centre-based deployment will remain in effect from four days before the election to two days after the polls, with returning officers and police superintendents authorised to adjust personnel numbers according to local circumstances.

Although the home ministry circular was issued on Tuesday, it was made public on Wednesday.

It said that the personnel would be allocated based on the geographical location and significance of each polling centre,

The circular categorised polling centres as general or important in metropolitan, non-metropolitan, and special areas, including hill tracts and remote regions.

It said that the Armed Forces, Border Guard Bangladesh, Coast Guard, Rapid Action Battalion, police, APBn, and Ansar battalions would operate as mobile and strike forces to maintain law and order in election areas.

BGB, RAB, APBn, and Ansar battalions would carry out their duties at district, upazila, and police station levels, while the Coast Guard would be responsible for coastal areas.

According to the Election Commission, the current election has approximately 12.75 crore registered voters. Voting would take place across around 43,000 polling centres with nearly 2.6 lakh voting booths in 300 constituencies.

More than 8 lakh members of the law enforcement agencies will be deployed to ensure election security, with around 5.5 lakh to 6 lakh Ansar and Village Defence Party personnel assigned specifically to polling centres.

About 1.5 lakh police officers will also be engaged in election duties. The Armed Forces, mainly comprising army personnel, are expected to number around 90,000.

The home ministry circular said that in non-metropolitan areas, general centres would have two armed police officers, one armed Ansar section commander, one armed Ansar responsible for the presiding officer’s security, one armed assistant Ansar where available, 10 baton-wielding Ansar, including four women and six men, and one to two baton-wielding Village Defence Party members.

Important centres in these areas would have three armed police and one armed assistant Ansar section commander in addition to the standard complement of Ansar and VDP members.

In metropolitan areas, with general centres staffed by three armed police, one armed Ansar, one armed Ansar for presiding officer security, 10 baton-wielding Ansar, and an armed assistant Ansar section commander, where available.

Important metropolitan centres would have four armed police officers, one armed Ansar section commander, one assistant section commander, and one armed Ansar for presiding officer security.

Special areas, including hill tracts and other remote locations, would follow the staffing model of non-metropolitan centres, with two armed police officers at general centres and three at important centres, supported by similar numbers of Ansar and VDP members.

To address geographical challenges, the Air Force would provide helicopter support for the transportation of election officials and materials.

Mobile teams would act under the guidance of returning officers to ensure a rapid response to any incidents.

According to the circular, the armed forces will be deployed under the ‘in aid to civil power’ framework, assisting law enforcement in sensitive locations and supporting rapid response units as required.

Judicial magistrates would oversee the enforcement of the electoral code of conduct and conduct summary trials for violations, while executive magistrates would lead mobile and strike forces, coordinate operations among agencies, and maintain law and order across all polling areas.

Law and Order Coordination Cells would be established at the home ministry, returning officers’ offices, and local constituencies, staffed by representatives of each of the security agencies.

A dedicated 999 emergency team will operate alongside these cells to ensure rapid response to complaints, while the Election Commission Secretariat and local monitoring cells will continuously observe conditions and relay real-time updates to relevant authorities.

It said that modern technology had been integrated into the election security framework and all Ansar personnel deployed at polling centres would use the ‘Election Security 2026’ mobile application to report real-time updates to mobile or strike forces.

Police personnel assigned to sensitive centres would be equipped with body-worn cameras to enhance accountability.

Priority will be given to deploying trained female police and Ansar members in women’s polling centres to ensure safe and respectful conduct of the election.

Temporary restrictions on movement and campaigning have been imposed to maintain order. From midnight on February 11 to midnight on February 12, taxis, microbuses, pickups, and engine-driven boats would face movement restrictions, while motorcycles would be restricted from February 10 to February 13.

Public meetings, rallies, and processions are prohibited during the 48 hours preceding and following polling in accordance with the Representation of the People Order.

title: Immersive medical anatomy learning app VirtuED launched
body:
Deputy managing director of Labaid Sakif Shamim has officially inaugurated VirtuED, medical anatomy learning app, says a press release.

This launch marks the formal journey of VirtucareBD, an initiative dedicated to overcoming the long-standing limitations of the healthcare sector in Bangladesh by establishing a modern, technology-driven, and smart health system.

The platform aims to integrate world-class technologies such as Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), and Mixed Reality (MR) directly into mainstream medicine.

Additionally, VirtucareBD has introduced surgical simulation and virtual hospital concepts to make medical education and services more realistic and accessible.

VirtucareBD functions as a high-tech ecosystem that creates a bridge between traditional medical methods and modern science. Its methodology is not limited to theoretical education but provides support at every level of clinical practice. Through AR technology, doctors can now observe a patient’s complex internal structures in 3D before performing surgery.

This serves as a digital map for surgeons, reducing the possibility of errors and ensuring patient safety. Furthermore, VR creates an artificial environment where young physicians can practice complex medical procedures repeatedly without any risk.

As a result, the quality of patient care in hospitals increases significantly, and doctors can work with greater confidence.

The flagship component of this ecosystem, VirtuED, is Asia’s first immersive digital anatomy learning platform.

Through this app, medical students have the opportunity to learn complex human anatomy using AR, VR, and 3D visualisation.

VirtuED moves medical education beyond the limitations of textbooks to create an interactive and future-oriented learning experience.

During the inauguration, Sakif Shamim, the managing director of VirtucareBD and deputy managing director of Labaid, stated that this is not just a single technology initiative. Instead, it is a well-planned effort to establish scientific standards in the health sector by unifying global medical data, modern research, and future-ready technology. He further mentioned that the core philosophy and goal of VirtucareBD are to improve the quality of medical education, increase physician skills, and ensure patient safety through data-driven decisions, immersive simulation, and remote assistance.

The event was attended by renowned physicians from various Labaid Group institutions as well as prominent experts from leading hospitals across the country.

title: Bangladesh RMG exports lose ground in US, EU
body:
Bangladesh’s ready-made garment exports lost momentum in most major destinations in the first half (July–December) of the current financial year 2025–26 amid mounting domestic and global challenges.

During the first half of FY26, exporters grappled with domestic issues, including political tensions that weakened buyers’ confidence in Bangladeshi manufacturers.

Global pressures, including weak demand, economic slow down, tariff-related complications, and inflationary pressures, also weighed on export performance.

According to detailed country-wise export data from the Export Promotion Bureau, Bangladesh exported RMG items worth $19.37 billion in the first half of FY26, marking a 2.63 per cent decline from $19.88 billion earned in the same period of FY25.

The downturn was more pronounced in the United States, European Union, non-traditional markets, and other destinations, although shipments to the United Kingdom and Canada narrowly avoided negative growth.

Exporters reported that buyers had lost trust in the country’s administration, leading them to either adopt a cautious approach or redirect their orders to alternative sourcing destinations.

Fazlee Shamim Ehsan, executive president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association, said that Bangladesh’s export slowdown could not be attributed solely to the weak global economy.

‘Buyers lost confidence due to political instability. For example, during 2024–25, the government failed to control unrest in major RMG hubs, particularly Ashulia, which sent negative signals to buyers,’ he said.

As a result, buyers shifted orders to alternative sourcing countries, he added.

‘Although US tariffs affected Indian exports, when European buyers considered shifting orders from Bangladesh, they opted for India instead,’ he said.

During July–December of FY26, Bangladeshi exporters recorded a 4.41 per cent decline in shipments to the EU—the largest destination for Bangladesh’s apparel exports—to $9.46 billion, down from $9.87 billion in the same period of FY25.

Export earnings from the EU accounted for more than 48 per cent of Bangladesh’s total RMG export revenues during the period.

Exports to major EU countries such as Germany, France, Denmark, and Italy declined in the first half of FY26, although moderate growth was recorded in Spain, the Netherlands, and Poland.

After witnessing positive growth for the first five months, export earnings from the United States also slipped into negative territory, falling by 0.1 per cent to $3.83 billion in July–December FY26, compared with $3.84 billion in the same period of FY25.

The US, the largest single-country destination for Bangladeshi apparel, accounted for around 20 per cent of total RMG export earnings, according to EPB data compiled by the Bangladesh Apparel Exchange, a private initiative promoting the country’s apparel and textile industry.

Bangladesh earned $2.21 billion from the UK in the first six months of FY26, registering a marginal 2.13 per cent increase from $2.16 billion in the same period of FY25.

From Canada, RMG exports reached $671 million during the reporting period, up 4.66 per cent from $643 million in the corresponding period of the previous financial year.

Exports to Germany declined by 11.4 per cent to $2.19 billion in July–December FY26, compared with $2.47 billion in the same period of FY25, EPB data showed.

Shipments to France fell by 10.89 per cent to $972 million from $1.09 billion, while exports to Italy declined by 5.04 per cent to $733 million from $772 million during the same period.

However, exports to Spain stood at $1.8 billion, while shipments to the Netherlands and Poland amounted to $1.08 billion and $864 million, respectively, all of which posted low to moderate growth in the first half of FY26.

In the apparel trade, the US, Canada, the UK, and the EU are considered traditional markets, while other destinations are classified as non-traditional.

Major non-traditional markets include Japan, Australia, Russia, India, China, South Korea, the United Arab Emirates, Malaysia, Brazil, and Mexico.

Despite hope, export earnings from non-traditional markets have declined since October.

During July–December FY26, exports to non-traditional destinations fell by 5.52 per cent to $3.18 billion, compared with $3.37 billion in the same period of FY25.

Non-traditional markets accounted for 16.45 per cent of Bangladesh’s total RMG exports during the period.

Among these destinations, exports to Japan declined by 0.75 per cent to $598 million in the first half of FY26, down from $602 million in the same period of FY25.

Exports to Australia plunged by 12.44 per cent to $377 million, while shipments to India declined by 10.44 per cent to $337 million. Exports to Mexico fell sharply by 18.66 per cent to $150 million, EPB data showed.

RMG exports to other major non-traditional markets also recorded declines.

Exporters also said that the withdrawal of incentives and certain government policies adversely affected the sector, particularly small and medium-sized factories.

Regarding incentives, BKMEA president Mohammad Hatem said that China and India were aggressively offering significantly lower prices in European and other markets.

‘The Indian government has introduced new incentive packages to support its exporters, while Bangladesh has been gradually withdrawing cash incentives,’ he said.

Exporters said that the new US tariff regime has created significant disruptions in global trade and negatively affected Bangladesh’s exports to the US and other regions.

Mohiuddin Rubel, former director of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, said that global demand had weakened significantly, while Bangladesh’s concentration on basic, low-priced products limited its pricing flexibility.

He emphasised the need for product and market diversification, along with a transition to higher-value products, to remain competitive.

Professor Mustafizur Rahman, distinguished fellow of the Centre for Policy Dialogue, described the persistent decline in exports as a warning signal.

He cautioned that the coming months would be challenging due to LDC graduation and the scheduled national election, adding that Bangladesh might struggle to meet its export target for the current fiscal year.

He stressed that innovation, reduced lead times, lower costs of doing business, and product and market diversification were now essential.

‘We must roll out these policies now, as the time to keep them on the shelf has ended,’ he said.

Exporters also expressed optimism that exports could rebound from May or June if a fair election restores political stability and buyers’ confidence.

In FY25, the RMG sector earned $39.35 billion from global markets.

title: Forex market stable amid strong remittance inflows
body:
Bangladesh’s foreign exchange market stayed largely stable throughout 2025 amid strong inflows of remittance and steady export earnings.

Subdued business activity, cautious investment and slow credit growth kept import-related dollar demand low, helping the exchange rate remain steady.

The dollar traded close to Tk 122 for most of the year, showing little volatility compared with previous years.

Bangladesh Bank played a key role in maintaining stability, purchasing about $3.5 billion from commercial banks since July to prevent excessive appreciation of the taka and rebuild depleted reserves.

The intervention began after the dollar briefly weakened to Tk 119.5 on July 12. Since then, the rate has stayed close to Tk 123 per dollar, helping exporters plan better and discouraging speculative movements in the currency market.

The stability marked a clear shift from earlier trends. The dollar stood at Tk 120 in December 2024, Tk 110 in December 2023, Tk 106 in June 2023 and Tk 93.45 in June 2022, showing that the pace of depreciation slowed sharply in 2025.

Bankers said that the stable exchange rate reduced uncertainty for traders and exporters, while discouraging speculative currency movements.

Zahid Hussain, former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office, told New Age that the foreign exchange market was the most improved and comfortable segment of the economy in 2025.

He said that the key indicators of this stability were a notable rise in foreign exchange reserves and a largely stable dollar rate throughout the year.

The current account also remained broadly balanced, mainly because of strong remittance inflows, he added.

Zahid noted that although external debt servicing increased, overall current account payments did not rise significantly, helping keep transactions in balance.

He cautioned, however, that two risks remain. Export growth has turned negative, and imports could rise once political uncertainty eases after the national election scheduled for February 12, 2026. These factors could put fresh pressure on the balance of payments, he said.

Even so, Zahid said that the current level of reserves should be sufficient to absorb such pressures in the near term.

As of January 1, Bangladesh’s gross foreign exchange reserves rose to about $33.18 billion, while reserves measured under the IMF’s BPM6 framework stood at $28.51 billion. At the end of 2024, reserves were significantly lower at $26.21 billion under the conventional method and $21.4 billion under BPM6.

At the beginning of 2024, reserves had fallen close to $18 billion after heavy dollar sales to pay for fuel, fertiliser and food imports amid global price shocks and domestic supply pressure.

Commercial banks played a key role in the turnaround.

With the exchange rate largely flat and the policy rate held at a tight 10 per cent, banks found it less attractive to hold dollars. Instead, they sold foreign currency to the central bank and invested in treasury bills and Bangladesh Bank facilities, which offered higher and more predictable returns.

Remittances provided the strongest support to the forex market.

Bangladesh received $32.82 billion in remittances in calendar year 2025, up sharply from $26.9 billion in 2024.

In the first six months of FY26, remittance inflows rose by 18.1 per cent to $16.26 billion.

Bankers attributed the surge to stricter action against hundi networks, improved monitoring of financial flows and a more market-aligned exchange rate.

Since January 2022, remittances sent through banks have been eligible for a 2.5 per cent cash incentive, making official transfers more attractive for migrant workers, particularly in the Middle East and Southeast Asia.

The political transition on August 5, 2024 further strengthened enforcement against money laundering and illegal transfers, narrowing the gap between official and open-market rates and reducing the space for hundi operations.

Export earnings remained steady but showed limited growth.

Exports during July–December of FY26 stood at $23.99 billion, slightly lower than a year earlier, reflecting weak global demand and slow diversification.

Imports, however, rose faster, widening the trade gap and keeping the current account in deficit at $749 million in July–October.

Despite this, the overall balance of payments turned positive, supported by a $2.17 billion surplus in the financial account.

title: NBR introduces online VAT refund system
body:
The National Board of Revenue on Wednesday launched an automated online Value Added Tax refund system, allowing refunds to be transferred directly to taxpayers’ bank accounts instantly.

The move would ease the long-standing hassles that taxpayers, especially businesses, face in claiming refunds, said the NBR authority at the launching event at the NBR Bhaban.

During the event, three business entities received their VAT refunds of worth Tk 45.35 lakh instantly through the automated system from three Dhaka-based VAT commissionerates, inaugurated by NBR chairman Abdur Rahman Khan.

‘We have initially replicated the existing manual refund procedure into an electronic format to ensure continuity, with plans to further simplify the process through legal and regulatory amendments if needed,’ said Abdur Rahman Khan.

He also said they first converted the existing manual process into an electronic system.

‘Once the system is fully operational, we will review whether the process needs further simplification. If necessary, we would amend the law and rules,’ he added.

Of 124 applications, the entire process for 4 had been completed in advance. Their refunds were finalised through the e-VAT system during the launch.

According to the NBR, it has added a new refund module to the e-VAT system to facilitate this. Under this arrangement, the system would connect with the Finance Division’s iBAS++ platform, enabling the direct transfer of refund amounts to taxpayers’ designated bank accounts through Bangladesh Bank’s BEFTN system.

Moreover, taxpayers could apply for refunds through their monthly VAT returns under the online refund mechanism.

After the relevant VAT commissionerate processes the application, the taxpayer’s bank information will be verified, and the refundable amount will then be automatically transferred to the taxpayer’s bank account.

The entire automated verification process involving the Bangladesh Bank and commercial banks would take about 30 minutes.

During the launch, Amber Group received its VAT refunds instantly.

After receiving the refund, Md Imran Hossain, chief financial officer of Amber Group, said that the system is a groundbreaking initiative of the NBR.

‘For those of us in the textile business, this is very important. Previously, the process was time-consuming and complicated. The system launched today is much more transparent and simpler,’ he added.

The initiative would enable them to receive refunds easily, he added, expressing optimism that the NBR would continue to take such industry-friendly and taxpayer-friendly initiatives.

Responding a question, NBR chairman said that the total amount of pending VAT and income tax refunds would be around Tk 4,000 crore in total, with VAT refunds accounting for about Tk 1,500 crore.

According to NBR data shared at the event, 115 refund applications have been submitted through the system so far, totaling Tk 124.49 crore.

‘We want to make the refund process completely transparent so that there is no scope for any irregularities,’ he added, saying that getting refunds is a right of the taxpayers as they have paid this money.

He also said that many taxpayers paid the advance VAT by taking high-interest bank loans, and that it has remained with the government for a long time.

The government is not paying them the interest, he added, noting that if the taxpayers still have to run from pillar to post to get their refunds, it would not be fair treatment.

‘If we earn Tk 4 lakh crore in revenue and need to return Tk 4,000 crore as refunds through a transparent process, there is nothing wrong with that,’ he added.

He also said that refunds are part of the system worldwide, and that Bangladesh should follow that principle.

title: Banks allowed to lend despite housing loan defaults
body:
Bangladesh Bank has allowed banks to continue disbursing housing loans even if their housing portfolios carry classified loans, setting revised loan ceilings that depend on the level of loan defaults in the sector.

In a circular issued on Tuesday, the central bank amended the Prudential Regulations for Consumer Financing, easing earlier restrictions that effectively limited housing loan disbursement once default levels rose.

The new rules allow banks to lend for housing within defined caps while directly linking lending limits to the quality of their housing loan portfolios.

Under the revised framework, banks with classified housing loans of up to 5 per cent of their total outstanding housing finance may sanction loans of up to Tk 4 crore per borrower.

If classified loans exceed 5 per cent but remain within 10 per cent, the maximum loan size will be Tk 3 crore.

For banks where classified housing loans cross 10 per cent, the ceiling will be reduced to Tk 2 crore.

The central bank said that the revision reflects rising construction costs and higher housing prices, particularly in major cities, which have made earlier loan limits outdated.

By allowing lending to continue under tighter caps instead of imposing a blanket restriction, Bangladesh Bank aims to support the housing sector while maintaining discipline in credit risk management.

Banks must ensure a maximum debt-to-equity ratio of 70:30, meaning borrowers must finance at least 30 per cent of the housing cost from their own sources.

Lenders must also verify that borrowers have adequate and stable income to meet repayment obligations.

The revised structure creates incentives for banks to reduce classified loans, as better portfolio quality allows higher lending limits.

Bangladesh Bank issued the directive under the Bank Company Act, 1991, and said all other consumer financing rules will remain unchanged.

title: December PMI witnesses a slight improvement
body:
The country’s overall Purchasing Managers’ Index in December witnessed a slight improvement by 0.2 points to 54.2 from the previous month, indicating a slightly faster pace of expansion, according to the latest PMI report published jointly by the Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce and Industry and Policy Exchange Bangladesh.

The PMI of Bangladesh was 54 points in October, a drastic 7.8-point decline from October’s 61.8 points, the report published on Wednesday said.

This latest slight improvement in December was driven by continued growth in the agriculture, manufacturing, and services sectors.

The agriculture sector recorded its fourth consecutive month of expansion, and at a faster rate.

The sector posted stronger expansion in the indexes of new business, business activity, employment, and input costs, while the order backlogs index showed a faster rate of contraction.

The manufacturing sector remained in expansion for the 16th consecutive month, although at a slightly slower pace, the report added.

Expansion was recorded across key indicators, including new orders, new exports, factory output, input purchases, imports, input prices, employment, and supplier deliveries.

The finished goods index returned to expansion, while the order backlogs index registered a slower rate of contraction.

However, the construction sector reverted to a marginal contraction after three consecutive months of expansion.

The sector posted a faster contraction rate for the new business index, while slower rates of expansion for the indexes of construction activity and employment, but a slightly quicker expansion rate for the input costs index.

The order backlogs index continued to contract, marking its fifth consecutive month of contraction, though at a slower rate.

The services sector recorded its 15th consecutive month of expansion, and at a slightly faster pace.

The sector posted expansion readings for the employment and input cost indexes.

However, contraction readings were recorded for the indexes of new business, business activity, and order backlogs.

Business sentiment remained subdued amid political uncertainty, a seasonal slowdown in demand, rising production costs, price instability, and weak sales. However, many respondents expect a gradual improvement from early next year.

In terms of the future business index, slower expansion was recorded across the key indexes of agriculture, manufacturing, construction, and services.

M Masrur Reaz, chairman and CEO of the Policy Exchange Bangladesh, said that the latest PMI readings indicated a marginal expansion of the economy, driven by strong agricultural sector performance.

‘Manufacturing sector experienced second straight month of slowdown, while the construction sector reverted to contraction,’ he added.

He also said that the future business index, however, remained in expansion across all key sectors of the economy, suggesting sustained optimism and continued growth momentum post-elections.

According to the MCCI and PEB, they developed the PMI with support from the UK government and technical assistance from the Singapore Institute of Purchasing and Materials Management.

PMI is a survey-based indicator of a sector or country’s business conditions, with monthly surveys that ask respondents to report changes in each variable compared to the prior month.

The Bangladesh PMI is designed to provide timely and reliable insights into the country’s economic conditions to support decision-making by businesses, investors, and policymakers.

A PMI reading above 50 indicates that the sector or economy is generally ‘expanding’, where 50 indicates ‘no change’ and below 50 indicates ‘contraction.’

title: US corn shipment arrives at Ctg port after 8 years
body:
The United States embassy in Dhaka on Wednesday welcomed the arrival of the first shipment of US corn to Bangladesh since 2018 at Chattogram port.

Unloading of the consignment started at about 11:20am at a Karnaphuli river ghat beside the port’s water transport licence office in the Sadarghat area in city.

The shipment contains 57,855 tonnes of yellow corn harvested in North and South Dakota and Minnesota in the 2025-26 crop year and shipped from Vancouver, Washington, the embassy said.

The consignment marks the first opportunity in eight years for Bangladeshi feed millers to use US corn as a source of animal nutrition.

US embassy Dhaka agricultural attaché Erin Covert visited the port to greet the vessel along with a consortium of buyers from three major feed milling companies Nahar Agro Group, Paragon Group and Nourish Poultry and Hatchery Limited.

At the event, Erin Covert said, ‘Our office is responsible for not only promoting American farm product exports, but also understanding better agricultural production in Bangladesh and how we can also work together in trade partnerships between businesses in the United States and businesses in Bangladesh.’

An official of the United Grain Corporation, a major US grain exporter, said, ‘We are honored to be a part of the first shipment of United States corn to Bangladesh in eight years. We appreciate the work of all those involved in making this possible and look forward to supplying Bangladesh with U.S. grains for years to come.’

Three Bangladeshi animal feed producers imported the corn. Nahar Agro Group brought in 10,000 tonnes, Paragon Group 19,000 tonnes and Nourish Poultry and Hatchery Limited 29,000 tonnes.

The corn arrived off Kutubdia on December 31 aboard a vessel named MV Beltokyo. From there, the cargo was sent on smaller lighter vessels to different destinations in Chattogram, Narayanganj and Noapara.

At Wednesday’s event, unloading was inaugurated from a lighter vessel carrying about 2,500 tonnes of corn.

title: BB caps passport endorsement fee at Tk 300
body:
The Bangladesh Bank has capped the passport endorsement fee charged by licensed money exchange houses at Tk 300 per passport, aiming to curb arbitrary charges and protect outbound travellers.

In a circular issued on Wednesday, the central bank said that money changers might not charge more than Tk 300 for endorsing an outgoing passenger’s passport, regardless of the amount of foreign currency sold.

Under existing rules, licensed money changers are allowed to sell foreign currency notes, coins and travellers’ cheques to Bangladeshi residents against their annual private travel entitlement.

Each transaction must be endorsed in the traveller’s passport and air ticket, where applicable, with the seal and signature of an authorised official.

The circular requires money changers to clearly display the Tk 300 endorsement fee at a prominent place in their business premises.

They must also issue a written receipt for the fee and maintain proper records of all such collections.

title: Two killed, 30 injured in clashes during protests in Iran: local media
body:
Clashes in southwest Iran on Wednesday killed two people and wounded 30, the Fars news agency said on the 11th day of a wave of protests in the Islamic republic.

Fars reported that shopkeepers were protesting in Lordergan when ‘rioters began throwing stones at the police’.

‘Among them, there were individuals with military and hunting weapons who suddenly opened fire on the police,’ Fars added, without specifying whether those killed were police officers or protesters.

title: BSEC, BMBA to work for market dev
body:
The Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission and the newly elected executive committee of the Bangladesh Merchant Bankers Association have committed to work together in enhancing the country’s capital market.

During a courtesy meeting held on Wednesday at the BSEC building at Agargaon in the capital, leaders from both organisations discussed strategic measures to strengthen the market’s foundation, said a press release.

Bringing quality companies to the market, BSEC chairman Khondoker Rashed Maqsood emphasised that the primary responsibilities of merchant banks included issue management, underwriting and portfolio management.

He noted that the recently gazetted and updated IPO rules had created significant opportunities to bring reputable and high-performing companies into the capital market.

The chairman expressed BSEC’s positive attitude toward assisting the listing of quality firms and urged BMBA members and issue managers to take the lead in this initiative.

He stated that BSEC would provide all necessary support to ensure that the market attracts companies that inspire investor confidence.

The discussion also focused on the need for merchant banks to enhance their capabilities in capital formation, portfolio management and corporate advisory services.

Khondoker highlighted that improvements in the efficiency, capacity, and ethics of merchant banks would naturally make the capital market more attractive to investors and other stakeholders.

BSEC commissioner Farzana Lalarukh addressed the importance of digital transparency, suggesting that every merchant bank and their association should maintain informative web pages and web portals.

She noted that providing authentic and detailed information through these platforms is essential for creating awareness among investors and preparing them to participate more effectively in the market.

Senior officials in attendance included BSEC commissioners Md Mohsin Chowdhury, Md Ali Akbar, Farzana Lalarukh and Md Saifuddin, along with executive directors and other senior officials.

The BMBA delegation was led by its president Iftekhar Alam and included general secretary Sumit Poddar, vice-president Md. Monirul Haque, treasurer Syed Rashed Hussain and executive members Gazi Mohammad Tareq, Suman Kumar Kundu and Md. Sohel Haque.

title: China launches anti-dumping probe into Japan chipmaking chemical
body:
China on Wednesday announced an anti-dumping probe into imports from Japan of a key chemical used in making semiconductors, a day after it banned the export to the country of goods with potential military uses.

The commerce ministry in Beijing said that ‘from 2022 to 2024, the quantity of dichlorosilane imported from Japan generally increased, while the price cumulatively decreased by 31 per cent’.

‘The dumping of imported products from Japan has damaged the production and operation of domestic industries,’ it said in a statement.

Japan is a major global supplier of dichlorosilane and the probe comes at a time of rising diplomatic tensions between the Asian giants.

China has ramped up pressure on its neighbour after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested in November that Tokyo may react militarily to an attack on Taiwan, which Beijing has vowed to seize control of by force if necessary.

China’s foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a news conference Wednesday that Takaichi’s ‘erroneous remarks regarding Taiwan... blatantly interfere in China’s internal affairs, and threaten military force against China’.

China on Tuesday blocked exports to Japan of ‘dual-use’ items with potential military uses.

While the export ban statement did not mention specific items, it has fuelled worries in Japan that Beijing may choke supplies of vital rare earth minerals, some of which are included in China’s list of dual-use goods.

China is by far the world’s biggest supplier of rare earths, which are crucial for a range of tech products from smartphones to fighter jets.

Masaaki Kanai, the top official in Japan’s foreign ministry for Asia-Pacific affairs, ‘strongly protested and demanded the withdrawal of these measures’.

Kanai said the bans ‘deviate significantly from international practice, is absolutely unacceptable and deeply regrettable’.

More than 70 per cent of Japan’s rare earth imports are from China, according to the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy.

That is in spite of Tokyo’s efforts to diversify supplies following a 2010 row that saw Beijing temporarily cut off shipments of the minerals to Japan.

Global risk consultancy Teneo said the ambiguous wording of the Chinese statement may be intended to press Takaichi to take a more conciliatory stance towards Beijing.

‘The brief statement by China’s commerce ministry is vague, and the impact of the new measures could range from almost entirely symbolic to highly disruptive,’ it said.

‘By triggering concern in Japan about the ongoing availability of critical Chinese industrial inputs, the announcement puts immediate pressure on Takaichi to offer concessions.’

Takahide Kiuchi, executive economist at Nomura Research Institute, said the impact on the Japanese economy would be ‘extremely severe’ if China included rare earths in export controls.

He estimated that a three-month ban could cost Japan 660 billion yen ($4.2 billion).

‘Particularly for rare earths like dysprosium and terbium, which are auxiliary materials for neodymium magnets used in EV (electric vehicle) motors, Japan is said to depend almost 100 per cent on China,’ he added.

Japan’s top government spokesman Minoru Kihara declined Wednesday to comment on the impact on Japan’s industries, citing ‘the numerous unclear points... including the scope of the measures’.

title: Islami Bank holds board meeting
body:
Islami Bank Bangladesh PLC on Wednesday held a meeting of the board of directors, said a press release.

Chairman M Zubaidur Rahman presided over the meeting held at Islami Bank Tower.

Among others, executive committee chairman Mohammad Khurshid Wahab, audit committee chairman Md Abdus Salam, risk management committee chairman M Masud Rahman and independent director Md Abdul Jalil were present.

Managing director Md Omar Faruk Khan and company secretary Md Habibur Rahman also attended the meeting.

title: SBAC Bank signs start-up financing deal with BB
body:
SBAC Bank PLC on Tuesday signed an agreement to participate in the Bangladesh Bank’s Start-up Refinance Fund of Tk 500 crore to facilitate innovation and development of new entrepreneurs, said a press release.

SBAC Bank managing director and chief executive officer SM Mainul

Kabir and BB’s SME and Special Programmes Department director Nawshad Mustafa signed the agreement at Jahangir Alam Conference Hall of the central bank on the day.

BB deputy governor Nurun Nahar oversaw the signing ceremony.

Among others, BB executive director Husne Ara Shikha, SBAC Bank deputy managing director Md Altaf Hossain Bhuyan and EVP and credit division head Md Abdul Mannan were present.

title: BSCL discusses strategic directions in coming years
body:
Bangladesh Satellite Company Limited organised a dialogue titled ‘Strategic Directions for BSCL in the Coming Years,’ said a press release.

The dialogue took place on Tuesday at Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel in the capital, where in-depth discussions were held on Bangladesh’s future direction in the satellite and space sector.

Adviser on environment, forest and climate change, water resources, and information and broadcasting Syeda Rizwana Hasan attended the event as chief guest.

BSCL chairman and secretary of the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications Abdun Naser Khan chaired the event.

Rizwana Hasan said that expanding the use of satellite technology in ensuring good governance, natural resource management and disaster response would deliver real benefits.

This would help ensure accountability, reduce corruption, and curb crime, she said adding that the multidimensional use of satellite technology was now a necessity of the time.

She further stated that satellites were essential for national security, capacity building, water resource management, and urban planning. In this regard, she stressed the need to further enhance the capacity of BSCL and called for increased coordination among relevant ministries.

Faiz Ahmad Taiyeb, special assistant to the chief adviser for the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology, congratulated BSCL for becoming a profitable company for the first time since its establishment. He said that through Earth Observation Satellites, BSCL would be able to address specific challenges faced by various government ministries.

Effective applications are possible particularly in agriculture, disaster management, weather forecasting, and the forestry sector, he said that, emphasising identifying problems through technology and finding practical solutions.

Abdun Naser Khan said that BSCL was working with new technologies in the satellite industry.

In today’s world, satellite technology is being used to solve a wide range of problems, and BSCL will also work in the coming years to diversify satellite technologies to address various challenges, he said.

Abu Taher Md Jaber, secretary of the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, said that there were currently around 30,000 fishing boats, which are difficult to track. If these boats can be tracked at an affordable cost, the safety of fishermen can be ensured, he said.

Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, said that remote sensing was a highly important sector. Joint space-based research activities will be conducted with BSCL for research and innovation.

He expressed optimism that within the next ten years, Bangladesh would be able to establish a visible position in the global space industry.

Md Emdad Ullah Mian, secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture, said that there was a 25-year long-term plan for the agriculture sector. To ensure food security, satellite technology will be used to determine crop production levels, provide weather forecasts, and analyze land use in hilly regions, he said.

The keynote paper was presented by Md Imadur Rahman, managing director and chief executive officer of BSCL.

At the dialogue, Rear Admiral (retired) Abul Kalam Azad spoke on the topic ‘Blue Economy: What BSCL Can Do for Bangladesh?’.

Additionally, Saifur Rahman Bakul, professor, Department of Aerospace Engineering at Bangladesh Aerospace University, spoke on ‘How Can Bangladesh Be at the Forefront of the Space Industry?’.

Speakers at the event provided strategic insights on satellite technology, the blue economy, and Bangladesh’s potential in the space industry, highlighting the crucial and strategic role of BSCL in these sectors.

title: PRAN rolls out special offers at DITF
body:
PRAN is participating in the 30th Dhaka International Trade Fair 2026 in Purbachal, with a wide range of special offers and discounts, said a press release.

The food processor is showcasing more than 1,000 diverse products across 10 pavilions and stalls.

On the occasion of the fair, PRAN is offering discounts of up to 33 per cent. The company has also introduced more than 100 new products at the fair.

A major attraction at the fair is pavilion no 10 of PRAN’s popular noodles brand ‘Mr. Noodles’. The Korean styled pavilion is offering special offers on 10 different noodle flavours.

PRAN’s popular biscuit brand ‘Bisk Club’, has set up a pavilion near the right side of the fair entrance, drawing significant attention from visitors. The pavilion features a wide range of biscuit and bakery products from the ‘All Time’ brand.

In addition, visitors can enjoy a variety of food items at attractive prices at the stalls of PRAN’s popular fast-food brands ‘Tasty Treat’ and ‘Fry Bucket’, sweet brand ‘Mithai’, and frozen-food brand ‘Jhotpot’.

Commenting on the initiative, Md Ali Hasan, senior general manager (marketing) at PRAN said, ‘To ensure that visitors can explore most of our products under one roof, we have set up a premier pavilion named ‘PRAN’. This spacious 2,500-square feet pavilion, located just behind the main building on the northern side of the fairground, is showcasing more than 1,000 products. On the occasion of the fair, visitors can purchase all PRAN products from this pavilion with a minimum discount of 10 per cent.’

Kamruzzaman Kamal, marketing director at PRAN-RFL group said, ‘Trade fair is an excellent platform to showcase new products and services to consumers. This year we have participated with a diverse range of products tailored to customer demand, and we are receiving a very positive response due to the special offers and packages.’

title: Sony Home Theatre Experience Centre launched
body:
Smart Technologies (BD) Limited, known as Sony-Smart, the official distributor of Japanese world-renowned brand Sony in Bangladesh, on Tuesday set up ‘Sony Home Theatre Experience Centre’ at Uttara in the capital, said a press release.

Sony International Bangladesh Branch head Joshua Quek, Bashundhara City Development Limited deputy managing director Captain (retired) Shaikh Ehsan Reza and Sony-Smart director Md Tanvir Hossain inaugurated the centre.

Among others, Sony-Smart sales head and general manager Md Sarwar Jahan Chowdhury, marketing head and deputy general manager Azad Rahman, employees of various levels of Sony-Smart and journalists from various media were present.

Marking the occasion of the inauguration of the Sony Home Theatre Experience Centre, Sony’s 75-inch TV is made available for Tk 1,62,500, along with a cash voucher worth Tk 1,62,500 for Gold’s Gym admission.

In addition, Sony’s sound system Bar 6 is available for just Tk 49,900. Only the first 30 buyers can enjoy these benefits when shopping from Sony-Smart Uttara showroom from January 6 to 8.

Sony-Smart also launched its New Year campaign on Tuesday with the title ‘Mind blowing Deals, Unbeatable Price’.

As a part of this campaign customers of Sony TVs of various sizes are getting attractive cash vouchers that can be used towards Gold’s Gym admission. There is a cash voucher of Tk 2.5 lakh for 98 and 85 inch TVs, Tk 1,62,500 for 75 inch TVs and Tk 1,55,000 for 65 and 55 inch TVs.

Additionally, under this New Year offer, buyers of Sony TVs of various sizes are getting special prices, digital warranties, and the convenience of purchasing products in interest-free installments using cards from various banks.

title: NRBC Bank celebrates new year 2026
body:
NRBC Bank has recently celebrated the arrival of the English new year 2026 with a modest ceremony at the bank’s headquarters, said a press release.

Chairman Md Ali Hossain Prodhania was present as chief guest.

Managing director and chief executive officer Md Touhidul Alam Khan and deputy managing director and COO Mohammad Abdul Qaium Khan, along with divisional heads were present in the ceremony.

Md Ali Hossain Prodhania stated that in 2025, the bank had seen significant growth in deposits, loans, recovery of non-performing loans, treasury operations, and remittances.

He highlighted that the bank has taken various initiatives, including forensic audits, to establish good governance in the past year.

This year, greater emphasis will be placed on financing the small and medium-sized enterprise sector, which plays a crucial role in job creation, entrepreneurial development, and achieving national economic growth milestones, he said.

He expressed optimism that in the new year, through renewed efforts and by leveraging opportunities and potential, the bank would achieve even better results.

title: Tally authorised NIT Creative Solutions opens office in Bogura
body:
Tally’s authorised partner, NIT Creative Solutions, inaugurated its new office in Bogura with a formal launch event held on Sunday at TMSS Community Centre, Nawab Bari in Bogura, said a press release.

The event marked a significant milestone in strengthening Tally’s outreach and support for the MSME ecosystem in the region and was organized with the support and active collaboration of the Bogura Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

The launch event was graced by Projit Kumar Das, country manager – Tally Bangladesh, and Mohammad Ishaq Ali, owner of NIT Creative Solutions, alongside representatives from the Bogura Chamber of Commerce and Industry, local business owners, professionals and key stakeholders.

During the session, speakers highlighted the growing importance of digital business management solutions and elaborated on the key features and benefits of TallyPrime, emphasising its ability to help businesses streamline operations, maintain statutory compliance, and drive sustainable growth in an increasingly digital economy.

A live demonstration of the newly launched TallyPrime Version 7.0 was also conducted, showcasing advanced capabilities such as Auto Backup and Smart Search.

Projit Kumar Das stated, ‘In today’s rapidly evolving digital landscape, businesses require solutions that are simple, reliable, and future-ready. TallyPrime is designed to empower MSMEs by simplifying accounting, compliance, and operational management, allowing entrepreneurs to focus on growth with confidence.’

Sharing his vision for the new office, Mohammad Ishaq Ali said, ‘With the launch of our Bogura office and the valuable support of the Bogura Chamber of Commerce & Industry, we aim to provide local businesses with timely guidance, reliable implementation, and continuous support for TallyPrime, enabling them to successfully adopt and benefit from digital business practices.’

NIT Creative Solutions will operate from its new office located at Moloya Bhaban, 484/A Raibahadur Road, Jaleswaritola in Bogura.

title: BRAC Bank introduces scholarship for employees’ children with disabilities
body:
BRAC Bank has introduced a scholarship programme to support the education of employees’ children with disabilities, reinforcing its commitment to inclusion, dignity and equal opportunity, said a press release.

Under the scholarship programme, BRAC Bank will provide monthly financial assistance for each eligible child. The programme was developed following an internal survey to identify employees with children with disabilities, so that support reaches those who need it most.

This scholarship is part of BRAC Bank’s Corporate Social Responsibility strategy, designed to create meaningful and lasting impact within the organisation and the wider community. It supports diversity and inclusion by fostering an equitable environment for employee well-being.

Tareq Refat Ullah Khan, managing director and chief executive officer of BRAC Bank, said, ‘This scholarship is a small but genuine step toward easing the educational path for children with disabilities and supporting our colleagues who face additional challenges every day. Our responsibility as an organisation extends beyond profits. It is about fostering a workplace and society where everyone has the chance to succeed.’

title: US seizes Russia-flagged oil tanker in North Atlantic
body:
The United States seized a Russian-flagged oil tanker in the North Atlantic on Wednesday after pursuing it from off the coast of Venezuela, in an operation condemned by Moscow.

Washington says the tanker is part of a so-called shadow fleet that carries oil for countries such as Venezuela, Russia and Iran in violation of US sanctions, and seized it despite the ship being escorted by the Russian navy.

The vessel had thwarted an earlier attempt to board it last month near Venezuela, where a US raid on Saturday toppled the country’s authoritarian president, Nicolas Maduro.

‘The vessel was seized in the North Atlantic pursuant to a warrant issued by a US federal court,’ US European Command, which oversees American forces in the region, said in a statement on X.

After the operation, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth posted that the US blockade on Venezuelan oil was in full effect ‘anywhere in the world.’

Russia’s Transport Ministry slammed the seizure, saying ‘freedom of navigation applies in waters on the high seas, and no state has the right to use force against vessels duly registered under the jurisdiction of other states.’

The US military also announced a second sanctioned tanker ship had been seized in the Caribbean Sea.

Homeland Security chief Kristi Noem posted on X that both vessels ‘were either last docked in Venezuela or en route to it,’ and included a video of US forces roping down from a helicopter onto an unidentified ship and proceeding toward the bridge with weapons ready.

Last weekend, US special forces snatched Maduro and his wife from Caracas and flew them to New York to face trial on drug charges.

Since then, President Donald Trump has said that the United States will ‘run’ Venezuela and US companies will control its critical oil industry.

In Caracas, after several days of shuttered shops and intermittent public transport, the capital’s streets were again busy Wednesday with pedestrians, street vendors, cars and motorbikes.

The North Atlantic operation came despite Russia reportedly sending a submarine and other naval assets to escort the empty tanker and saying the vessel was sailing under the Russian flag.

The vessel, formerly known as the Bella-1, in recent weeks switched its registration to Russia, changed its name to the Marinera and the tanker’s crew reportedly painted a Russian flag on the tanker.

It had been en route to Venezuela before it evaded the US blockade, and has been under US sanctions since 2024 over alleged ties to Iran and Hezbollah.

Trump said Tuesday that Venezuela said 30-50 million barrels of ‘high‑quality, sanctioned’ Venezuelan crude will be shipped to US ports, with the revenue -- perhaps more than $2 billion at current market prices -- placed under his personal control.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright added Wednesday that Washington will control sales of Venezuelan oil ‘indefinitely.’

It was not clear whether Venezuela’s new ruler -- interim president Delcy Rodriguez -- had agreed to hand over the oil, how the plan would work, or what its legal basis would be.

Rodriguez -- a long-time member of Maduro’s inner circle as vice president and energy minister -- has vowed cooperation with the United States amid fears that Trump could pursue wider regime change.

title: Vintage Nasir keeps Noakhali winless
body:
Nasir Hossain’s career-best 90* led Dhaka Capitals to a convincing seven-wicket win over Noakhali Express in the ongoing Bangladesh Premier League at the Sylhet International Stadium on Wednesday.

After restricting Noakhali to 133-6 in 20 overs, Dhaka cruised to 134-3 in 14.1 overs. This was Dhaka’s first win after three consecutive defeats, while Noakhali were yet to win a match after playing five.

Being put into bat first, Noakhali’s top order faltered again as they lost three wickets for only 18 runs. They lost five inside the first 10 overs while putting only 40 on the board.

However, a 90-run partnership off 64 balls for the sixth wicket between Mohammad Nabi and the skipper, Haider Ali, gave Noakhali something to bowl with.

Nabi remained unbeaten on 42 off 33, while Haider made 47 off 36. All six bowlers were among the wickets for Dhaka, as they each took one. Nasir registered 1-24 from three before his batting extravaganza.

However, after Hasan Mahmud took two wickets in his first two overs, Nokhali hinted at fighting back. But Nasir took the game away from their hands.

He put on a 59-run partnership off 28 balls with Irfan Shukkur, where the latter contributed 12. However, his later partnership with Imad Wasim was comparatively even, where the latter made 29 off 16.

Nasir reached his fifty in just 21 balls, which is the fastest by any batter this season. He went on to surpass his previous best of 80—which he made back in the 2013 BPL—as he struck 14 fours and two sixes.

He also now has the third-highest joint number of fours in an innings in the BPL.  Nasir later said that batting up in the order helped him to play a big innings.

‘No one gave me a chance [in the BPL] at three (laughs)! Of course, it feels good. Because wherever you perform, it will feel good. And especially in the T20s, I enjoy batting up in the order,’ he said.

The all-rounder also didn’t want to keep any regret after missing out on the chance of scoring a hundred.

‘No, we lost three consecutive matches. So as a team we needed this win badly to gain some momentum,’ he said.

The 34-year-old also said that he wanted to continue playing for five or six years more.

‘I won’t say this is the later part of my career. By the grace of Allah, if I am well, I will be able to play for five to six years more. I always try to play well according to my knowledge,’ said Nasir.

‘I try to read the wicket both while batting and bowling,’ he added.

title: Bethell slams maiden century to give England glimmer
body:
Jacob Bethell fulfilled his rich potential with a chanceless maiden Test century Wednesday as England built a fragile 119-run second-innings lead with two wickets remaining to give themselves a glimmer of hope in the final Ashes Test.

At the end of day four at the Sydney Cricket Ground, England had reached 302-8 with Bethell imperious on 142 not out and number 10 Matthew Potts yet to score.

England are desperate for another morale-boosting win after victory in the previous Test at Melbourne. Australia lead 3-1 and have already retained the Ashes.

It was the 22-year-old Bethell who kept their faint hopes alive after Zak Crawley fell early and first-innnings centurion Joe Root departed cheaply.

He powered to his hundred off 162 balls by smashing a lofted drive over midwicket for four.

‘It’s pretty special, it’s not really sunk in yet. I haven’t really had time to kind of reflect on it,’ Bethell told reporters.

Bethell had his parents in the stands and raised his bat towards them as he passed the milestone.

‘To do that and have the family there was very special,’ said the left-hander.

‘My dad was a cricketer so he knows how it feels to be out there batting, but I don’t think that stops him from getting any less nervous.’

It was not just Bethell’s maiden Test ton but the only one he has scored in red-ball cricket, with his previous best 96 against New Zealand.

Bethell was recalled for Melbourne to replace the under-performing Ollie Pope, scoring a gritty 40 in difficult batting conditions.

He proved to be England’s rock, but soon saw wickets tumbling at the other end as Harry Brook was trapped lbw for 42 and Will Jacks caught without scoring in the space of three balls from part-time off-spinner Beau Webster.

‘I certainly didn’t think I would (impact) with spin this game,’ said Webster, who is more usually employed as a seamer, but returned figures of 3-51.

Webster believed the pitch had begun to take turn. ‘There was a bit of wear and tear there from Starcy’s footmarks,’ he said. ‘And we managed to make the most of it in that session.’

A mix-up saw Jamie Smith run out for 24 just as he and Bethell were threatening to take the game away from Australia with a sixth-wicket partnership that had reached 45.

Ben Stokes then came in at number eight with the score 264-6 after limping off with groin injury while bowling, but the captain lasted only five balls.

Australia were dismissed for 567 before lunch on the back of Travis Head’s 163 and 138 from skipper Steve Smith, a first-innings lead of 183 runs.

England needed a solid start, but chief tormentor Mitchell Starc once again conjured up a first-over breakthrough -- his 29th wicket for the series.

A beautiful inswinger was misjudged by Crawley who shouldered arms as it thudded into his pad and he was out lbw for one.

Fellow opener Ben Duckett was dropped on 38, but failed to capitalise and was bowled by Michael Neser on 42, his highest score in a wretched series.

Root, fresh from his first innings 160, was terrorised by Starc and Neser. He finally fell lbw after facing 37 balls for just six runs to the relentless Scott Boland.

Bethell knew he would now have to shepherd the tail on the fifth morning as England try to eke out a competitive target.

‘I’m  going to have to be smart around how we let Pottsy and (Josh) Tongue come in and what they face,’ said Bethell.

‘But I’m just going to have to hit the gaps. It’s a big outfield, so there are plenty of gaps and I just have to try and hit them.’

title: Chattogram regain top spot
body:
Chattogram Royals regained their position at the top after beating Sylhet Titans by 14 runs in the ongoing BPL at the Sylhet International Stadium on Wednesday.

Batting first, Chattogram made 198-5 in 20 overs, the highest total by any team so far in this season. In reply, Sylhet were all out for 184 runs in 19.4 overs.

Adam Rossington and Mahmudul Hasan shone at the top, followed by Mahedi Hasan toward the end, helping Chattogram to post a big score.

After a 60-run powerplay, Rossington and Mahmudul put on a 60-run partnership off 38 balls to lay a strong base for Chattogram.

Rossington, on the back of three consecutive fifties, made 49 off 38, while Mahmudul stormed with a 21-ball 44 with three fours and four sixes.

After Mahmudul’s departure, Rossington carried on with Hasan Nawaz before the latter was joined by Asif Ali to keep the momentum going.

Mahedi then finished with an unbeaten 33 off just 13 with four fours and a six. Ruyel Mia took 3-41 for Sylhet.

Sylhet, however, couldn’t get the momentum to put themselves ahead in the game. Some of them got the start but couldn’t capitalise on that.

After losing Parvez Hossain early in the innings, Sylhet scored 50 runs in the powerplay but lost two more wickets.

Afif Hossain, who top-scored with 46 off 33, didn’t get much support from others in the middle overs. Sylhet then tumbled toward the end when the required run rate kept climbing.

Pakistani pacer Aamer Jamal took 4-34 runs, while Shoriful Islam picked up 2-39.

title: Black Caps go spin heavy for T20 WC
body:
New Zealand named a spin heavy squad on Wednesday to travel to the T20 World Cup in India and Sri Lanka next month, led by captain Mitchell Santner.

Three of New Zealand’s four pool games will be played at the spin-friendly Chepauk Stadium in Chennai, which is a familiar hunting ground for former Chennai Super Kings Devon Conway, Rachin Ravindra, Daryl Mitchell and Santner.

Joining Santner in the spin bowling ranks are Ish Sodhi -- New Zealand’s second-highest wicket taker in the format -- as well as all-rounders Michael Bracewell, Glenn Phillips, and Ravindra.

Coach Rob Walter also named a strong pace-bowling quartet, led by the ICC’s second-ranked T20I bowler Jacob Duffy in his first World Cup.
