The commission notes that in the event of rights violations, there are no other agencies but the courts, which are burdened with more than 4,500,000 pending cases.

The chair of the inquiry commission, which has suggested massive reforms in the intelligence agencies, including the Directorate General of Forces Intelligence and the National Security Intelligence, to stop them from being engaged in grabbing banks and media houses or interfering in politics, notes that the country needs the Directorate General of Forces Intelligence and that the agency needs reforms. The Forces Intelligence, the chair says, was involved in the takeover of Islami Bank for a business group during the Sheikh Hasina-led government. In the same vein, there should also be a rapid response unit of the police. Therefore, the Rapid Action Battalion, which was set up out of necessity, may continue either in its present form or under another name, but it must be thoroughly restructured with stringent checks and balances so that it cannot engage in rights violations. The battalion has already earned infamy for violating rights, torturing citizens, running detention centres and, as the inquiry commission says, even for destroying most of the evidence of the detention centres it ran after the fall of the Awami League government on August 5, 2024, which has harmed the inquiry commission’s investigation during the tenure of the interim government, which assumed office on August 8 that year.

Whilst the government should thoroughly restructure security and law enforcement agencies, make them accountable, heavily amend the legislation to keep them in check and train the personnel to prevent rights violations, the political parties that would come to power should show the will to make all this happen.

title: Business-as-usual approach won’t end road chaos
body:
AN INCREASE in road accidents and the resulting deaths and injuries in 2025 compared with the previous year exposes the authorities’ persistent failure in road safety. The annual Passenger Welfare Association of Bangladesh report shows that at least 9,111 people were killed and 14,812 others injured in 6,729 accidents in 2025, marking a rise of 5.79 per cent in deaths, 14.87 per cent in injuries and 6.94 per cent in accidents compared with 2024. Of the dead, 622 were children. The Road Transport Authority has, like previous years, showed a conservative figure. Official data say that 5,286 people died in 2025 in road accidents. Motorcycles remained the most dangerous mode of transport, accounting for more than 37 per cent of accidents and nearly 38.5 per cent of fatalities. Besides the heavy toll on roads, hundreds more were killed or injured in railway and waterway accidents, highlighting a wider transport safety crisis. Pedestrians continued to be among the most vulnerable, with at least 1,146 deaths recorded. The financial cost was equally alarming, with losses estimated at more than Tk 60,000 crore, imposing a heavy burden on victim families and the economy.

Most accidents involved, as the Passenger Welfare Association report says, vehicles running over pedestrians, head-on collisions or drivers losing control, pointing to poor driving skills, disregard for traffic rules and defective road design. Motorcycles, trucks and buses dominated the accident statistics while transport workers, students and even law enforcement personnel were among the dead. The report identifies reckless driving, over-speeding, reckless overtaking, road construction defects, the movement of unfit vehicles, carelessness of passengers and pedestrians and unskilled drivers, and a sharp increase in motorcycles and technically faulty three-wheelers as reasons for the increased number of accidents. A lax enforcement of road laws and poor planning compounded the situation. Road policies and practices have, in fact, largely remained unchanged, with the interim government admitting its failure to discipline the sector amid weak administration and low morale among traffic police personnel. The persistence of chaos on the roads demands more than ad hoc measures and excuses. While steps such as identifying accident-prone spots, installing road signs and mandating training hours for driving licences are necessary, they remain insufficient without strict enforcement of the law.

The government must, therefore, act on its commitment to ensure road safety. It must enforce the Road Transport Act and adequately address issues such as unskilled and rash driving, unfit and unregulated vehicles and road construction defects. Political parties preparing for the next national elections should also commit to road safety and public transport reforms in their manifestos. Without sustained political will and coordinated action, the daily loss of lives on the roads will continue as a tragic reality.

title: E3 Solution to help implement HEAT Project
body:
A significant framework contract agreement was signed by the Higher Education Acceleration and Transformation (HEAT) Project, funded by the government and the World Bank at the HEAT project office in Dhaka on Tuesday.

The project will be implemented by the University Grants Commission, and Extreme Exhibition and Event Solution (E3 Solution) Limited by July 2028, said a press release.

Under this framework agreement, E3 Solution will provide comprehensive event management services for organising national and international conferences, workshops, and seminars for the HEAT Project.

Speaking at the ceremony, Professor Asaduzzaman, project director of the HEAT Project, expressed optimism that the partnership would ensure the timely and effective execution of all event-related activities. He emphasised the importance of professional event management in achieving the objectives of the HEAT Project.

Rezaul Karim Bhuiyan, managing director of E3 Solution, thanked the HEAT Project authorities and all stakeholders for their trust and confidence in the company. He reaffirmed E3 Solution’s commitment to delivering high-quality services and successfully completing all assigned responsibilities under the agreement.

The signing ceremony was attended by Professor Khurshid Alam, deputy project director of the HEAT Project, and Madhu Sudan Saha, director of E3 Solution, among other officials.

This collaboration is expected to strengthen the HEAT Project’s capacity to organise impactful national and international events that contribute to the advancement and transformation of higher education in Bangladesh.

title: Narayanganj Charukola recalls Samiran Chowdhury
body:
Narayanganj Charukola Institute remembered its founder principal, artist Samiran Chowdhury on the Institute campus in Narayanganj on Tuesday.

Samiran Chowdhury died on January 3 at a hospital in Dhaka.

The event, chaired by Dhaka University associate professor and the governing body president of the institute Reza Asad Al Huda Anupam, consisted of a song and discussion session about the recently passed artist and his works, said a press release.

Narayanganj-based cultural activist Rafiur Rabbi, Narayanganj Charukola Institute principal Md Shamsul Alam Azad and the family members of the artist also spoke at the event.

Samiran Chowdhury was born on November 20, 1962, at Ulukandi village of Araihazar upazila, Narayanganj. He passed his SSC examination in 1979 from Narayanganj Bar Academy before joining Dhaka’s Institute of Fine Arts. After the institute joined the University of Dhaka, he completed his BFA in 1985 and his Master’s degree in 1987.

In 1985 his first solo painting exhibition was held at Narayangonj and he organised 14 solo exhibitions at home and abroad. He also participated in more than 20 group exhibitions.

He exhibited widely, his works acquired by collectors and museums across multiple continents.

In 1994, he founded the Narayanganj Institute of Fine Arts and became the first principal of the Institute.

title: Omega-3 fortified broiler meat set to hit market
body:
Omega-3 fortified broiler chicken is set to enter the Bangladeshi market for the first time, following successful research led by Bangladesh Agricultural University in collaboration with Bengal Meat.

Bengal Meat made the announcement at a launching event at its office in the capital’s Tejgaon on Tuesday.

Since October 2024, a group of researchers under the supervision of the BAU Research and Innovation Centre has been working to develop the Omega-3 enriched broiler under a project titled ‘Dietary Supplementation of Nutraceutical Feed Additives for the Production of Omega-3 Enriched Designer Broiler Meat’. The project is funded by the World Bank through the ICT Division.

While Omega-3 fortified eggs are already available in the local market, this marks the first successful commercial development of Omega-3 enriched broiler meat in Bangladesh, said chief coordinator of the BAU Research and Innovation Centre Professor Md Abdul Awal.

Omega-3 fortified broiler refers to poultry meat enriched with omega-3 fatty acids through dietary modification of chicken feed, allowing consumers to intake essential nutrients directly from meat.

Academicians said that the innovation could play a vital role in improving public health, as a large section of the population lacks adequate access to Omega-3 sources due to low consumption of sea fish and other Omega-3-rich foods.

Omega-3 fatty acids are essential nutrients that support the proper functioning of vital organs, including the heart, brain and eyes, and help reduce the risk of cardiovascular diseases.

Bengal Meat chief executive officer AFM Asif said that they were ready to market Omega-3 fortified broiler meat.

‘It may take one and a half months for us to go for large scale of production,’ he said.

Professor Awal said that broiler chicken was selected for Omega-3 fortification because it was widely consumed by people of all ages and income groups in the country.

Bengal Meat developed the Omega-3 enriched broiler using feed additives that were safe for consumption, researchers said.

One of the researchers, Md Imrul Kayes, said that various feed additives were tested at different stages of the research, but flaxseed, chia seed and fish oil proved to be the most effective.

Health ministry joint secretary Most Yeasmin Akhter said that the innovation was highly significant from a public health perspective, though affordability would be a major challenge.

She urged Bengal Meat and other potential producers to consider export opportunities while ensuring that the product remained affordable for domestic consumers.

Bangladesh Agricultural University former vice-chancellor Professor Dr Mostafizur Rahman said that there was growing demand for Omega-3 enriched broiler meat among health-conscious consumers.

Speakers at the event said that the enriched meat, produced by incorporating fish oil, linseed or chia seed into standard broiler feed, not only helped address nutritional deficiencies but also contributed to reducing cardiovascular health risks.

They also noted that the initiative could increase farmers’ income, create new employment opportunities and ensure the supply of premium-quality, healthy meat in the market.

Researchers said that Omega-3 enriched broiler meat was expected to cost up to Tk 40 more per kilogram than conventional broiler meat.

title: Exhibition for Children of Gaza inaugurated at AFD
body:
The HopeWave Foundation organised a four-day children art exhibition titled Echoes of Hope for the Children of Gaza, inaugurated at Alliance Française de Dhaka in Dhanmondi on Tuesday.

Curated by Mubtasim Alvee, the exhibition displayed drawings, handwritten letters, photographs, and project documentation created by children from Ukhiya, including refugee, indigenous, and underserved communities.

All exhibited works is an outcome of a three-day psychosocial art campaign conducted with children in Ukhiya.

The exhibition was inaugurated by Alliance Française de Dhaka director François Chambraud. On the opening ceremony, founder of HopeWave Foundation poet-activist Munimah Mahreen said that the exhibition is not only about charity but solidarity.

‘These artworks created by children can still teach adults how to be human,’ she said.

‘Displayed artworks reflect the truest form of humanity—shared empathy, children’s thoughts and expressions are the purest form of that truth,’ said Mubtasim Alvee.

The exhibition comprise a Psycho-Social session by Fabliha Bushra today, while a creative documentary filmmaking workshop by Yeasir Arafat would be conducted on Thursday, and a music composition workshop by Samin Yasar and Hassan Munhanmanha would be held on Friday.

The exhibition will end on Friday with a cultural evening at the venue.

title: Prof Mahbub joins NSU architecture department
body:
Professor Mahbubur Rahman, an eminent architect, academician, and administrator, has joined the Department of Architecture at North South University, further strengthening its academic and professional leadership.

Professor Rahman is widely recognised for his significant contributions to architectural education, research, professional practice, and the development of national policy.

Prior to joining NSU, he served as pro-vice-chancellor of Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology and also held the position of acting vice-chancellor in 2024.

Professor Rahman, a Commonwealth Scholar and Robert McNamara Fellow, started teaching at BUET in 1985.

His academic career spanning four decades has taken him to several countries, including Canada, the United Kingdom, Malaysia, Oman, Bahrain, and Saudi Arabia.

This has enabled him to gain extensive experience in curriculum development, accreditation, and quality assurance in higher education.

A prolific researcher and scholar, he has published more than 165 peer-reviewed papers and book chapters, and has authored or edited nine books. His acclaimed publication, City of an Architect, which documents and critically examines Dhaka’s architectural heritage, received the prestigious Baku Book Prize in 2023.

The Department of Architecture at North South University warmly welcomes Mahbubur Rahman and looks forward to benefiting from his extensive experience, leadership, and continued contributions to architectural education and research.

title: Tk 25cr assets of Shahjalal Fertiliser ex-chief accountant seized
body:
The criminal investigation department of police has seized land, flats, shares, vehicles and bank accounts worth at least Tk 25 crore in connection with the embezzlement of funds from the Shahjalal Fertilizer Factory project in Sylhet.

The seizure follows preliminary findings that Khandaker Muhammad Iqbal, former head of the accounts department of the Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation’s Shahjalal Fertilizer Factory project, misappropriated project funds by submitting fake bills and receipts.

The assets were allegedly acquired in his own name and in the name of his wife, Halima Akhter.

According to CID officials, the seized properties include 23.5 kathas of land, 11 shares covering area of 392.7323 decimals, and 12 flats.

While the deed value of the flats stands at Tk 8.47 crore, their current market value is estimated at around Tk 25 crore.

In addition, Tk 30.65 lakh has been frozen in three bank accounts following court orders.

The CID filed a case under the Money Laundering Prevention Act on April 26, 2023, after investigating allegations that Iqbal embezzled funds from the Shahjalal Fertilizer project by channelling money through two companies-TI International and Nusrat Traders-registered in his wife’s name.

Investigators said Iqbal joined the Shahjalal Fertilizer Factory as an assistant accountant in 2005 and later rose to become head of the accounts department.

During his 14-year tenure, he allegedly amassed vast wealth, including multiple flats in Dhaka, department stores, large tracts of land in Dhaka and Gazipur, and ownership records of 91 vehicles.

He was dismissed from the factory five years ago over embezzlement allegations.

The case statement notes that Tk 388.327 million was fraudulently withdrawn from the BCIC project using fake bills and receipts.

The Anti-Corruption Commission is also probing 26 separate cases related to the alleged fraud.

During the investigation, CID seized six flats in Dhaka’s Ramna and Airport areas and land in Dhaka, Gazipur and Mymensingh with a deed value exceeding Tk 7.11 crore.

Data from the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority shows that 91 vehicles were registered in the names of Iqbal-linked organisations, of which 21 minibuses and two pickup vans have been seized.

On court orders, the additional inspector general of police of CID, Dhaka, has been appointed receiver of the 21 minibuses, which are currently being rented out at the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant.

Rental income amounting to Tk 53.8 lakh has so far been deposited into the state treasury.

The financial crime unit of the CID is conducting the investigation.

Officials said efforts are underway to uncover the full extent of the crime, identify other individuals involved, and proceed with further legal action.

title: Rajshahi hospitals struggle as patients with cold-related diseases surge
body:
Public hospitals across Rajshahi division are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in cold-related patients as a moderate cold wave grips the region, triggering a surge in respiratory and seasonal illnesses, particularly among children and the elderly.

On Tuesday, the Rajshahi Meteorological Observatory recorded the season’s lowest temperature — and the lowest in the country — at 7.0 degrees Celsius.

Rahidul Islam, a senior observer at the Rajshahi Meteorological Observatory, told New Age that temperatures between 8°C and 10°C are classified as a mild cold wave, 6°C to 8°C as a moderate cold wave, and below 6°C as a severe cold wave.

‘Rajshahi is now experiencing a moderate cold wave which may persist for several more days,’ he added.

Doctors at public hospitals said that the number of daily patients seeking treatment for cold-related complications had risen sharply since temperatures began dropping significantly in the past week, accompanied by dense fog and biting winds.

Hospital authorities reported that they were struggling due to severe shortages of beds, manpower, and other resources as admissions in paediatric and medicine wards surged with cases of pneumonia, acute respiratory infections, asthma complications, fever, cough, cold, and diarrhoea.

Rajshahi Medical College Hospital is facing severe overcrowding, with 2,537 patients currently admitted against its official capacity of 1,200 beds. During the same period in the past year, RMCH reported 2,066 patients against its 1,200-bed capacity.

The majority of the patients are children and the elderly, said hospital spokesperson and emergency department in-charge physician Sankar K Biswas.

‘Every day we are receiving a high volume of patients with cold-induced illnesses. Children suffering from pneumonia and elderly patients with breathing difficulties are the most affected. Many cases are becoming severe due to delayed treatment and prolonged exposure to the cold,’ he said.

Md Shadin, who brought his ailing mother to RMCH from Nazipur under Mohadevpur upazila in Naogaon, said that they admitted her on Monday but she was not allotted a bed and was forced to stay beside the staircase of Ward No 33.

Doctors at RMCH’s paediatric unit said that admissions had reached nearly three times the capacity, with a total of 143 children currently undergoing treatment against 53 beds.

Professor Shahida Yeasmin, head of the RMCH paediatric department, said that most admitted children were suffering from the common cold, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and diarrhoea, with the cold weather worsening their symptoms.

Hospital officials said that the accommodation crisis, compounded by manpower shortages, had severely strained services.

‘Although RMCH was upgraded from a 500-bed to a 1,200-bed hospital, it is still being operated with the previous manpower,’ Sankar said.

Similar conditions were reported at district hospitals in Bogura, Naogaon, and Chapainawabganj, where health officials confirmed a sharp rise in cold-related outpatient visits and admissions over the past week.

Md Najmul Haque, additional director of Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Medical College Hospital in Bogura, told New Age that the hospital had an approved capacity of 500 beds, though an extended capacity of about 1,200 beds — including around 400 floor allocations — was being utilised.

‘At present, more than 1,800 patients are undergoing treatment, far exceeding our capacity,’ he said, adding that many were being kept on the floor due to the acute shortage of beds.

He added that the pressure continued to rise as cold-related illnesses spread across the region.

Md Masud Parvez, superintendent of the 250-bed Chapainawabganj District Hospital, said that a total of 350 patients were currently receiving treatment at the hospital.

‘About 20 days ago, the number was below 300. Now it has risen to around 350. The rise is largely due to cold-related illnesses,’ he said.

Physician Parvez noted that although the hospital was upgraded from 100 to 250 beds, staffing levels remained inadequate.

‘Even for the original 100 beds, we do not have full manpower. Doctors and consultants are working at around 50 per cent capacity. We are managing services with limited resources,’ he added.

Md Mir Sufian, acting superintendent of Naogaon 100-bed district sadar hospital, told New Age that a total of 222 patients were receiving treatment at the hospital against its 100-bed capacity.

‘Most of the admitted patients are suffering from cold-related complications, particularly children. We are also seeing an increase in diabetes-related cases during this period,’ he said.

Public health experts have warned that patient numbers could rise further if the cold wave persists, urging people — especially low-income households, outdoor workers, and rural residents — to take preventive measures, including wearing warm clothing, ensuring safe drinking water, and seeking early medical care.

title: Five killed in clashes between Syria govt, Kurdish forces
body:
Clashes between government personnel and Kurdish-led forces in the north Syrian city of Aleppo killed at least five people on Tuesday, with both sides trading blame over who started the fighting.

Progress has stalled on implementing a March deal to merge the Kurds’ semi-autonomous administration and military into Syria’s new Islamist government, and tensions have occasionally erupted into clashes, particularly in Aleppo, which has two Kurdish-majority neighbourhoods.

State news agency SANA reported that the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces had ‘targeted the area near the Shihan roundabout, resulting in the death of one defence ministry member’.

It later said ‘three civilians, including two women’ were killed in ‘SDF bombing of residential buildings in Aleppo city’s Al-Midan neighbourhood’.

The SDF, in a statement issued before the state media reports, said groups affiliated with the government ‘targeted the Sheikh Maqsud neighbourhood with a reconnaissance drone’, resulting in ‘the death of one resident and the wounding of two others’.

Aleppo’s Kurdish-majority Sheikh Maqsud and Ashrafiyeh neighbourhoods have remained under the control of Kurdish units linked to the SDF, despite Kurdish fighters agreeing to withdraw from the areas in April.

Separately, the SDF accused factions affiliated with Syria’s army of attacking the town of Deir Hafer, around 50 kilometres east of Aleppo, and near the strategic Tishreen Dam to the city’s northeast.

The Kurdish-led force affirmed its right to ‘respond legitimately to these attacks’.

The SDF controls large swathes of Syria’s oil-rich north and northeast, and with the support of a US-led international coalition, was integral to the territorial defeat of the Islamic State group in Syria in 2019.

Its integration into the state following the ouster of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad a year ago has proven complicated, and the original March agreement was supposed to be implemented by the end of 2025.

On Sunday, SDF chief Mazloum Abdi held further talks with officials in Damascus on integrating the Kurdish-led forces, but state media said no tangible results were achieved.

The Kurds have repeated calls for decentralisation — which Syria’s new Islamist authorities have rejected.

Last month in Aleppo, deadly clashes killed five people, in violence that came after Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan of Turkey — a close ally of the new authorities — urged the SDF during a visit to Damascus not to be an obstacle to Syria’s stability.

title: Swiss officials admit inspections failure at burnt-out bar
body:
Swiss local authorities admitted Tuesday that fire safety inspections had not been carried out for the past five years at a bar where 40 people died and dozens were injured in a New Year blaze.

‘Periodic inspections were not conducted between 2020 and 2025. We bitterly regret this,’ Crans-Montana mayor Nicolas Feraud told a press conference in the Alpine ski resort, five days after the disaster at Le Constellation bar.

The authorities have said they believe the fire started when people celebrating New Year raised champagne bottles with sparklers attached, setting light to sound insulating foam on the ceiling of the bar’s basement.

In a statement issued at the press conference, the Municipality of Crans-Montana said it had gone through all the documents in the file submitted to the Wallis canton public prosecutor’s office following the fire.

It said the documents detail ‘administrative procedures relating to the establishment’s compliance’.

‘Although more than 1,400 fire inspections were carried out in the municipality in 2025 alone, the municipal council deeply regrets discovering that this establishment had failed to undergo periodic inspections between 2020 and 2025.’

The council said it would commission a specialist external agency to inspect all public establishments and would ban pyrotechnic devices indoors.

‘The Municipality of Crans-Montana remains fully committed to supporting the victims of this tragedy and their families and loved ones, who are constantly in its thoughts,’ the statement said.

‘It will continue to do everything in its power to ensure that such a tragedy never happens again.’

Wallis police said Monday it had identified all 116 people injured in the blaze, of whom 83 remained in hospital.

title: Lee snaps Xi selfie with Chinese ‘backdoor’ phone
body:
South Korean president Lee Jae Myung snapped a selfie with Xi Jinping using a smartphone gifted to him by the Chinese leader, who had joked at their last meeting that the device might be capable of spying.

Lee posted a selfie of himself, Xi and their wives on social media platform X on Monday during a visit to Beijing.

‘A selfie with President Xi Jinping and his wife, taken with the Xiaomi I received as a gift in Gyeongju,’ Lee wrote.

‘Thanks to them, I got the shot of a lifetime,’ he said.

‘I will communicate more frequently and collaborate more closely going forward.’

Lee’s office also posted a short YouTube video of the scene, with Xi complimenting the South Korean leader’s photo skills.

The Xiaomi handset made headlines in November when Xi cracked a joke to Lee on the sidelines of an APEC summit in South Korea.

When Lee asked if the communication line on the device was secure, the Chinese leader urged him to ‘check if there is a backdoor’ — referring to pre-installed software that could allow third-party monitoring.

The banter was a rare display of humour from the Chinese leader, who is not often seen making jokes, let alone about espionage.

Lee has said Xi was ‘unexpectedly quite good at making jokes’.

During their 90 minute summit on Monday, Xi urged Lee to join Beijing in making the ‘right strategic choices’ in a world that is ‘becoming more complex and turbulent’.

Lee’s visit to China followed a US military operation in Caracas that captured Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and brought him to New York to face narco-trafficking charges — a raid condemned by Beijing and Pyongyang.

Lee’s selfie post sparked heavy interest online and was shared more than 3,400 times in the first few hours.

One user quipped: ‘Sir, Do you know Nicolas Maduro used the same phone?’

The South Korean leader, who took office in June following the impeachment and removal of his predecessor over a martial law declaration, has sought to improve ties with China after a years-long diplomatic deep freeze.

On Tuesday he met in Beijing with Chinese premier Li Qiang, charged with economic policy, hailing improving ties as the ‘irreversible trend of the times’.

The South Korean leader then headed to China’s economic powerhouse city of Shanghai.

title: Israeli strikes undermine efforts to prevent escalation: Lebanon
body:
Lebanese president Joseph Aoun on Tuesday condemned Israel’s latest strikes on his country, saying they undermine efforts to prevent escalation.

Aoun’s criticism came after Israel launched a series of strikes in southern and eastern Lebanon on Monday, saying it hit Hezbollah and Hamas targets.

The attacks began with strikes on four villages where Israel had issued evacuation warnings, though later bombing including a strike in the early hours of Tuesday came without prior notice.

In a statement, Aoun said that ‘Israel’s continued attacks aim to thwart all efforts made locally, regionally and internationally to stop the on-going Israeli escalation, despite the response shown by Lebanon to these efforts at various levels’.

In spite of a year-old ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah, Israel has carried out frequent strikes on Lebanon, usually saying it is bombing Hezbollah sites and operatives, and occasionally Hamas targets.

On Tuesday, the Israeli military said its operations the day before struck infrastructure ‘belonging to the Hezbollah and Hamas terrorist organisations in several areas in Lebanon’.

According to the military, the targets included ‘several weapon storage facilities and military structures, both above and below ground’.

The strike early on Tuesday targeted Ghazieh, near the southern coastal city of Sidon, destroying a building and damaging its surroundings, causing a fire on site which firefighters deployed to combat, according to an AFP photographer.

The latest strikes come with the committee monitoring the ceasefire, which includes the United States, France, Lebanon, Israel and the United Nations, set to meet on Wednesday.

Lebanon’s cabinet will also convene later this week to discuss the Lebanese military’s progress in disarming Hezbollah, a plan launched under heavy US pressure and amid fears of expanded Israeli strikes.

The Lebanese army was expected to complete the disarmament south of the Litani River — about 30 kilometres from the border with Israel — by the end of 2025, before tackling the rest of the country.

In his statement, Aoun said the government’s plan to ‘extend its authority over the south of the Litani’ was ‘implemented by the Lebanese army with professionalism, commitment and precision’.

Israel has previously questioned the Lebanese military’s effectiveness and has accused Hezbollah of rearming.

Israel’s foreign minister Gideon Saar on Sunday called the disarmament efforts far from sufficient.

title: 31 killed in New Year’s migrant boat sinking off Gambia
body:
At least 31 people drowned when an overloaded boat carrying undocumented migrants capsized on New Year’s Eve off the coast of Gambia, the government said on Monday, hiking the previous toll.

‘Many others are missing and feared dead,’ the government said in an update.

Thousands of people, most of them young, have tried to reach Europe from west Africa, mainly via the Spanish Canary Islands, on overcrowded and often dilapidated boats due to restrictions on visas and tighter border security.

Migrant boats have been forced to leave from further south, notably from The Gambia and Guinea, adding to the journey — and dangers — at sea, after Senegal, Mauritania and Morocco increased maritime patrols.

In the latest such tragedy, a boat loaded with more than 200 people made a distress call overnight December 31 to January 1 near the North Bank region.

The Gambian Navy launched a hunt for survivors after midnight, involving several vessels and a fishing boat. The stricken vessel was later found on a sandbank.

‘Fifteen bodies are confirmed to be recovered from the Gambia and 16 in Senegal,’ said the government in its update, hiking the previous toll of at least 7 dead. 102 people were rescued, 23 of whom were hospitalised.

President Adama Barrow said on Friday that the country was in mourning over the disaster.

title: Mahathir Mohamad hospitalised with hip fracture
body:
Malaysia’s 100-year-old former prime minister Mahathir Mohamad is being treated for a hip fracture after falling at his residence on Tuesday, an aide said.

Mahathir has suffered health problems in recent years and was previously hospitalised for fatigue after a picnic celebration for his centenary in July.

He was taken conscious by ambulance to the National Heart Institute in Kuala Lumpur earlier Tuesday after the fall, aide Sufi Yusoff said.

In a statement issued later in the day, Sufi said ‘after medical assessment, it has been confirmed that Tun (Mahathir) suffered a fracture to the right hip’.

The former premier ‘is expected to be admitted for the next few weeks for treatment and observation’, Sufi added.

He fell while ‘transiting from one part of the balcony to the living room’, according to the aide.

Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim and his wife Wan Azizah Wan Ismail prayed for Mahathir’s recovery.

‘Azizah and I pray for Tun’s (Mahathir’s) well-being and speedy recovery, God willing,’ Anwar said in a Facebook post.

Mahathir, Anwar’s mentor turned political rival, has previously undergone bypass surgeries for heart problems.

He was prime minister from 1981 until 2003, and again from 2018 to 2020.

He reached the age of 94 during his second stint and was the world’s oldest elected leader at the time.

title: No major damage reported from strong Japan quake
body:
A strong 6.2-magnitude earthquake shook western Japan on Tuesday but no tsunami warning was issued and no major damage was reported.

The tremor was recorded at 10:18am (0118 GMT) in Shimane prefecture at a shallow depth, the Japan Meteorological Agency said.

The US Geological Survey recorded a slightly lower 5.8 magnitude reading which it then lowered to 5.7.

The quake measured upper-five on Japan’s Shindo scale of shakiness in the western city of Yasugi.

At that level, heavy furniture may fall and drivers can have trouble steering.

The JMA said that the same region was hit soon afterwards by smaller quakes with magnitudes of 4.5, 5.1, 3.8 and 5.4, also with no tsunami alerts.

No abnormalities were detected at the Shimane nuclear plant as of 10:45 am, broadcaster NHK said, citing utility company Chugoku Electric.

Parts of the Shinkansen bullet train network were suspended due to a power blackout, operator JR West said. It was unclear if this was related to the quakes.

The military said it was conducting an aerial damage assessment and had established a disaster response liaison office.

‘The government is collecting information on damage. People in the regions that were hit by strong shakes please continue to be careful about more quakes of the same strength,’ prime minister Sanae Takaichi said.

Japan sits on top of four major tectonic plates along the western edge of the Pacific ‘Ring of Fire’ and is one of the world’s most seismically active countries.

The archipelago, home to around 125 million people, experiences around 1,500 jolts every year.

The vast majority are mild, although the damage they cause varies according to their location and depth.

Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed around 18,500 people.

In 2024, the JMA issued its first special advisory of a possible ‘megaquake’ along the Nankai Trough.

This 800-kilometre undersea trench is where the Philippine Sea oceanic tectonic plate is ‘subducting’ — or slowly slipping — underneath the continental plate that Japan sits atop.

The government has said a quake in the Nankai Trough and subsequent tsunami could kill as many as 2,98,000 people and cause up to $2 trillion in damages.

The JMA lifted the 2024 advisory after a week but it led to panic-buying of staples like rice and prompted holidaymakers to cancel hotel reservations.

It issued a week-long second ‘megaquake’ advisory in December 2025 after a magnitude-7.5 tremor struck off the northern coast.

The December 8 quake triggered tsunami waves of up to 70 centimetres and injured more than 40 people, but no major damage was reported.

title: AI, social media misuse warned ahead of election
body:
Speakers at a dialogue on Tuesday warned against the misuse of artificial intelligence and unregulated social media, saying that they could seriously undermine the credibility of the coming national election, urging urgent regulatory and institutional reforms to protect democratic processes.

The dialogue, focusing on the digital economy, governance and electoral integrity, was organised by the Centre for Governance Studies at the CIRDAP Auditorium in the capital, said a press release.

At the event, Centre for Policy Dialogue distinguished fellow Debapriya Bhattacharya said that the use of social media and AI-driven content manipulation posed a new and dangerous challenge to electoral integrity.

‘During the August movement, internet shutdowns showed how essential digital connectivity is, but also how easily it can be abused. In this election, AI-based disinformation and online disorder may have long-term negative impacts,’ he said.

He criticised the Election Commission for its alleged failure to act against online hate speech and digital violence, saying civil society had long demanded effective regulation of social media platforms.

Debapriya also called for the creation of a unified national data repository, stressing that it must be an autonomous and accountable institution, independent of both the Election Commission and the Ministry of Home Affairs.

CGS president Zillur Rahman said that while digitalisation was widely promoted over the past decade, it had often been used as a cover for misgovernance rather than genuine reform.

‘Simply owning a mobile phone does not make a country digital. In the name of digitalisation, massive financial crimes occurred, including the theft of central bank funds,’ he said, adding that unverified information from social media was increasingly shaping public opinion and even influencing mainstream media coverage.

CGS executive director Parvez Karim Abbasi said that Bangladesh’s growing digital footprint—nearly eight crore internet users, including 6.5 crore on social media—offered opportunities but also serious risks.

‘Low digital literacy and inequality are fuelling cybercrime and misinformation. While freelancing has grown rapidly, training in advanced areas, such as artificial intelligence, remains limited,’ he said.

Bangladesh Chamber of Industries former president Shahedul Islam Helal said that digital tools could reduce corruption and increase transparency if used responsibly, citing automation and remote monitoring in industrial production.

Former National Board of Revenue chairman Muhammad Abdul Mazid cautioned that digitalisation alone would not deliver results without ethical governance.

‘Without accountability and a change in mindset, technology will only magnify existing failures,’ he said.

Several political leaders, academics, entrepreneurs and banking professionals also spoke, echoing concerns over digital security, AI misuse and the urgent need for safeguards ahead of the election.

Among others, former president of Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry Asif Ibrahim, Daffodil Group chairman Sabur Khan, former president of BARVIDA Abdul Haque, former chairman of National Board of Revenue Dr Muhammad Abdul Mazid, organising secretary of Nationalist Democratic Movement Barrister Shahedul Alam and associate relationship manager of City Bank PLC Tanha Kate spoke at the programme.

title: BCG rescues 9 fishermen, arrests one at Maheshkhali
body:
The Bangladesh Coast Guard rescued nine fishermen and arrested a suspected robber during an operation in Maheshkhali of Cox’s Bazar Monday afternoon.

A press release, signed by BCG media officer Lieutenant Commander Siam-ul-Haq and issued on Tuesday, said that a fishing boat named FB Allah Dan was robbed at around 4:00pm in the Paraban channel adjacent to Baradia area under Maheshkhali police station. After receiving the alert through the emergency service number 16111, the coast guard station Maheshkhali launched a prompt rescue operation.

During the drive, coast guard personnel successfully rescued all nine fishermen who were being held by the robbers and detained one suspect. The boat used in the robbery was also recovered.

The arrested suspect and the seized boat were handed over to Maheshkhali police station for legal proceedings.

title: Man sent to jail after wife’s slit-throat body found
body:
The police have recovered the slit-throat body of a housewife named Arifa Akhtar, 17, from a house at Kuakata of Kalapara upazila in Patuakhali district on early Tuesday.

The body was recovered in a bloody state from a rented house at Ward No. 3 in Kuakata Municipality area under Mohipur Police Station at about 12:10 am.

Mohabbat Khan, officer-in-charge, said that the husband of the deceased, Rifat Hossain, 21, was taken into police custody as his words were incoherent.

He added that the body was sent to Patuakhali morgue for autopsy and the husband was sent to Patuakhali district jail on Tuesday noon and further legal action was under way.

According to the police and local sources, the couple had been living in Kuakata area four the last four months and Rifat worked in a restaurant at Kuakata coastal town.

Local people also said that hearing the sound of crying suddenly at midnight, they went inside the house and saw her lying on the floor in a bloody state while Rifat was sitting next to her and crying.

title: SEU holds special prayers for Khaleda Zia
body:
Southeast University organised a discussion and special prayers, honouring former prime minister and chairperson of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party Khaleda Zia, at the Multipurpose Hall of the university in Dhaka on Monday.

SEU vice-chancellor Professor Yusuf Mahbubul Islam presided over the programme while pro–VC Professor M Mofazzal Hossain addressed as special speaker, said a press release.

The event began with opening remarks by Professor Md Serajul Islam, dean of Southeast business school and convener of the event organising committee.

Following his speech, a documentary highlighting the life and political contributions of Khaleda Zia was screened.

At the conclusion of the programme, special prayers were offered seeking eternal peace and forgiveness for the departed soul of Khaleda Zia.

The prayer session was conducted by Mufti Nasir Uddin, imam of Rahim Metal Jame Mosque.

title: BREB distributes warm clothes to members
body:
The Bangladesh Rural Electrification Board and the sports, culture and welfare councils of 80 Palli Bidyut Samity have come forward to distribute warm clothes to its members across the country.

For this purpose, the BREB and PBS inaugurated a blanket distribution programme at several districts on Monday, said a press release.

Through the programme, blankets are being distributed to the people affected by the continuous cold wave across the country.

The BREB and 80 rural electricity associations will continue such public welfare work in the future.

title: Many challenges lie ahead in 2026
body:
Bangladesh’s readymade garment sector is likely to face another challenging year in 2026 amid weak global demand, political uncertainty, banking sector stress, and mounting pressure from least developed country graduation, business leaders and economists said.

They warned that the sector, which struggled throughout 2025 due to tariff shocks and volatility in key export markets, might continue to face headwinds unless political stability was restored through a credible national election and supportive policy measures are taken.

According to data from the Export Promotion Bureau, Bangladesh exported RMG products worth $38.83 billion in 2025, a marginal 0.89 per cent increase from $38.48 billion in 2024.

Despite modest annual growth, exports remained on a negative trajectory from July to December, raising concerns among exporters about the sustainability of growth this year.

During July-November of the 2025-26 financial year, exports to the European Union declined by 1.03 per cent to $7.83 billion, while shipments to the United States grew by only 3.06 per cent to $3.22 billion.

Exports to non-traditional markets also fell by 3.19 per cent to $2.67 billion during the period.

Business leaders said that deteriorating law and order, a fragile banking sector, declining exports, and prolonged stagnation in new investment and job creation added to the sector’s woes in 2025.

Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association, said that both new investment and expansion of existing factories were virtually absent amid political uncertainty and weak law and order.

‘There are no signs of improvement in the short term. Restoration of law and order and a credible election could help restore confidence among local entrepreneurs and attract foreign investment,’ he said.

Exporters said that many garment manufacturers faced difficulties in opening back-to-back letters of credit due to poor health of the banking sector, while rising non-performing loans — estimated at around 36 per cent of total loans — eroded confidence among depositors and businesses.

‘The banking sector is going through a severe crisis and businesses are suffering the most because of it,’ Hatem said, adding that urgent reforms were needed.

Shovon Islam, managing director of Sparrow Group, said that international buyers closely monitored political situation in sourcing countries.

‘Buyers are currently in a state of observation and caution, particularly regarding the February election,’ he stated, noting that a return to political stability could potentially spark a recovery from April to May.

He described 2025 as one of the most challenging years for the RMG sector, comparing it to the shocks experienced during the abolition of the quota system, the Rana Plaza tragedy and the Covid-19 pandemic.

The sector also continues to grapple with the impact of higher US tariffs.

In April 2025, the United States imposed sharply higher reciprocal tariffs on apparel imports from several countries, including Bangladesh, initially raising duties to 37 per cent.

The rate was later reduced to 35 per cent, then to 20 per cent, following negotiations concluded on July 31, 2025.

Since August 7, 2025, Bangladeshi apparel shipments to the US have been facing a 20 per cent reciprocal tariff in addition to the regular 16.5 per cent duty, exporters said, noting that the measures further slowed global demand.

Exporters said that competitor countries had aggressively pushed into the EU and other markets to offset losses from the US market.

Inamul Haq Khan, senior vice-president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, said that China, India and other competitors entered the EU and new markets more aggressively following the US tariff measures, squeezing Bangladesh’s market share.

He = said that Bangladesh failed to attract the expected volume of orders shifting from China, as Vietnam, Indonesia and Myanmar captured a larger share.

Bangladesh is scheduled to graduate from least developed country status in November 2026, leaving less than 11 months to prepare for the loss of preferential market access.

Industry leaders warned that the country remained inadequately prepared for the post-LDC era due to weak infrastructure and logistics, limited product and market diversification and high production costs.

They said that pushing ahead with graduation without adequate preparation could result in an annual export loss of at least $8 billion.

Hatem alleged that the government lacked a clear roadmap for LDC graduation and had failed to engage adequately with business stakeholders to prepare for the transition.

Exporters also expressed concern that Bangladesh had yet to sign preferential trade agreements or free trade agreements with major trading partners, risking the loss of duty-free access after graduation.

Mohiuddin Rubel, former BGMEA director, stressed the need for advanced policy planning to address the realities of the gradual withdrawal of tariff preferences and exceptional facilities.

Meanwhile, recent labour law amendments and ratification of International Labour Organization conventions — C190, C155 and C187 — have raised compliance costs for the industry, although worker rights groups welcomed the reforms.

Global fashion outlooks also remain cautious for 2026, as McKinsey & Company said in its State of Fashion 2026 report that weak consumer confidence, geopolitical instability and economic volatility would continue to weigh on the global fashion industry.

The report noted that fashion markets in the US, EU and China were growing at only low single-digit rates, a trend likely to persist into 2026.

Professor Mustafizur Rahman, a distinguished fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue, said that Bangladesh had failed to address structural weaknesses that continued to erode competitiveness in 2025.

He warned that 2026 would be particularly challenging due to LDC graduation and the national election, adding that Bangladesh might struggle to meet its export target for the current fiscal year.

‘Innovation, reduced lead time, lower cost of doing business, and diversification of products and markets are now essential. The time to keep these policies on the shelf has ended,’ he said.

Inamul Haq Khan said that industry players remained cautious about recovery amid ongoing global turmoil but expressed hope that an elected government could restore buyers’ confidence.

Hatem said that while China and India were offering significantly lower prices backed by new incentive packages, Bangladesh was gradually withdrawing cash incentives for exporters.

‘Without adequate policy support, the survival of many exporters would be at risk,’ he said, adding that engagement with industry stakeholders after the election could help restore export growth from mid-2026.

Industry leaders also urged stronger logistics, political and social stability, financial sector reform, factory-level efficiency improvements, and greater investment in research, innovation and marketing.

title: Insurers asked to reassess damages from July 2024
body:
The Insurance Development and Regulatory Authority has directed insurance companies to reassess insurance claims from industrial units that were subject to widespread vandalism and arson during the July–August 2024 uprising.

In a circular issued on Sunday, the IDRA also rejected a blanket classification of the incidents as ‘Popular Rising’ for denying compensation.

In a statement, Bangladesh Textiles Mills Association on Tuesday said that the directive followed prolonged efforts by industry associations to challenge insurers’ refusal and delay in settling claims for damaged factories, warehouses, and industrial establishments across the country.

During the uprising, many industrial units suffered extensive losses from vandalism, looting, and fires, severely disrupting production and causing significant financial losses for entrepreneurs.

Most affected establishments had valid fire and allied-peril insurance coverage, obtained through regular premium payments, the BTMA said.

However, insurance companies allegedly delayed claim settlements by citing procedural complexities, while in many cases signalling outright rejection of claims by invoking riot and strike damage and political disturbance-related exclusions.

Industry leaders argued that such blanket rejection contradicted fundamental insurance principles and left damaged factories unable to resume operations, placing thousands of workers at risk of unemployment.

The dispute intensified after a meeting held on March 3 of this year, organised by the state-owned Sadharan Bima Corporation, where incidents occurring after July 15, 2024, were broadly categorised as ‘Popular Rising’, paving the way for denying insurance and reinsurance claims.

Following sustained engagement by the BTMA and a series of consultations, IDRA convened a high-level stakeholders’ meeting at its headquarters with representatives from BTMA, Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association, Sadharan Bima Corporation, and several insurance companies.

In the meeting, BTMA president Showkat Aziz Russell emphasised the adverse economic and employment consequences of unresolved insurance claims.

IDRA took two key decisions following the meeting, including instructing the Sadharan Bima Corporation to withdraw its March 3 meeting decision and directing all non-life insurance companies not to treat all claims as ‘Popular Rising’ cases.

Moreover, the IDRA also directed all insurers to appoint surveyors in accordance with insurance laws and regulations and proceed with claim settlements based on survey reports.

In a statement, BTMA said the decisions would significantly facilitate faster settlement and compensation of insurance claims for member mills of BTMA, BGMEA, and BKMEA, as well as other affected industrial units damaged during the July–August 2024 mass uprising.

title: NEIR crucial to curb illegal phones, recover Tk 6,000cr tax loss: MIOB
body:
Mobile Phone Industry Owners Association Bangladesh urged strict implementation of NEIR to curb the sale of illegal handset, protect consumers, and prevent Tk 6,000 crore in revenue losses from the grey market.

‘The grey market deprives the state of Tk5,000–6,000 crore in tax revenue annually, and NEIR is the best tool to curb this leakage,’ said Ziauddin Chowdhury, executive member of MIOB and country manager of Xiaomi Bangladesh while presenting a keynote address at a press conference in InterContinental Dhaka.

MIOB organised the press conference on Tuesday under the theme ‘Towards a Safer Bangladesh through NEIR.’

MIOB executive member and managing director of Smart Technologies, Mohammad Zahirul Islam, moderated the press conference.

According to MIOB, NEIR will help detect illegal or cloned IMEI handsets, curb phone-related crimes, and boost consumer confidence.

They welcomed the January 1 rollout of NEIR alongside reduced import duties, calling it a timely step to promote fair competition and legal imports.

They further said NEIR would increase government revenue and strengthen the digital economy.

MIOB said combining both local and foreign capital, more than BDT 3,000 crore has been invested in 18 smartphone manufacturing facilities in Bangladesh.

The sector directly employs around 50,000 skilled workers and supports another 50,000 people through dealers, DSRs, service centres, and retail operations.

Around 30 per cent of the workforce is women, the association said.

Ziauddin Chowdhury said that nearly 20 per cent of smartphones entering the country come through informal channels.

He said that the grey market has had a particularly damaging impact on officially imported and locally manufactured smartphones, especially those priced above the Tk30000 segment remain unsold.

Responding to claims by protesting traders that NEIR would shut down 20,000 shops and threaten the livelihoods of two million families, Chowdhury dismissed the figures as misleading and exaggerated.

Citing a study conducted by Insight Metrics, he said Bangladesh has around 13,000 smartphone retail points nationwide.

‘About 90 per cent of these outlets already sell official products. Only around 1,000 to 1,500 shops deal exclusively in used or unofficial phones,’ he said. ‘The narrative of mass unemployment is being deliberately created to gain public sympathy and resist regulation.’

However, Chowdhury urged to review of the recently introduced 43 per cent smartphone tax, arguing that rational taxation alongside NEIR would boost the formal market and increase government revenue.

MIOB president Jakaria Shahid called NEIR a positive step for discipline and fair competition in the mobile industry.

He commended the government’s initiative while strongly condemning the vandalism at the BTRC office.

With consistent policies, he believes the industry can greatly contribute to the national economy.

Zahirul Islam said, ‘We want people to buy mobile phones at lower prices and are working to manufacture them locally. We believe NEIR’s initiative will strengthen our digital economy and boost state revenue.’

Earlier on January 1, Mobile phone handset traders under the banner of Mobile Business Community Bangladesh allegedly attacked the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission Bhaban (headquarters building) at Agargaon in the capital, following the launch of NEIR.

title: Govt to import essentials ahead of Ramadan
body:
A meeting of the advisory council committee on government purchase on Tuesday approved a number of proposals to procure essentials food items ahead of the holy month of Ramadan.

Presided over by finance adviser Salehuddin Ahmed the meeting at secretariat approved purchase of 10,000 tonnes of lentil through the local tender at a cost of around Tk 71.87 crore with each kilogram of lentil costing Tk 71.87.

Payel Automatic Food Processing Mills of Chattogram won the tender called by Trading Corporation of Bangladesh under the ministry of commerce.

Another proposal from same TCB--- procurement of 1,35,75,000 litres of soybean oil under the international direct procurement method at a cost of Tk 178.47 crore—was also approved.

Prime Corp World Company Limited will supply per litre soya bean oil at Tk 131.47 after importing those from Thailand.

The finance adviser said the import of edible oils would strengthen the stock of the item ahead of Ramadan, the fasting month in the Muslim majority country.

On December 7, the Bangladesh Vegetable Oil Refiners and Vanaspati Manufacturers Association, the trade body of edible oil traders, announced new prices for edible oils after a meeting with the commerce ministry, hiking soya bean oil prices by up to Tk 6 a litre.

The price of bottled soya bean rose to Tk 195 a litre from that of Tk 189 a litre and the unpackaged soya bean oil was set at Tk 176 a litre from Tk 172 a litre and the unpackaged palm oil at Tk 166 a litre from Tk 150 a litre.

The price hike of edible oils kept the inflation at elevated level of more than 8 per cent in December, according to the monthly inflation update released by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistic on Monday.

Responding to a query on rising inflation for two months in a row until December, the day’s procurements are linked to efforts to streamline supply of essentials.

The committee also approved import of 40,000 tonnes oif urea from Saudi Arabia with per tonne costing $390.

Earlier, a meeting of the advisory council committee on econiomic affairs presided also by the finance adviser at the same venue approved a proposal in principle for procuring the vaccines being used in the Expanded Programme on Immunization  for the current financial year of FY26 through direct procurement method.

The procurement will be conducted under the project titled ‘Loan 4078 (COL)/4079-BAN: Responsive COVID-19 Vaccines for Recovery Project under the Asia Pacific Vaccines Access Facility (APVAX).’

title: Low-income workers suffer as biting cold hits Jhenaidah
body:
A spell of cold weather has disrupted normal life in Jhenaidah as a cold wave continues to sweep over the northern and northwestern districts of the country, pushing working and labouring people into acute hardship.

For the last one week, the intensity of cold has sharply increased in the district, leaving daily life almost paralysed. The working and labouring communities have been the worst sufferers, with many struggling to manage their families due to the scarcity of work.

According to the Jashore and Chuadanga Regional Meteorological Office, temperatures have dropped across Chuadanga, Jashore, Meherpur, Jhenaidah, Kushtia and Magura districts since the middle of last week. A moderate cold wave is currently sweeping over Jashore and Chuadanga.

Day temperatures have fallen in Maheshpur, Harinakundu, Kotchandpur, Kaliganj and Sadar upazilas of Jhenaidah, while night temperatures have been hovering between 12 and 14 degrees Celsius almost every day. The cold has intensified further with the onset of chilly northern winds blowing across the district.

The prolonged cold spell has severely affected low-income labourers, including van and rickshaw pullers, agricultural workers and brick kiln labourers, who are finding it increasingly difficult to secure work.

Many are unable to work due to the biting cold, while opportunities for temporary and migrant labourers have declined alarmingly, forcing many to remain unemployed at home.

At the Post Office intersection area of Jhenaidah town, day labourer Samad Hossain of Rajapur village was seen waiting for work. He said he comes to the town in search of work, as employers usually pick up labourers from the spot.

‘But because of the cold, no one is coming to hire workers. Even those who comes take labourers at lower wages, as there are more workers than jobs,’ he added.

Another day labourer, Daud Ali, said that their livelihood depended entirely on physical strength. ‘As long as our bodies support us, our families survive. The cold has become so intense that even standing is painful. Still, we come and wait for work, but opportunities have decreased due to the cold,’ he said.

Anwar Hossain, a resident of the Pagla Kanai area of the town, told BSS that city residents often hired temporary labourers for household work. ‘The cold has increased and labourers are harder to find. At the same time, there is no sunshine throughout the day, which makes it difficult for us to carry out household work even if we want to. Both residents and labourers are suffering,’ he said.

As the cold intensifies, the distribution of warm clothes has begun across the district, including the district town, upazila towns, large markets and villages.

Sources said that warm clothes were being distributed among the homeless, destitute and labouring people through personal initiatives, social and voluntary organizations, as well as administrative efforts.

title: Govt approves fuel oil import from India
body:
The advisory committee on government purchase at a meeting on Tuesday approved a proposal to purchase fuel oils at a cost of Tk 1,462 crore from India amid tensions between Dhaka and New Delhi over a series of incidents.

The latest was Dhaka’s decision to shut down the broadcasting of the Indian Premier League after Bangladesh pace bowler Mustafizur Rahman, also known as Fizz, was released by IPL franchise Kolkata Knight Riders, following directives by the Indian Cricket Board.

Dhaka has also asked India to sift Bangladesh matches in the forthcoming  T20 World Cup to Sri Lanka from India on ground of security of national cricketers.

Finance adviser Salehuddin Ahmed, who presided over the meeting of the advisory committee on government purchase, called the rows over Mustafizur disappointing.

The release of the pace bowler all of a sudden was unfortunate, he said, adding that the fallout of the incident was also unexpected.

There have been diplomatic rows between Bangladesh and India since New Delhi gave shelter to deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina who fled there amid a mass uprising on August 5, 2024.

Salehuddin, however, said that the Mustafizur issue had not put any impact on the procurement of goods from India under the government purchase.

At Tuesday’s meeting, a Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation proposal to import 1.8 lakh tonnes of refined diesel from India’s Numaligarh Refinery Limited for the January-December period at a cost of Tk 1,462 crore was approved.

The import price of a litre of diesel from Numaligarh Refinery in Assam has been estimated at Tk 88 while the average price of a litre of diesel on the international market recently was about $1.24, equivalent to Tk 175.

Responding to questions from reporters about diesel imports from India amid the tensions, energy adviser Muhammad Fouzul Kabir Khan said that the diesel import was being carried out under an agreement signed previously.

‘This is a 15-year contract signed long ago,’ he said, adding that the latest import was part of the contract.

The day’s meeting also approved three more proposals on imports of fuel oils with the overall amount standing at 30.6 lakh tonnes at an estimate cost of Tk 24,150.84 crore.

The imports are to meet the country’s fuel oil demand until June.

The BPC will import 15 lakh tonnes of crude oil from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia for state-run Eastern Refinery Limited at a cost Tk 11,863 crore.

It will import 13.80 lakh tonnes of refined fuel oils from seven companies from six countries under government-to-government arrangements at an estimated cost of Tk 10,826 crore.

The six countries are India, China, Malaysia, the UAE, Thailand and Indonesia.

title: Chinese brands lead EV sales in Germany
body:
Electric vehicle sales rebounded strongly in Germany in 2025, official data showed Tuesday, with Chinese manufacturers making inroads from a low base in the EU’s largest economy despite tariffs.

EV sales rose 43.2 per cent last year to 545,142 in total, the KBA federal transport authority said, representing 19.1 per cent of all new cars sold.

Chinese EV giant BYD -- which last year overtook Elon Musk’s Tesla to become the world’s largest electric carmaker -- saw its German sales rise over 700 per cent to more than 23,000 cars, giving it 0.8 per cent of the overall auto market.

‘International vehicle manufacturers with affordable battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids have contributed disproportionately to growth in these segments,’ said Imelda Labbe, head of the VDIK foreign carmakers’ lobby in Germany.

The European Union in 2024 introduced higher tariffs on Chinese-made electric cars, alleging that they benefitted from unfair subsidies.

That has not stopped sales of Chinese cars rising across the bloc, with the country’s carmakers keen to crack foreign markets amid cut-throat competition at home.

Rising EV sales are also some rare good news for Germany’s beleaguered carmakers, which have invested heavily in the technology in recent years, and are seeking to comply with European Union environmental rules.

Though the European Commission in December proposed scrapping a planned 2035 ban on new combustion-engine vehicles, carmakers would still have to cut emissions by 90 per cent from 2021 levels under its latest plan, and need to see dramatic sales growth.

The rise in EV sales last year comes after a fall of almost 30 percent in 2024 following the withdrawal of government subsidies, and Germany’s electric car market is still smaller than optimists had hoped for.

‘We haven’t seen a real boom yet,’ EY analyst Constantin Gall said.

‘The hoped-for surge in e-mobility in Germany is proving to be much more protracted and difficult than expected.’

After the decline in the market in 2024, the government said in December it would introduce subsidies again.

Some motorists will be able to benefit from 5,000 euros ($5,855) for the purchase of new EVs or hybrids so long as their components are largely made in Germany.

But industry figures say that better charging infrastructure and cheaper power would be needed to really boost EVs and warned that the planned subsidy would have limited impact.

‘The state subsidies will only be available to households on low and middle incomes,” Gall said. “But it is high-earners who tend to buy new electric cars.’

Weak sales at home have compounded the challenges facing Germany’s car industry.

It was already contending with the costs of investing in EVs and cratering sales in key market China even before US President Donald Trump last year slapped tariffs on cars and auto parts.

Volkswagen, Europe’s largest carmaker, is in the process of cutting 35,000 jobs in Germany by 2030 under a deal reached with unions in a bid to slash costs.

Overall car sales in Germany rose just 1.4 per cent last year to about 2.9 million vehicles, the KBA said -- roughly 750,000 fewer than were sold in 2019 before the Covid pandemic and Germany’s economy sank into stagnation.

‘The weak economy, increasing job insecurity and the multitude of political, social and economic crises are taking their toll,’ Gall said.

title: Oil prices gain, as equities extend record run higher
body:
Oil prices gained slightly and stock markets hit new heights Tuesday as investors tracked developments surrounding crude-rich Venezuela as well as the outlook for the global economy.

The United Nations voiced deep concern over the dramatic US operation in Venezuela, warning that it clearly ‘undermined a fundamental principle of international law’.

‘States must not threaten or use force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state,’ Ravina Shamdasani, spokeswoman for the UN rights office, told reporters in Geneva.

Oil prices have experienced choppy trading since the surprise US raid Saturday on Caracas that saw Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife taken to New York.

They pleaded not guilty to drug trafficking and other charges while appearing at a court in the city on Monday. A judge ordered them to remain behind bars until the next hearing due March 17.

While Venezuela sits on about a fifth of the world’s oil reserves, observers pointed out that a quick ramp-up of output would be hamstrung by several issues including its creaking infrastructure, low prices and political uncertainty.

‘With the country pumping less than one per cent of the world’s oil after years of underinvestment, any major near-term disruption looks more bark than bite,’ Matt Britzman, senior equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, noted Tuesday.

Brushing off geopolitical concerns, some major stock markets have begun the new year with new all-time highs, having smashed records in 2025.

Seoul rose more than one per cent Tuesday to top 4,500 points for the first time, helped by another strong rally in chip giant SK hynix.

That mood was reflected on Wall Street, where the Dow ended at a record high Monday, boosted by a rally to share prices of technology titans Amazon and Meta.

London’s benchmark FTSE 100 index reached a new high Tuesday above 10,000 points, with investors expecting more cuts to British interest rates in 2026.

‘Global equities are likely to keep looking through the geopolitical shock unless it threatens the broader supply chain or tightens financial conditions, because geopolitics has become a persistent feature rather than a surprise,’ said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets.

‘Equities can continue grinding higher if earnings expectations, liquidity, and rate expectations remain supportive, especially in tech,’ she added.

Traders are awaiting key US jobs data due Friday for fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates.

The Federal Reserve is expected to keep cutting American borrowing costs this year, but how many times remains unclear.

title: OECD finalises deal on global minimum tax with US carveout
body:
The United States, along with more than 100 countries, has finalised an agreement exempting American firms from certain foreign taxes — an update that follows Washington’s push for exclusions from a global minimum tax.

Countries had struck a deal in 2021 to tax multinational companies, in an agreement negotiated under the auspices of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

The deal contains two ‘pillars,’ the second of which sets a minimum global tax rate of 15 per cent.

But US President Donald Trump has pushed back on the global tax agreement, saying the proposed pact would have no force or effect for the United States.

On Monday, the US Treasury Department said that it had worked to ‘reach agreement with the more than 145 countries in the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework to have US-headquartered companies remain subject to only US global minimum taxes while exempting them from Pillar Two.’

‘This side-by-side agreement recognizes the tax sovereignty of the United States over the worldwide operations of US companies and the tax sovereignty of other countries over business activity within their own borders,’ the Treasury added.

The update came after the Group of Seven nations agreed in June to exempt US multinational companies from a global minimum tax imposed by other countries.

At the time, treasury secretary Scott Bessent said he had asked Congress to remove a provision from a draft of Trump’s ‘One, Big, Beautiful Bill’ that had been dubbed a ‘revenge tax,’ following progress on this agreement among the G7.

The provision would have allowed the government to impose levies on firms with foreign owners, and on investors from countries deemed to impose unfair taxes on US businesses.

title: JnUCSU polls vote counting suspended over technical glitches
body:
Vote counting in the first-ever Jagannath University Central Students’ Union elections was suspended on Tuesday night due to technical glitches.

According to officials, voter turnout in the JnUCSU elections was recorded at 65.33%, with hall union elections seeing an even higher participation rate of around 77%.

The voting process, which began at 9:00 am, was met with enthusiastic participation from students, eager to take part in the historic elections. However, as the counting process began at 7:45pm using optical mark recognition (OMR) machines, technical glitches quickly emerged.

At 8:45 pm, the university administration announced the suspension of vote counting due to these technical difficulties. In a statement, authorities clarified that discussions with stakeholders were ongoing and that a new time for restarting the counting process would be communicated later.

The university authorities were holding a meeting with the VP and GS candidates from different panels to discuss how they should proceed with the counting as OMR machines were initially malfunctioning till 11:00pm.

Chhatra Dal candidates were pressing for counting votes manually while Shibir candidates wanted the votes to be counted through the OMR machines.

title: BB allows electronic submission of export documents
body:
Bangladesh Bank has allowed the electronic presentation and processing of export documents under documentary collection arrangements, aiming to align export procedures with ongoing digitalization initiatives.

In a circular issued to authorised dealer (AD) banks on Tuesday, the central bank said exporters’ documents under both Documents against Payment (DP) and Documents against Acceptance (DA) modes may now be handled through secure bank-to-bank electronic channels.

The move follows the Uniform Rules for Collections (URC 522) and its Supplement for Electronic Presentation (eURC), subject to strict compliance with the prescribed conditions.

Under the new framework, electronic processing will be permitted only where there is prior mutual agreement between local AD banks and their overseas collecting or presenting banks.

The parties must also agree on document formats and the designated place of presentation.

Export sales contracts will need to clearly state that documentary collections will be handled electronically in line with eURC standards.

The circular outlines different treatment based on local legal recognition of Electronic Transferable Records (ETRs).

Where ETRs are permitted, all export documents, including title documents, may be presented electronically while preserving their legal validity and transferability.

Where ETRs are not recognised, banks may submit most documents electronically, but title or transferable documents such as bills of lading and bills of exchange must be sent physically. In some cases, authenticated electronic copies may also be provided alongside physical documents.

Bangladesh Bank has also allowed digital endorsement of title documents using recognised electronic platforms, digital signatures, Digitally Signed Endorsement Certificates, or SWIFT-based messages, provided audit trails and legal enforceability are maintained.

AD banks have been instructed to ensure secure transmission, maintain complete audit trails, store electronic records as required by law, and verify digital signatures.

title: Bumper harvest, plunging prices put Chandpur’s potato market in crisis
body:
Rows of unsold potato sacks in Chandpur’s cold storages reflect a season of deepening losses, turning what was once a lucrative crop into a source of financial despair for thousands of farmers.

In local markets, old potatoes are fetching as little as Tk 7-8 per kilogram, well below production and storage costs, leaving farmers with little incentive to withdraw their stored produce, locals said.

Outstanding dues for seed potatoes purchased on credit last season remain unpaid, while storage fees continue to accumulate, they said.

Agriculture officials said the district’s 56,860 potato farmers are concentrated mainly in Chandpur Sadar, Matlab South, and Kachua upazilas, where some 5,000 hectares are under potato cultivation.

Despite the market downturn, they said, planting continues, though many farmers have scaled back their operations in response to last season’s losses.

‘The absence of syndicates this season has kept potato prices low,’ said Mobarak Hossain, officer at the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE).

‘Last season, syndicates pushed prices up to Tk 80 per kilogram. That situation does not exist this year,’ he said.

The ripple effect is felt throughout the supply chain. Cold storage operators in Kachua upazila are struggling as farmers hesitate to withdraw their produce.

Mangal Khan and Yasin Mia, managers of local facilities, said that with market prices so low, even selling the stored potatoes fails to cover storage costs.

A bumper harvest last season exacerbated the problem. Good-quality old potatoes now sell for Tk 8-10 per kg, while new potatoes are priced around Tk 20 per kg. Farmers who invested heavily are counting losses.

‘I produced 100 maunds of potatoes and made no profit at all-everything turned into a loss,’ said Bachchu Miji, a grower and trader at Bakila Bazar in Hajiganj upazila. Others, including farmers from Shah Mahmudpur in Chandpur Sadar, echoed his frustration.

Hanif Patwary, whose 33 sacks of potatoes stored at Baborhat BSCIC cold storage sold for just Tk 3,000 per 50 kg sack, said, ‘After suffering such losses, I will not cultivate potatoes again.’

The situation is mirrored in Kachua upazila, where more than half of stored potatoes remain in cold storage past the usual withdrawal period of November-December, frustrating both farmers and storage operators.
